From Numbers to Systems
Section 1 of 1

From Numbers to Systems (Draft version 2026-11-08)

How Mathematics Was Always an Algebraic Machine

Luke Hanley

Introduction

9 min read

Every year, mathematics education introduces rules that later become wrong. A child cannot subtract a larger number from a smaller one. Years pass, the child learns about negative numbers, and the rule is retracted. You cannot divide evenly by all numbers. The rule becomes fractions. Multiplication is repeated addition, except for irrational numbers and matrices and complex numbers, where it means something else entirely. At each transition, students must accomplish two things simultaneously: they must learn the new rule, and they must carefully set aside the intuitions they developed using the old one.

The students who succeed are those who can tolerate this pattern. They learn to treat each level of mathematics as a separate system, unrelated to what came before, complete unto itself until the next transition makes it obsolete. That requires a peculiar kind of resilience. It also requires forgetting. The students who struggle are often those who trusted the model they were given and built strong intuitions from it, only to discover that the model was a provisional approximation, not the thing itself.

This is not a teaching failure. It is a consequence of the underlying representation. A number-line model, where numbers are points and operations are procedures applied to those points, has no clean way to introduce fractions, negative numbers, or complex numbers without reaching points where the prior model breaks. The representation cannot accommodate them. So new representations are introduced, each replacing the last, each requiring students to rebuild their intuitions from the ground up.

The book you are reading is about a different representation entirely. It is not a variant of the number-line model. It is a different foundation for mathematics, one that eliminates those discontinuities and makes arithmetic not harder but simpler.

What Is Wrong with How Mathematics Is Taught

Something is wrong with mathematics education, and the people who teach it often sense it even if they cannot name it precisely.

Not wrong in the way that individual topics are explained poorly. Wrong in the way that the subject acquires discontinuities that seem unnecessary. A kindergartener can understand counting. A middle schooler understands that you can subtract past zero. A high schooler learns that you can take the square root of a negative number. Each of these represents progress. But the progress feels like replacement rather than extension. The old rule was not incomplete; it was wrong. It must be discarded.

Mathematics educators are often told this is simply the natural progression from concrete to abstract. Kindergarteners need simple rules. Older students need sophisticated mathematics. So the rules change as students advance. That explanation has the shape of wisdom, but it does not survive scrutiny. The rules that are discarded are not simple approximations to complex truths. They are genuine contradictions. The claim that you cannot subtract a larger number from a smaller one is not a simplified version of the claim that you can. It is the opposite claim.

The structural problem runs deeper than pedagogy. It affects the content itself. Because the number-line model cannot accommodate negation, fractions, or complex numbers without special mechanisms, these get added as special cases. Negation becomes a separate number type. Fractions become a different operation with their own rules. Complex numbers become an invented extension. Each is a patch that makes the system work but obscures the underlying structure.

The result is that students do not experience mathematics as a coherent body of knowledge. They experience it as a series of unrelated systems, each replacing the previous one, each with its own rules and intuitions. The students who naturally enjoy following rules and fitting into systems often do well. The students who want to understand the underlying reason why the rules work often become frustrated. They sense that something should be simpler, more connected, more inevitable. That intuition is correct.

The Central Claim

The argument of this book is that that intuition points toward something real. Mathematics is not a series of disconnected systems. The discontinuities are artifacts of the representation. They are not necessary. They do not exist in a different model, one where the algebraic system comes first and numbers are understood as states inside that system.

That model is not a mere reinterpretation of existing mathematics. It is the underlying structure that existing mathematics has always been approximating. The factorial algebraic system is what every mathematical operation was always building toward. The conventional number-line model is a useful projection of that structure onto a line, but a projection nonetheless. It discards dimensions, elides properties, and replaces structural facts with procedural rules.

When the full system is visible, none of the discontinuities occur. The factorial odometer that a kindergartener uses to count is the same structure that a doctoral student uses when working with infinite series. The orientation relationship that handles negation in third grade handles complex conjugates in graduate mathematics. The scope-proportion relationship that handles fractions in fourth grade handles p-adic numbers in advanced number theory. No rule learned at any level is ever abandoned. Intuition compounds. Knowledge accumulates.

The argument is that the difficulty students experience with mathematics is not necessary difficulty. It is the difficulty produced by the wrong representation, and it can be substantially reduced by making the right one visible.

How This Book Is Built

The book proceeds through six parts, each addressing a distinct piece of the argument.

The first part establishes the foundation. Before any number appears, before any operation is named, the book builds the algebraic system itself. What structure must exist before a number can mean anything? What is a dimension? How does the system generate one distinguishable state after another, each preserving all prior structure? This part answers those questions by building the factorial odometer step by step.

The second part introduces the formal structure. Once the odometer exists, the book brings in variables, values, relationships, and constants. A single variable named x becomes the simplest possible algebraic system. A second variable with a relationship between them extends it. The constant e, defined by an infinite series, shows that mathematical constants are not magic numbers but variables with specific relationships assigned to their values.

The third part makes the central inversion visible. All arithmetic operations are relationship state machines. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation, fractions, and complex numbers are all the same kind of thing. They are not different number types. They are different relationships. This part walks through each one and shows how they fit into the system without exception or special case.

The fourth part examines the deep structure that makes operations tractable. Factorial boundaries are complete knowledge states. Residues are not computed separately but carried in the representation from the moment a number is generated. Primes are not fundamental atoms but structural absences. This part shows why the factorial basis works and what becomes visible when you can see into the structure directly.

The fifth part addresses calculus. Calculus is not about infinitely small numbers. It is about boundaries. The derivative measures proximity to a boundary. The integral measures accumulated occupancy. When this is understood clearly, calculus becomes a natural extension of the arithmetic that came before, not a separate system requiring a new vocabulary and conceptual framework.

The sixth part explores implications. The algebraic system does not need to be translated into computation. It is computation. When you apply this to education, the curriculum discontinuities vanish. Students build intuitions that never need revision. Knowledge compounds rather than requiring replacement.

What This Book Assumes About You

This book does not assume you remember algebra or calculus. It does not assume you were good at mathematics or that you struggled with it. Both experiences are equally relevant. The students who struggled may have been struggling exactly because they trusted the model they were given. The students who succeeded may have been succeeding despite the model, not because of it.

What the book does assume is that you are open to the possibility that mathematics might be different from what you were taught, and that the difference might make it simpler rather than more complex. The book also assumes you can follow a sustained argument through multiple chapters if the chapters are clear and short and each one earns its place in a running argument.

If you have read From Numbers to Systems, this book will feel immediately familiar in structure and approach. Both are built on the same foundation. Both argue that the domain was built on a structure that served for a time but eventually creates friction. Both show that a different structure eliminates that friction. Mathematics and computing were always built on the same machine. This book and Fixing Fragile Software explain that machine from different starting points.

How to Use This Book

Read this book in sequence. Each chapter builds directly on what came before. Skipping ahead or reading chapters out of order will create the same experience you have had with mathematics education: encountering new terminology without the foundation that makes it clear.

Each chapter is short enough to finish in one sitting. Read one chapter, then put the book down. Let the concept settle before moving forward. If a chapter does not make sense on first reading, reread it. The issue is likely not that you are missing something about mathematics. The issue is likely that the explanation needs to land more clearly, and a second reading often does that work.

Pay particular attention to the examples. The book carries a running example throughout the opening chapters. A single variable x becomes the simplest algebraic system. Later, a second variable y is added, and a relationship between them is defined. That running example is not decoration. It is the argument made concrete. When abstract concepts appear, the running example shows what they mean in practice within two paragraphs. Follow the example carefully. It is doing the explanatory work.

You will encounter diagrams and sketches of the factorial odometer. Study them. The visual carries information that prose cannot convey as efficiently. Looking at the structure of the odometer illuminates what is happening in ways that words alone cannot achieve.

The appendices at the end contain formal definitions for readers who want precision after understanding has been established. Do not read the appendices first. The appendices are for readers who have finished the main argument and want to see the formal specification. Read the main book first. The appendices will be clearer and more useful once you have built intuition about what the system is doing.

One final note: this book is not a reference. It is a sustained argument. Each page assumes you remember what the previous pages established. If you set the book aside and return to it weeks later, you may need to reread the last few chapters you covered. That is not a flaw in how the book is written. It is a consequence of arguments that move forward sequentially rather than standing independently.

Now begin. What follows will ask you to reconsider what numbers are and how they work. The reconsideration will be worth your time.

Part 1

Starting from Nothing

Chapter 1Why Numbers Feel Like They Come First (They Don't)

8 min read

At some point, every child asks where numbers come from. The question usually happens when a child is learning to count. One, two, three, four. At some point the child stops and asks: “But where does one come from? Why do we start there?”

The answer given is a redirection. We start at one because that is where counting starts. We move to two because two comes after one. The numbers are an ordering, and the ordering is natural. This answer does not actually resolve the question. It simply moves past it. The child is left with the impression that numbers are something that simply exist, that the ordering is intrinsic, that asking why is less important than moving ahead.

This exchange contains an assumption that structures all of mathematics education. The assumption is never stated explicitly. It is simply inherited. The assumption is that numbers are primitive. They come first. Everything else follows from them. Operations are things you do to numbers. Relationships are connections between numbers. Structure emerges from the interactions of numbers themselves.

That assumption is wrong. It is not a simplification. It is not a useful approximation for young students. It is simply wrong. And the wrongness creates all the problems that follow.

What the Assumption Hides

Start by observing what every number actually is.

Take the number seven. It is written as a symbol. It appears on a number line. It has properties: it is odd, it is prime, it is less than ten. We treat seven as if it is a simple, irreducible thing. One of the atoms that makes up arithmetic.

But seven carries structure that the assumption never shows. Seven is the state you reach after the first dimension of the counting system is full and the second dimension begins. Seven can be divided by one and by seven but by nothing else. Seven has a specific relationship to every other number. When you add seven to something, there are patterns in the result that depend on what the something is. When you multiply seven by something, other patterns appear.

That structure is not derived from the fact of the number seven. The number seven is read off from that structure. Seven is what you get when the structure advances through its progression. But conventional mathematics never shows you the structure. It shows you the number and asks you to treat it as a starting point.

Here is a more concrete example of what is hidden. Consider the number twenty-four. We can divide it by one, two, three, four, six, eight, twelve, and twenty-four. We cannot divide it evenly by five, seven, nine, or many other numbers. Where do those divisibilities come from? Where do those impossibilities come from?

The conventional answer is that twenty-four happens to have those properties. We factorize it, discovering that twenty-four is two cubed times three. From that factorization we can derive the divisibilities. But this treats the divisibilities as something we discover after the fact, not something that is already contained in what the number is.

In the structure beneath the number line, the divisibilities are not discovered. They are visible immediately. The number twenty-four occupies a position in a structure where what can divide it is already determined by that position. The divisibilities are not properties the number has. They are relationships the structure carries.

The Assumption Creates Gaps

The assumption that numbers are primitive creates a problem that echoes through mathematics education. If numbers are the starting point, what do you do when you encounter something that does not fit the number-line model?

You invent something new. You invent negative numbers to handle the fact that you can subtract a larger number from a smaller one. You invent fractions to handle the fact that division does not always come out to a whole number. You invent complex numbers to handle the fact that you cannot take the square root of a negative number in the traditional sense. You invent limits and infinitesimals to handle the behavior of functions near boundaries.

Each of these inventions is presented as if it extends the system of numbers to a new realm. Negative numbers are numbers on the other side of zero. Fractions are ratios of numbers. Complex numbers are numbers in two dimensions. Each is treated as an addition, an expansion of what a number can be.

But this framing creates a structural gap. If numbers are the primitive, then these extensions should not exist. They should be impossible by definition. Yet they clearly need to exist for mathematics to work. The solution is to add them as special cases, as exceptions to the rule that numbers are simple, indivisible primitives. Each exception requires new definitions, new rules, new ways of thinking.

This is what creates the curriculum discontinuities. The rule that you cannot subtract a larger number from a smaller one is not a simplified version of the rule that you can. It is an obstacle that must be overcome when the model is extended. The discovery that multiplication means something different when you multiply by an irrational number is not a refinement of the concept. It is a contradiction that must be managed.

The source of these contradictions is not the mathematics. The source is the wrong assumption about where mathematics begins.

What Is Actually Primitive

The problem is not that numbers exist. The problem is that we start there.

What is actually primitive is not the number. What is actually primitive is the structure that generates numbers. What is actually primitive is the system within which numbers exist, the system that determines which divisions are possible, which relationships are valid, what properties each number carries.

When you start with structure instead of numbers, everything that caused problems becomes inevitable. Negative numbers are not an invention. They are what you get when you introduce orientation into a system. You can point in two directions. If you have left and right, forward and backward, you need language to describe both directions. Negation is not a number type. It is a relationship direction.

Fractions are not an invention either. They are what happens when you constrain one variable as a proportion of another within a scope. You do not invent fractions. You define a relationship and fractions emerge from the relationship’s structure.

Complex numbers follow the same logic. They are not an invented extension. They are the natural result of adding a second dimension to the values a variable can take.

The question that the child asked at the beginning of their mathematics education, “where do numbers come from,” has an answer. Numbers come from the structure. The structure comes first. Numbers are states within that structure. The structure generates them one at a time, each preserving what came before, each carrying forward the relationships that earlier states established.

The Structure You Have Always Known

Here is what makes all of this particularly interesting. You already understand this structure. You have understood it your whole life. You use it every day without realizing you are doing it.

When you count, you are advancing through the structure. When you add two numbers, you are combining states within the structure. When you notice that some numbers divide evenly by two and others do not, you are reading a property that the structure carries. When you multiply, you are combining dimensions within the structure.

The conventional mathematics education teaches you all of these things. But it teaches them while directing your attention toward the numbers, not toward the structure. It is as if you were taught to drive by focusing on how fast the car goes rather than on the road you are traveling on. You could potentially reach your destination. But you would have no idea how you got there or why any particular turn made sense.

The remainder of this book is about shifting your attention. Not from numbers to something entirely different. Simply from numbers to the structure that numbers are part of. You will recognize almost everything in this book. You have done all these operations your whole life. What will be new is seeing the structure that makes the operations meaningful, and realizing that the structure is simpler, more unified, and more inevitable than the number-line model suggests.

What Comes Next

This chapter has established a single question: if numbers are not primitive, what is?

The answer is the factorial algebraic system. It is a structure that generates states one at a time, each preserving prior structure, each carrying forward the relationships that made earlier states possible. Numbers are names for those states. Operations are the relationships that determine how those states transition. Properties like divisibility are not computed from numbers. They are carried in the structure from the moment a state is generated.

The next chapter builds that structure from the beginning. It starts with nothing and asks the simplest possible question: what is a single distinguishable state? From that question, the structure grows. The factorial odometer advances. Numbers emerge, not as atoms but as the states the odometer reaches.

That is where the real mathematics begins.

Chapter 2The Machine That Generates Counting

12 min read

The previous chapter established that numbers do not come first. The structure comes first. Numbers are states within that structure. This chapter builds that structure. It begins with nothing and asks how one distinguishable state emerges from nothing. Then it asks how additional states follow. The answer is the factorial odometer, a state machine that generates counting.

Starting with Nothing

Imagine a structure that contains no states at all. There is nothing. No number, no dimension, no possibility of distinction. This is the starting point.

Now ask the simplest possible question: how does this structure produce a single distinguishable state?

The answer requires creating one position where something can be different from nothing. Call that position the first digit. In that position, you can be in one of two conditions: either you have not occupied that position yet, or you have. Call the first condition zero and the second condition one.

That is all. A single position, two conditions. The state where you have not yet occupied the position is the absence state. The state where you have occupied the position is the presence state. This distinction is the origin of counting. The absence state is what we call zero. The presence state is what we call one.

But zero in this system is not a number sitting on a number line. Zero is the state before any position has been occupied. It is an absence, not an entity. Zero is what exists when nothing has changed, when no state machine has been activated, when the system remains in its default configuration.

In conventional mathematics, zero is treated as a number like any other. It sits on the number line next to one and two. But in the structure of the algebraic system, zero is not stored. Zero is what you get when you have not yet moved anything. It is the inferred state.

The First Position Fills

Once you have created a position and it has two possible conditions, the next question is what happens when that position fills. When the presence condition is fully realized, when the first position has been occupied completely, what comes next?

The answer is that you need a second position. The first position has only two conditions, occupied or not occupied. It cannot represent three distinct states by itself. So a second position is created. The first position continues to track whether it has been occupied. The second position tracks whether the two-state configuration of the first position has been fully explored.

This is how the system advances. Each position has a maximum value it can reach. The first position can take values zero or one. When the first position reaches its maximum, the second position advances, and the first position returns to its minimum. This is exactly how an odometer works. When the rightmost digit fills up, the next digit advances and the rightmost returns to zero.

But in this structure, the maximum value of each position is not arbitrary. The first position has a maximum value of one. The second position has a maximum value of two. This is the factorial structure. Position n can have values from zero to n.

This is the key insight. The structure does not assign arbitrary limits to each position. The limit to each position is determined by how many distinct states that position must represent. The first position must represent two states, so it can hold zero or one. The second position must represent three states (the three distinct configurations of positions one and two combined), so it can hold zero, one, or two. The third position must represent four states, so it can hold zero, one, two, or three.

This is why it is called the factorial odometer. The value of position n is bounded by n. The number represented by this structure is the sum of d_i times i factorial, where d_i is the digit at position i.

Counting as State Generation

Now observe what happens as this structure advances.

Start at the state where no position has been occupied. This is zero, the absence state. The odometer has not moved. Now advance the odometer by one. The first position moves from zero to one. This state represents the number one. Advance again. The first position has reached its maximum value of one, so it returns to zero and the second position advances to one. This state represents the number two. Continue advancing. First position moves back to one. This is state three. Continue again. First position reaches its maximum and resets. Second position advances to two. This is state four.

Counting is not adding one repeatedly. Counting is the odometer advancing through its configurations. Each configuration is a distinct state. The odometer generates these states in sequence. Numbers are simply names for those states.

Notice what each advance does. It never changes a digit in an arbitrary way. When a position advances, it moves by exactly one. When a position reaches its maximum, it returns to zero and the next position advances by one. This is the only way the odometer moves. No other transitions are possible.

Most importantly, notice that a position holding zero because it has never been reached is different from a position holding zero because it was advanced and then reset by a later carry. A freshly created variable’s positions are all in this first condition: no transition has ever touched them, and because the system knows their value must be the default, nothing needs to be stored for them. They are inferred rather than recorded. But once a position has been touched by at least one transition, it carries a history, even if a subsequent carry has reset its digit back to zero. Six, reached by the odometer, has its first and second positions at zero. That zero is the result of carry resetting those positions after they filled; it is not the same as a position that has never been reached at all. The distinction becomes important later: a variable with no realized values state machine behaves differently from a variable whose values state machine is realized and currently reads zero, even when both report the same scalar value.

This is why an untouched variable’s zero is not stored in the algebraic system. When a variable has never received any event, no state machine has been activated for it, no digit position has been occupied, and the variable carries no information, so nothing is stored. That zero state is implicit in the structure: it is the default when nothing has occurred. A variable that has received events and later reads zero again — because a carry reset its digits, or because some later relationship drove it back to the default — is a different case. Its values state machine has been activated and may carry a history even though its current scalar reading is zero. The chapters on relationships and on multiplication return to this distinction, because the two kinds of zero behave differently once other variables depend on them.

Dimensions as Natural Boundaries

The factorial odometer naturally generates dimensions as its structure grows.

Imagine you are counting using just the first position. You can reach values zero and one. That is it. The first position defines a complete one-dimensional space. You can be at zero or one, nowhere else.

Now you need to represent three distinct states. A single position cannot do this. The first position is full. You must create a second position. Now you have two positions, and they can combine to represent multiple distinct states. The first position takes values zero and one. The second position takes values zero, one, or two. This combination creates not just more numbers, it creates a second dimension.

This is crucial. A dimension does not come from spatial intuition. A dimension emerges from the need to represent more states than the current position can hold. When you fill a position, you need another dimension to continue. The dimension is not imposed on the structure. The dimension emerges from the structure’s own limitations.

As you continue counting, each time you fill a position, you create a new dimension. The structure grows. It becomes two-dimensional, then three-dimensional, then higher. But these dimensions are not metaphorical. They are actual expansions of the state space necessary to represent new distinct configurations.

The conventional number line is a one-dimensional projection of this multi-dimensional space. When you line numbers up on a single line, you are collapsing the factorial odometer into a single dimension. That projection is useful for calculation. It is also misleading. It hides the structure that makes the numbers what they are.

The Residue Structure Emerges

As the odometer advances and the structure grows, a fundamental property becomes visible. Every number carries information about its relationships to other numbers.

Take the number six. It is reached after six advances of the odometer from zero. In the factorial basis, six is represented as one-zero-zero. The third position holds one, the second position holds zero, and the first position holds zero: [d3=1, d2=0, d1=0]. This configuration is the state that the odometer reaches on the sixth advance, because one unit at the third position is worth three factorial, which is six, and positions one and two together have already been exhausted by that point. Position one alone has two possible digit states, zero or one. Position two alone has three possible digit states, zero, one, or two. Together, positions one and two can form six distinct joint configurations, which is exactly why the odometer needs a third position the moment it reaches six: the two-position space has been completely used up.

Now observe: what numbers divide six evenly? The number two, the number three, and the number one. Not four or five or any higher number. Where does that divisibility come from?

The answer is in the structure of six itself, read from its low-order positions rather than inferred from the presence of a high-order digit. Divisibility by two is read directly from the first position: when the first position holds zero, the number is divisible by two. Six has first position zero, so six is divisible by two. Divisibility by three is read from a combination of the first two positions: when twice the second position plus the first position is divisible by three, the number is divisible by three. Six has second position zero and first position zero, so that combination is zero, which is divisible by three. Because six is divisible by both two and three, it is divisible by six as well — and this is exactly why positions one and two are both zero for six: nothing is left over in the lower positions once the single unit at the third position accounts for the entire value. A non-zero third-position digit does not, by itself, signal divisibility by six for every number that has one; the number seven, for instance, also has a one in the third position, but seven is not divisible by six, because seven’s first position holds a one rather than a zero.

No computation is required to determine these divisibilities. The structure says it directly. The digit configuration of any number encodes what divides it, what does not, and all the relationships that number has to every other number within that scope. These relationships are called residues. They are not computed from the number. They are carried by the number from the moment the odometer generates it.

This is why residues are important, and it is why they are visible immediately in the factorial basis representation. A number is not just a quantity on a line. A number is a configuration of a structure, and that configuration carries information. The divisibilities are not separate facts about the number. They are the structure itself made visible.

What Counting Actually Is

Looking back at the opening of this chapter, we can now answer the child’s question: where do numbers come from?

Numbers come from the odometer advancing. Counting is the process of the odometer moving from one configuration to the next. Each advance generates a new distinct state. The names we assign to those states are the numbers.

Counting does not mean adding one repeatedly. When you count one, two, three, you are not performing three addition operations. You are simply naming the first, second, and third states that the odometer reaches. The odometer generates these states by advancing its configuration. You are reading off the states and naming them.

This may seem like a minor difference. It is not. It changes what counting is fundamentally. Counting is not a procedure. It is the progression of a state machine through the valid states it can reach. Numbers are the names of those states.

This also explains why zero is the starting point and why the first position can hold zero or one. Zero is the state before any position has advanced. One is the state after the first position has advanced once. These are not arbitrary labels. They are the states that the structure naturally reaches.

The chapter that follows will expand this structure further. It will introduce the idea of positions and what happens when you need more of them. It will show how the structure naturally generates dimensions as it grows, and why geometry is not something imposed on numbers but something that emerges from their structure. But the foundation is now in place. Numbers come from the structure. The structure comes first. Counting is the odometer advancing through its configurations, and numbers are the states it generates.

That is the foundation of mathematics. Not a number line, but a state machine that generates numbers one state at a time, each preserving all the structure that came before.

Chapter 3Dimensions Without Distance

10 min read

The previous chapter introduced the factorial odometer and showed that counting is not adding one repeatedly but the progression of a state machine through its configurations. Numbers are the states the odometer reaches. As the odometer advances, something else emerges: dimensions. This chapter addresses what dimensions are, where they come from, and why they have nothing to do with distance or spatial intuition.

When One Position Is Not Enough

The first position of the odometer can take values zero or one. It represents two distinct states. You can count zero and one with just this position. You cannot count three, four, or five. The first position is full. It has reached its maximum.

When you need to represent a third distinct state, the first position alone is insufficient. You must create a second position. This is not a choice made for convenience. It is a necessity of the structure. Given that the first position can only take two values, a second position must exist to represent additional states.

Now the question is: what values can the second position take?

The answer comes from the structure itself. The second position must represent the states that result from the first position being fully utilized. The first position goes from zero to one. That is two states. The second position must be able to represent three states: the case where the first position is zero, the case where the first position is one, and the case where the first position is full and needs to advance further. So the second position can take values zero, one, or two.

This is the origin of the factorial structure. The maximum value of position n is n. Position one has maximum value one. Position two has maximum value two. Position three has maximum value three. As each position reaches its maximum, the next position is required.

The Multi-Dimensional Odometer

Observe what happens when you visualize the odometer with multiple positions.

With only the first position, you have a line:

[0] or [1]

With two positions, you have something more complex. You can arrange the states in a two-dimensional structure:

Position 2 = 0:  [0,0]  [1,0]
Position 2 = 1:  [0,1]  [1,1]
Position 2 = 2:  [0,2]  [1,2]

This is not a line anymore. This is a two-dimensional grid. The states do not arrange in a one-dimensional progression. They arrange in a two-dimensional space.

With three positions, the structure becomes three-dimensional. With four positions, four-dimensional. The structure that was once described as a one-dimensional number line is actually a multi-dimensional space. Successive advances of the odometer trace a path through this space, but the space itself is multi-dimensional from the beginning.

This is a crucial observation. The number line is a projection. It is a useful projection, useful for many calculations. But it is not the territory. The actual structure of the odometer is multi-dimensional. The number line collapses that structure onto a single line, hiding the dimensions that are really there.

What a Dimension Actually Is

In conventional geometry, a dimension is understood as a direction in which you can move through space. A one-dimensional line has one direction. A two-dimensional plane has two directions. A three-dimensional space has three directions. These dimensions are taken as primitives, as the fundamental building blocks of space itself.

In the algebraic system, dimensions are something different. A dimension is not a primitive. A dimension is a position in the odometer. Each position can be thought of as a separate direction in which the system can advance. The first position can advance from zero to one. That is one direction. The second position can advance from zero to one to two. That is another direction. The third position can advance from zero to one to two to three. That is a third direction.

The number of dimensions in the system is determined by how many positions are needed to represent the states the odometer has reached. If the largest number you have reached requires three positions, your system is three-dimensional. If you later reach a number that requires four positions, the system becomes four-dimensional.

Dimensions are not imposed on the odometer from outside. Dimensions emerge from the odometer’s own needs. When one position fills, a new dimension is required. When that position fills, another dimension is needed. The structure grows in dimensionality as it grows in the numbers it can represent.

This has a striking implication. Adding a new number to the system is not just adding an entry to a list. It is potentially expanding the system into a new dimension. When the odometer advances to the first number that requires a new position, the system itself becomes higher-dimensional.

Geometry Without Distance

Conventional geometry is built on the idea of distance. Points are located in space according to their distances from an origin. Lines are paths through space. Curves are smooth paths that change direction. All of geometry flows from the primitive notion of distance.

The factorial algebraic system generates geometry from a different foundation. Distance is not primitive. Distance is derived from scope relationships. In the odometer, each position has a finite range. Position two can go from zero to two. Position three can go from zero to three. The distance between two states is not measured in units on a line. The distance is measured by how many steps the odometer must advance to get from one state to the other.

More importantly, geometry emerges naturally from the multi-dimensional structure of the odometer without any appeal to spatial intuition. A two-dimensional state space is generated automatically when two positions are needed. A three-dimensional space is generated when three positions are needed. The structure of the odometer creates geometric relationships directly.

For example, in a two-dimensional odometer space, you can move in two directions. You can advance the first position while keeping the second position fixed. Or you can advance the second position while keeping the first position fixed. Or you can advance both simultaneously. These different movements correspond to moving along different geometric directions in the space.

The shape of this space is not a standard Euclidean grid. It is a simplex. The states of the two-position odometer do not form a rectangle. They form a triangle. Three corners, six edges if you count diagonals, one face. This is the geometry that emerges naturally from the factorial odometer structure.

A three-position odometer generates a three-dimensional simplex. A four-position odometer generates a four-dimensional simplex. The geometry is not imposed. It emerges from the structure.

The Number Line as Projection

Now you can understand why the number line is a projection.

The factorial odometer is multi-dimensional from the start. Each position represents a dimension. The progression of states through the odometer traces a path in that multi-dimensional space. The number line captures that path but discards the multi-dimensional structure around it.

Imagine taking a multi-dimensional object and projecting it onto a single line. You cast a shadow. The shadow captures some information about the object. It tells you the order in which the object’s points appear along the line. But the shadow discards the object’s shape, its volume, its internal structure. You can reconstruct the one-dimensional order from the shadow, but you cannot reconstruct the multi-dimensional structure from the one-dimensional projection.

This is what the number line does to the odometer. It captures the sequence of states the odometer reaches. It discards the multi-dimensional relationships between those states. When you work entirely with the number line, you lose access to the geometric structure that is actually present.

This explains why dimensions feel like they must be introduced separately in conventional mathematics. The number line has no room for them. When you need geometry or multiple dimensions, you must add them as new concepts. You must introduce the idea of coordinates, axes, and spatial relationships. These feel like new ideas because you have been working with a one-dimensional projection all along.

In the algebraic system, dimensions are not new. They are there from the start. They are implicit in the structure of the odometer. When you need to use multiple dimensions, you simply make explicit what was always present.

Dimension and Scope

There is one more relationship to establish. The dimensionality of the system is linked to the scope of the numbers it can represent.

Position n can take values from zero to n. With positions one through k allocated, the largest representable value has every position at its maximum simultaneously, which is (k+1) factorial minus one. If your system has reached the number six, which is one-zero-zero in factorial notation — digit one at the third position, zero at the second and first — the third position has just activated for the first time, and the system is using three positions. The system is three-dimensional.

Positions one through three continue to cover every value up to twenty-three, which is one less than twenty-four, or four factorial. Only when the system reaches twenty-four does it need to expand to four positions. A new dimension is added at that point. The fourth position takes its first non-zero value, and positions one through three all reset to zero. The system becomes four-dimensional there, not at seven.

This is not metaphorical. The geometric structure of the system actually becomes higher-dimensional when the odometer expands into a new position. The number of dimensions in the system is always equal to the number of positions currently in use.

So scope and dimensionality are the same thing. A system with large scope is a system with many dimensions. A system with small scope is a system with few dimensions. These are not separate properties. They are two ways of describing the same thing.

Why This Matters

Conventional mathematics teaches dimensions as a feature that must be added to the number line when needed. First you learn about one-dimensional problems. Then you learn about two-dimensional problems. These feel like different subjects because they are taught as additions.

In the algebraic system, all problems are inherently multi-dimensional from the start. The number line is a special case, a one-dimensional projection of a naturally multi-dimensional structure. When you work with multiple variables, you are not moving into a different domain. You are making explicit the dimensions that were always present in the structure.

This also explains why higher-dimensional geometry, non-Euclidean geometry, and other geometric structures that seem exotic in conventional mathematics are actually natural extensions of the factorial odometer. The simplex geometry is not an invention. It is what the factorial odometer generates naturally. Curved spaces emerge from the way the odometer’s positions interact.

The geometry you need for any problem is already present in the algebraic system. You do not need to invent it. You only need to make it explicit by working with the multi-dimensional structure instead of projecting it onto a line.

Looking Forward

This chapter has established that the factorial odometer is naturally multi-dimensional and that dimensions emerge from the structure itself as new positions are needed. The next chapter will examine what else emerges from this structure: the residues that carry information about relationships between numbers, the properties that are visible in the structure from the moment a number is generated.

But the key insight to carry forward is this: dimensions are not spatial intuitions imposed on numbers from outside. Dimensions are the natural consequence of a structure that needs more positions to represent more states. The number line is useful for one purpose, but it hides the real multi-dimensional nature of what numbers are.

Chapter 4Residues Are Not Calculated, They Are Carried

14 min read

The previous three chapters have introduced the factorial odometer and shown that it naturally generates multiple dimensions as it grows. They have shown that numbers are states within this structure, not primitives that exist before the structure. This chapter addresses what else the structure carries: the residues that define which numbers divide other numbers evenly, which do not, and all the divisibility relationships that make arithmetic tractable.

What Divisibility Actually Is

Start with a concrete question: what numbers divide evenly into twelve?

The answer is one, two, three, four, six, and twelve. Not five, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven. Where does this list come from?

In conventional mathematics, you discover divisibility by testing. Does twelve divide evenly by two? Yes. By three? Yes. By five? No. You perform repeated division until you find the divisors. Divisibility is something you compute from the number.

But this is not the only way to think about divisibility. You can also think about it structurally. The number twelve is represented in the factorial basis as two-zero-zero: the third position holds two, the second position holds zero, and the first position holds zero, [d3=2, d2=0, d1=0]. Checking the weights: two times three factorial, plus zero times two factorial, plus zero times one factorial, equals twelve plus zero plus zero, which is twelve.

Divisibility by two is read directly from the first position: when it holds zero, as it does here, the number is divisible by two. Divisibility by three is read from a combination of the first two positions: when twice the second position plus the first position is divisible by three, the number is divisible by three. Here that combination is twice zero plus zero, which is zero, divisible by three. Because twelve is divisible by both two and three, it is divisible by six as well. Divisibility by four is read from a combination of the first three positions: when six times the third position plus twice the second position plus the first position is divisible by four, the number is divisible by four. Here that combination is six times two plus zero plus zero, which is twelve, divisible by four.

The divisors of twelve are not discovered by testing each candidate in turn. They are read from the low-order positions using a fixed set of combinations, each tied to a specific factorial weight. A non-zero digit at the third position, by itself, does not determine divisibility by two, three, four, or six; the digit at the third position tells you how many complete blocks of six the number contains, and the lower two positions tell you what divisibility relationships the remainder carries.

This is the foundation of residues. A residue is not a separate computation applied after the fact. A residue is a structural property of the number that is visible from the moment the number is generated.

The Configuration Carries the Information

The concept of a residue is often introduced in number theory as something you compute. You take a number, divide it by another number, and find the remainder. That remainder is the residue. You compute residues when you need them.

In the algebraic system, residues are not computed. They are carried. The very structure of the number in factorial notation encodes which residues it has.

Take the number twenty. In factorial notation, this is three-one-zero: the third position holds three, the second position holds one, and the first position holds zero, [d3=3, d2=1, d1=0]. Checking the weights: three times six, plus one times two, plus zero times one, equals eighteen plus two plus zero, which is twenty.

What divides evenly into twenty? The number two divides twenty. How do you know this? Because the first position holds zero, and divisibility by two is read directly from the first position. The structure says twenty is divisible by two. Does three divide evenly into twenty? Reading the combination of twice the second position plus the first position gives twice one plus zero, which is two. Two is not divisible by three, so twenty is not divisible by three — which matches the ordinary arithmetic fact that twenty divided by three leaves a remainder.

Does five divide evenly into twenty? The structure’s low-order positions do not expose this directly, because five is not among the factorial weights. Factorials are one, two, six, twenty-four, one-hundred-twenty, and five is not in that sequence. So the position-by-position residue rules that work for two, three, four, and six do not give a one-step reading for five. The divisibility is still present in the number — twenty is in fact divisible by five — but confirming it from the structure alone requires either the ordinary scalar check or a scope large enough to reach a factorial boundary that is itself a multiple of five, such as one hundred twenty, which is five factorial. Twenty itself equals three copies of six plus one copy of two plus zero copies of one, and that decomposition is visible in the digits without needing to test divisors one at a time, even though the five-specific reading requires a larger scope than two, three, four, or six do.

This principle extends to all residues. The digit configuration is the residue structure made visible. Reading the positions and their values tells you everything about what divides the number, what does not, and how the number relates to all other numbers at the same scope level.

Why Factorial Boundaries Are Complete

The previous chapter introduced the idea of factorial boundaries. Position n has maximum digit n. With positions one through k allocated, the largest representable configuration has every position simultaneously at its maximum, giving a value of (k+1) factorial minus one. The very next state, (k+1) factorial, cannot be reached by any configuration of positions one through k alone; it requires activating position k+1, whose single unit is worth the entire block that positions one through k could represent, plus one more. At that boundary, position k+1 holds digit one and every position below it resets to zero. A factorial boundary is where a new position activates at its minimum nonzero digit, not where the existing positions are all full — full occupancy is the state immediately before the boundary, and the boundary itself is the opposite: a fresh position with everything below it at its default.

Now you can understand why factorial boundaries are special, with one qualification. At a factorial boundary (k+1) factorial, divisibility by every integer that divides some factorial at or below (k+1) factorial — two, three, four, six, and so on — is directly readable from the low-order positions using the combination rules established for each one. This is a strong form of completeness, but it is not completeness for every integer divisor. A divisor such as five, which is not itself a factorial weight and does not evenly divide two, six, or twenty-four, does not get a comparably simple positional reading until the scope reaches a factorial boundary that is itself a multiple of five — the first one is one hundred twenty, which is five factorial. Below that boundary, five’s relationships to other numbers still exist; they are simply not exposed by a short position-based rule the way two, three, four, and six are.

At the number one, you know nothing yet. One position, one value. At the number two, you have entered the second position, and some relationships become visible. At the number six, which is three factorial, position three activates for the first time, holding one unit while positions one and two reset to zero. The divisibility relationships for two, three, and six are now directly readable for every number up to this boundary using the rules already established.

When you reach twenty-four, which is four factorial, position four activates in the same way, holding one unit while positions one through three reset to zero. The same divisibility rules for two, three, four, and six remain directly readable for every number up to this new boundary.

This is why factorials feel like natural stopping points. They are. They are the states where a position has just activated at its minimum, and the structure resets beneath it. They mark where a new position’s worth of range becomes available, and where the position-based divisibility rules already defined continue to apply without needing a new rule for each new boundary.

Primes as Structural Signals

Here is a remarkable consequence of understanding residues this way. Prime numbers, which are often taught as the fundamental building blocks of arithmetic, are actually something quite different, once a distinction is made clear.

A prime number is a state that has no divisors other than itself and one. That fact about a number does not change with scope: ten is composite at every scope, because it is two times five regardless of how much of the structure has been built out, and five is prime at every scope, because no integer between two and four divides it evenly, at any scope. Primality itself is not scope-dependent.

What is scope-dependent is how directly a number’s relationships to other numbers can be read off from the factorial-basis digit positions, using the kind of short combination rules established earlier in this chapter for two, three, four, and six. Those rules exist because two, three, four, and six are all divisors of a small factorial. Five is not a divisor of any factorial smaller than one-hundred-twenty, which is five factorial. Below that scope, there is no comparably short rule that reads divisibility by five directly from a handful of low-order positions. The number ten, for instance, is already composite with five as a factor well before scope one-hundred-twenty is reached — that fact does not wait for any scope to become true — but the factorial-basis positions do not expose a one-step divisibility-by-five reading until the scope reaches a factorial boundary that is itself a multiple of five.

This has an implication worth stating carefully. A prime is not a fundamental atom from which other numbers are assembled; its divisibility relationships to every other number are determined the moment the number exists, not constructed afterward by combining smaller pieces. But the ease of reading those relationships directly from the digit structure, without separate computation, does depend on whether the prime in question divides a factorial at or below the current scope. Primes that divide no small factorial — five, seven, eleven, and most primes in general — do not get a short positional rule until the scope reaches a factorial boundary built from a multiple of that prime. This is a statement about the representation’s directness, not about whether the number has divisors.

This reframes what primes are without overstating the reframing. They are not the foundation of arithmetic in the sense of being the raw material other numbers are built from, because the odometer generates every number, prime or composite, by the same single mechanism. But primes that divide no small factorial remain diagnostically distinct for longer: the structure does not hand you a short rule for their relationships until the scope catches up to them.

Inferred and Realized Zero Positions

Return to the structure of twelve, which is two-zero-zero in factorial notation: [d3=2, d2=0, d1=0]. The third position has a non-zero value. The first and second positions have zero values.

What does it mean that the first and second positions are zero here? It depends on how the odometer reached twelve. If the odometer arrived at twelve by advancing through eleven, ten, and the states before them, then positions one and two were touched repeatedly along the way and reset to zero each time a carry passed through them; they are realized positions currently reading zero, carrying a history of having been occupied, not positions that were never reached. A position is in its inferred, unstored absence state only when no transition has ever touched it at all — which, for a variable that has been advanced all the way to twelve, is not true of positions one and two.

This distinction matters for a freshly created variable rather than for a variable that has already advanced through many states. A brand-new variable’s positions are all inferred: no transition has touched any of them, and nothing needs to be stored. The moment any event moves that variable, the positions it passes through become realized, whether their final digit lands on zero or on something else.

This has a consequence for how numbers are represented and what space they consume, stated precisely: an inferred position, never touched, needs no storage. A realized position, even one currently reading zero, may still need to record that it has a history, depending on what the surrounding relationships require. The system is minimal in the first sense — it never pays to store a position nothing has touched — without claiming that every zero-valued digit is automatically free of history.

This principle extends beyond numbers to the algebraic system as a whole. A variable that has never received any event is inferred at zero and consumes no space. A variable that has received events and now reads zero, whether through an explicit assignment or through carries that happened to cancel out, is a realized variable whose current value happens to be zero. The two cases look identical when you only ask “what is the value,” and they can behave differently once other variables depend on them, as later chapters on relationships and multiplication show.

Residues Across the System

The final insight is that residue structures are not isolated to individual numbers. They form a web across the entire system.

When the odometer reaches twelve, it has already passed through all numbers from one to eleven. The residue structure of twelve is not separate from the residue structures of the numbers that came before. Twelve’s residues are extensions and completions of the residues that earlier numbers began to establish.

The number twelve has six as a divisor. That relationship was already present, in a sense, in the number six itself. The number six established that six is a state in the odometer. The number twelve extends that by saying twelve is a multiple of six. The residue structure grows. It does not jump in at random points. It evolves continuously as the odometer advances.

This is why residues are carried rather than computed. The structure at any number incorporates all the structure that came before. Residues are not properties that numbers have in isolation. They are relationships that the entire structure up to that point establishes.

The Simplification This Creates

Looking back at the opening question of this chapter: what numbers divide evenly into twelve?

In conventional arithmetic, you answer this by testing. In the algebraic system, you answer it by reading the structure. The configuration of the number twelve in factorial notation tells you directly which divisions work. You do not perform them. You read them from the structure itself.

This is not a minor convenience. This is a fundamental simplification. You do not compute residues. You observe them in the structure. This means divisibility problems that seem computationally complex in conventional arithmetic become simple observations in the algebraic system. You see the structure, and the divisibilities are visible.

This also means that several problems that require sophisticated algorithms in conventional mathematics become more direct in the algebraic system, with a caveat tied to what was established in the previous two sections. Testing divisibility by two, three, four, or six becomes reading the structure rather than performing division. Testing divisibility by a prime that does not divide any small factorial, such as five or seven, still requires either an ordinary test or a scope large enough to reach a factorial boundary built from a multiple of that prime. Finding greatest common divisors and factoring both benefit from the same pattern: the factorial-related divisors are visible immediately, and the rest follow the same rules ordinary arithmetic always required.

The algebraic system does not hide these properties. They are visible in the representation from the moment a number is generated. The structure carries the information. You only need to learn to read it.

Completing Part 1

Part 1 has now established the foundation of the algebraic system. The factorial odometer generates numbers one state at a time. Numbers are not primitives. They are states within a structure. That structure is naturally multi-dimensional. And the structure carries all the information about divisibility and relationships from the moment each number is generated.

The next part will expand this to the full algebraic system. It will introduce variables, values, relationships, and constants. It will show how the simple odometer structure extends to a system where multiple variables can interact, where constants like e and π are defined by relationships, and where the algebraic system as a whole becomes a machine for managing complex relationships.

But the foundation is solid. Every concept that follows builds on the structure you have now seen: a state machine that generates numbers sequentially, preserving prior structure with each advance, carrying residue information in its very configuration.

Part 2

Building the Algebraic System

Chapter 5What an Algebraic System Actually Is

9 min read

Part 1 built the foundation. Numbers are states in a structure. Counting is the advance of the factorial odometer. Dimensions emerge as scope grows. Residues are carried in the representation. That foundation now allows the next question.

What is the full thing that contains these states?

Most people would answer with a familiar phrase. Algebra is the use of symbols to represent numbers and relations. That description sounds reasonable, but it keeps the old assumption in place. Symbols still stand in for numbers. Numbers still come first. Relations still sit on top of numbers as secondary objects.

This chapter starts somewhere else. The algebraic system comes first. Variables, values, and relations exist inside that system. A number is one kind of state that a variable can occupy. The system is primary. Numbers are one output of the system.

The Mistake in the Usual Picture

The standard classroom picture says a variable is a box that can hold a value. Write x on the box. Put 3 in the box. Later remove 3 and put 7 in the box. Then write equations that connect boxes.

This picture is easy to teach. It is also misleading. Boxes do not explain how values are constrained, how transitions are validated, or how relationships are maintained when one variable changes. Boxes hide the structure that actually matters.

A variable is not a container. A variable is a state machine.

A state machine has three core elements. It has a set of valid states. It has rules that define which transitions are valid. It has events that trigger those transitions. When you model a variable as a state machine, the variable no longer means a box that holds an object. The variable means a named position in a structured space that can move only through valid transitions.

The box picture collapses all of that into one vague gesture. The state machine picture makes all of it explicit.

Start with the Whole, Not the Piece

An algebraic system is an entity with identity. That identity answers a simple question. Which system are we talking about?

If you have one equation in one notebook, identity seems unnecessary. In real mathematics and real computation, identity matters immediately. The same variable name can appear in multiple systems with different meanings. The same relation can hold in one scope and fail in another. Identity prevents ambiguity.

So the algebraic system begins as an entity. Inside that entity are state machines. The first state machine names which variables exist in the system. The second set of state machines tracks values for each variable. The third set of state machines tracks relationships between variables. The fourth set tracks constraints that bound valid configurations.

This is not extra complexity. This is the minimum structure required for coherent behavior.

When people say algebra is symbols plus rules, this is what that phrase points toward but never states clearly. Symbols are variables in a naming state machine. Rules are constraints and relations in relationship state machines. Values are current states in value state machines. The algebraic system is the entity that holds all of it together.

The Smallest Working Algebraic System

Build the smallest possible case.

Create one algebraic system entity. Name it S.

Inside S, create one variable named x in the variable naming state machine.

Now create a value state machine for x. That value state machine uses factorial basis positions exactly as earlier chapters described.

At this moment x has not transitioned. Therefore x is in the inferred default state. The value is zero.

Notice something important. Zero is not stored. No value state needs materialization until an event moves x away from the default. The system can answer the question “what is x” with zero even when no explicit storage exists for x values yet.

Now trigger one event that advances x by one valid transition. The value state machine for x materializes at the minimal scope required. x now occupies the state named one.

Trigger another event. x advances again. If the current position is full, carry propagates as scope expansion. x now occupies the state named two.

Nothing in this sequence required equations. Nothing required external procedures. The variable exists as a state machine. The value changes through valid transitions. The system remains coherent because every change passes through explicit structure.

That is the first complete algebraic system.

Why the System Must Be Primary

Suppose you begin with numbers instead. You write x equals 2. Later you write x equals 3. Then you ask whether this is valid.

Where does validity come from?

If validity lives outside the assignment, then every assignment needs external checks. If validity lives inside the structure, the transition itself carries validity rules. The second approach is simpler and safer.

Now add one relation. Let y equal x plus 1.

In the box model, changing x requires procedural code that also updates y. If that update is missed, y becomes stale. If updates happen in the wrong order, transient inconsistency appears. If two updates race, the relation can break.

In the algebraic system model, y equals x plus 1 is a relationship state machine. It is not a note written next to boxes. It is an active structural rule. When x transitions, the relationship state machine constrains y to the matching valid state. If no matching state exists at current scope, scope expansion occurs as a valid structural event.

This is why the system must come first. Coherence is a property of structure, not a side effect of good habits.

Variables as Named Capabilities

In conventional language a variable is usually described as an unknown. That description works in elementary exercises and fails in advanced work.

A variable is better understood as a named capability for occupying states within bounded scope.

The name gives identity inside the system. The value state machine gives possible states. The transition rules give valid movement. Relationships connect movement across variables.

This view unifies basic algebra and advanced mathematics.

In early arithmetic, x might occupy small counting states. In polynomial algebra, x might move under constraints defined by equations. In calculus, x might occupy boundary-near states where derivative behavior matters. In complex analysis, x may require orthogonal dimensions.

The variable remains the same kind of object in every case. Only scope and constraints deepen.

That continuity is one reason this model avoids curricular discontinuities. The object never changes type midstream. The learner keeps one coherent concept and applies it at increasing depth.

The Role of Relationships

An algebraic system with only isolated variables is incomplete.

Mathematics becomes meaningful when variables relate. A relation says which combined states are valid. In this model a relation is a state machine that evaluates and constrains joint configurations.

Consider a simple relation: z equals x plus y.

This relation does four jobs.

It names the participating variables. It defines the validity condition for their joint state. It defines transition consequences when one member changes. It defines required scope behavior when current scope cannot represent the next valid joint state.

In textbook algebra these jobs are distributed across symbols, informal understanding, and procedural manipulation. In the algebraic system they are explicit in one structure.

That explicitness eliminates ambiguity. It also enables execution. A relationship state machine can run.

Constraints as First Class Structure

Relationships alone do not define all valid behavior. You also need constraints that are not reducible to one equation.

A constraint may say x remains nonnegative in a given scenario. Another may say two dimensions remain orthogonal. Another may cap scope at a fixed boundary for a finite problem.

If constraints remain informal assumptions, systems drift. If constraints become first class state machines, systems stay coherent under change.

This point matters in both mathematics and computation. People often treat assumptions as background context. Background context is fragile. First class structure is durable.

When a constraint is explicit, every transition can validate against it. When a constraint changes, the system can revalidate affected states deterministically. That behavior is impossible when assumptions live only in prose.

This reframes what it means to solve an equation. In the conventional picture, solving is a procedure: apply rules to symbols until the unknown is isolated. In the algebraic system, solving is a structural question: which states of the variable satisfy all the constraint machines simultaneously? The answer is the set of states where no constraint machine reports a violation. The solving process is not manipulation of notation. It is the search for configurations that the system permits. The answer is found when the constraints are satisfied, not when the symbols have been rearranged.

The Shift in Intuition

At first this model can feel heavier than familiar notation. That feeling comes from visibility. You can now see structure that conventional notation hides.

After that initial adjustment, the model becomes lighter in practice.

You stop asking which trick applies to this special case. You ask which state machine governs this transition.

You stop memorizing exceptions for number types. You represent the relation and let the same structural rules apply.

You stop treating consistency as maintenance work. You get consistency as a property of the system design.

This is the same shift readers saw in From Numbers to Systems for computing. When structure carries behavior, behavior no longer depends on scattered procedures.

From One Variable to a Real System

This chapter introduced the smallest complete system with one variable. The next chapter expands that system to two variables that share one entity and one value space.

That expansion matters for two reasons.

First, it makes relationships concrete. You can watch a change in one variable constrain another variable in real time.

Second, it reveals a property that conventional algebra usually hides. Two variables can occupy the same value state without duplicating storage. In this model shared value space is natural. If x and y occupy the same state, the system can represent that state once and bind both names to it until divergence occurs.

That property will matter later for efficiency, coherence, and the elimination of unnecessary computation.

For now keep the central point clear.

An algebraic system is not numbers plus symbols.

An algebraic system is an entity that contains variable naming, value states, relationships, and constraints as explicit state machines. Numbers are names for occupied states. Operations are valid transitions under relationships. Coherence comes from structure.

Once that point is clear, the rest of algebra stops looking like a bag of techniques and starts looking like one machine.

Chapter 6Variables as State Machines

8 min read

The previous chapter established the full frame. An algebraic system is an entity that contains variable naming, value states, relationships, and constraints. That chapter answered what the system is. This chapter answers what a variable is inside that system.

The usual answer is familiar. A variable is a box that stores a value. Put five in the box. Replace five with seven. Continue as needed.

That picture is simple. It is also the source of repeated confusion. Boxes do not explain validity, transition order, scope expansion, or relationship consistency. Boxes hide the structure that governs change.

A variable is not a box. A variable is a state machine.

The Difference Between Holding and Occupying

A container holds an object. The object can be inserted or removed. The container itself does not define which objects are valid, which changes are allowed, or how one change affects another object elsewhere.

A state machine works differently. A state machine occupies a current condition inside a bounded set of valid conditions. It also defines which transitions are valid between those conditions. A variable in this model occupies a state. It does not hold a value as cargo.

This difference appears abstract until you watch change happen.

Suppose x is in state three. An event arrives that requests an increment by one. In a container model, the operation means fetch value, add one, store result. In a state machine model, the operation means evaluate whether the transition from state three to state four is valid under current constraints and scope. If it is valid, transition occurs. If it is not valid at current scope, scope expansion may be required before transition can occur.

The state machine model carries meaning that the container model leaves implicit.

A Variable Has a Defined State Space

When people first hear that a variable is a state machine, they often imagine infinite possibilities and open ended movement. That is still too loose.

A variable state machine has a defined state space at any moment. The state space is bounded by current factorial scope. Within that scope, each state is valid and identifiable. Outside that scope, states are undefined until scope expands.

This boundedness matters because mathematics is not only about what is possible in principle. Mathematics is also about what is valid under current assumptions.

If current scope supports states zero through twenty four, then a transition request to forty must trigger one of two outcomes. Either the system expands scope first and then transitions, or the transition is rejected under a fixed scope constraint. Both outcomes are explicit. Neither outcome depends on hidden procedural behavior.

The variable does not float in an unlimited number line. The variable occupies a bounded state space that can grow under explicit rules.

Zero as Inferred Default

This is where the model departs sharply from conventional storage thinking.

In the algebraic system, zero is not a stored value by default. Zero is the inferred state before any event has moved the variable.

Create a variable named x in the variable naming state machine. Do nothing else.

What is x?

x is zero.

Where is that zero stored?

Nowhere. No transition has occurred. No value state machine needs materialization for x yet. The answer zero is inferred from absence of transition.

This is not a storage trick. This is the semantics of the model. If no event has moved x, x remains in default state. Default state is zero. Therefore zero is true without explicit storage.
