Now trigger an event that increments x by one. At that moment the value state machine for x materializes at minimal scope required for the new occupied state. x becomes one.

Trigger a decrement back to zero. If no remaining relationship or constraint requires explicit representation, x can collapse back to inferred default. The system may remove explicit value realization and still preserve correct meaning.

This is why the model says zero is inferred, not stored.

Events Drive Change, Not Assignment Syntax

In conventional notation, change is often written as assignment.

x equals x plus one.

This syntax mixes three separate things. It names current state, defines requested transition, and asserts next state. The reader mentally executes the middle step.

In a state machine, these parts separate cleanly.

Current state exists as explicit machine condition. Requested change arrives as event. Transition validity is evaluated against constraints. Next state is occupied only if transition is valid.

This separation improves clarity and reliability.

Clarity improves because each part has one role. Reliability improves because invalid transitions are impossible to apply silently.

The point is not to ban assignment syntax from writing. The point is to remember that assignment syntax is shorthand for event driven transition in a state machine.

Once you keep that structure visible, many algebraic confusions disappear.

Carry Is a Transition Event, Not a Side Effect

In base ten arithmetic, carry is often taught as a bookkeeping side effect.

In the factorial algebraic system, carry is an explicit transition event at a boundary.

Suppose x occupies the highest state in current position while lower positions are also at boundary. An increment request arrives. The transition cannot occur in place. A boundary event triggers. The current position resets to default. The next position increments. If needed, scope expands.

Nothing about this sequence is accidental. Each step is part of the variable state machine definition.

This matters because it unifies elementary arithmetic and advanced structure. The same transition logic handles simple counting and deep scope expansion. You do not switch mental models when numbers become large. You follow the same state machine rules at larger scope.

Why the Container Metaphor Breaks Under Relations

A single variable can be explained with a container metaphor if you ignore enough detail. Relations expose the failure quickly.

Suppose y is constrained by relation y equals x plus one.

If x and y are treated as independent boxes, a change in x requires procedural code that also updates y. If code misses one path, relation breaks. If update order changes, transient inconsistency appears. If concurrent writes occur, race behavior appears.

If x and y are state machines connected by a relationship state machine, consistency is structural. A transition in x triggers relationship evaluation. Valid next state for y is determined by relation and constraints. If current scope cannot represent required y state, scope event occurs according to explicit rules.

The system does not hope that procedural updates stay synchronized. The system enforces synchronization through structure.

That enforcement starts with the variable model. Variables must be state machines for relationships to remain coherent under change.

A Variable Is a Named Trajectory

Another useful way to state the concept is this.

A variable is not a place where values sit. A variable is a named trajectory through valid states.

At time t0, x occupies state two. At time t1 after event e1, x occupies state three. At time t2 after event e2, x remains state three because e2 requested no valid change. At time t3 after event e3, x occupies state six after scope event.

This sequence is the meaning of x over time. The value at any single moment is only one snapshot from that trajectory.

This view makes the no change principle concrete. If an event yields no state change, no transition occurred in meaningful terms. The variable trajectory does not move. The system remains unchanged.

That principle will matter in later chapters for identity operations such as adding zero and multiplying by one.

Keeping One Concept Across All Levels

One reason mathematics education feels discontinuous is that the object called variable keeps changing meaning.

In early algebra, variable means unknown number. In functions, variable means input axis. In calculus, variable means changing quantity with limits. In complex analysis, variable may include orthogonal dimensions.

Students are told these are connected, but the object itself seems to mutate each time.

In the state machine model, variable keeps one meaning.

A variable is a named state machine with bounded scope, valid transitions, and event driven change.

Early lessons use small scope and simple transitions. Later lessons use larger scope, richer constraints, and additional dimensions.

The object does not change type. Depth changes. Structure remains.

That continuity is not a cosmetic benefit. It is a cognitive benefit. Learners can build intuition once and extend it instead of replacing it repeatedly.

What This Changes in Practice

When you model variables as state machines, several practical shifts happen.

You stop asking what value is inside x as if x were a container. You ask which state x occupies under current scope.

You stop writing transition logic as scattered procedural steps. You define transition validity in one structural place.

You stop treating zero as data that must always be stored. You treat zero as inferred default until events require explicit realization.

You stop handling carry as arithmetic housekeeping. You treat carry as explicit boundary transition.

Each shift removes hidden assumptions. Hidden assumptions are where fragility accumulates. Explicit structure is where coherence comes from.

What Comes Next

This chapter has established the core concept of Part 2. Variables are bounded state machines, and zero is inferred default before any event moves a variable.

The next chapter adds a second variable inside the same algebraic system. That step will make relationships concrete. You will see why z equals x plus y is not a procedure that runs after changes. It is a relationship state machine inside the entity itself. When one variable moves, relation constrained transitions keep the full system coherent.

At that point the algebraic system starts to look less like notation and more like an executable structure.

Chapter 7Two Variables, One System

8 min read

The previous chapter showed that a variable is a state machine, not a container. It has a defined state space, valid transitions, and an inferred default state of zero before any event moves it. A single variable named x is the simplest complete algebraic system.

Now add a second variable.

The move seems simple. Two boxes instead of one. But the moment you add a second variable and relate the two, the container model begins to fail. The state machine model reveals its advantage.

Adding y

Start with the same system from the previous chapter. One entity called S. One variable x in the naming state machine. One value state machine for x, currently in default state, currently occupying zero.

Now extend the naming state machine to include y. A second value state machine materializes at minimal scope when needed. Until an event moves y, its state is inferred as zero.

At this point x and y are independent. They share one entity but do not constrain each other. Both are in default state. If you increment x to three, y remains at zero. If you then increment y to five, x remains at three. The system holds both states simultaneously, each tracked by its own value state machine.

That independence is real and useful. Two variables in one system, neither affected by the other.

The situation changes when you add a relationship.

Defining the Relationship

Write the relation: z equals x plus y.

In conventional algebra, this is read as an equation to solve or as a formula to evaluate. You substitute values of x and y, perform addition, and compute z. The relation is a procedure waiting for inputs.

In the algebraic system, this relation is a different kind of thing entirely. It is a relationship state machine.

A relationship state machine does not evaluate when called. It exists continuously inside the entity. Its job is to enforce a constraint on the joint state of z, x, and y. Specifically, it says that at all times the state of z must equal the combined states of x and y. That constraint is active at all times, not only when you decide to evaluate it.

This distinction carries significant consequences.

What Happens When x Changes

Return to the system with x at three, y at five, and z constrained by z equals x plus y. At this point z is eight, inferred from the constraint.

Now an event arrives that increments x by two.

In the container model, you update x to five. If you then want z, you evaluate the formula. If you forget to re-evaluate, z remains stale at eight. Stale state is a silent error.

In the state machine model, incrementing x to five triggers the relationship state machine. The relationship state machine evaluates whether z’s current state is still consistent with the constraint. It is not. z must now be ten. The relationship state machine drives z’s value state machine to transition to ten. The system never holds an inconsistent state because structure enforces consistency rather than relying on procedural discipline.

The transition in x causes a constrained transition in z. No manual update required. No path exists where z can be forgotten.

The Relationship Is Inside the Entity

This is the structural point that the conventional model misses.

When you write z equals x plus y on paper, you are noting a relationship. When you write it in a spreadsheet formula, you are creating procedural dependency. When you implement it in code, you are writing logic that must be found and executed at the right time.

In each of those cases, the relationship is something you create outside the variables and attach to them afterward. The variables themselves remain simple containers.

In the algebraic system entity, the relationship state machine lives inside the entity alongside the variable naming state machine and the value state machines. It is not attached afterward. It is part of the definition of what this system is.

This changes what the system means. A system without the relation between x, y, and z is a different system than one with it. Not a less complete version of the same system. A genuinely different system with different valid states and different valid transitions.

When you define the relation as part of the entity, the entity becomes aware of what it is and what it must maintain. That awareness is structural, not procedural.

Scope Expansion Through a Relation

A practical consequence deserves examination.

Suppose x is at twenty and y is at ten. The relation says z equals x plus y. Therefore z must be thirty.

But suppose the system was defined with maximum scope at twenty-four, which is four factorial. Can z occupy state thirty at that scope?

No. Thirty exceeds the current maximum.

The relationship state machine detects this. The system cannot satisfy the constraint at current scope. Two outcomes are possible, depending on whether scope is fixed or expandable.

If scope is expandable, a scope expansion event occurs before the transition in z. The value state machine for z materializes at the new scope required to represent thirty. Then the constrained transition occurs. The system remains coherent at larger scope.

If scope is fixed by a constraint, the increment that would have moved x to twenty is invalid. The transition request is rejected before x changes. The system remains in its last valid state.

Both outcomes are explicit. Neither produces silent inconsistency. The system always knows whether it can satisfy its constraints. When it cannot, the response is a defined structural event, not unpredictable behavior.

Variables That Share Value Space

Here the model reveals something that the container picture cannot express at all.

Suppose x and y both occupy state five. In the container picture, you have two boxes, each containing the value five. Two representations of the same value exist.

In the state machine model, x and y are names. Their value states are positions in a shared factorial basis space. If x and y both occupy state five, they both point to the same position in that shared space. One representation exists.

This is not a memory optimization layered on top of the model. This is the natural behavior of state machines in a shared value space. Two names bound to the same position are the same as two names bound to the same state.

The consequence becomes visible when one of them changes. Suppose an event increments x by one. Before the increment, x and y share state five. After the increment, x occupies state six. y still occupies state five. The two names are no longer at the same position. Divergence has occurred.

At the moment of divergence, y does not need to copy anything. y is already at five. Only x has moved. The system reflects reality without duplication, because shared value space means identical values need no separate representation.

This principle will matter later in the book when the efficiency of the algebraic system is compared to conventional base-ten arithmetic.

Relationships and the No-Change Principle

The previous chapter introduced zero as inferred default. A variable at zero requires no explicit value state machine. That principle extends to relationships.

Suppose the relation is z equals x plus y, and the current event increments x by zero. In the state machine model, incrementing by zero is a request for a transition that produces no change. No transition occurs, because a transition that produces no change is indistinguishable from no transition at all.

Since x did not change, the relationship state machine has nothing to evaluate. z does not need to change. The entire sequence of events produces no observable difference in the system.

This is not a special rule invented to handle zero. It is the natural consequence of what transitions are. Transitions are changes. No change means no transition. No transition means no evaluation cascade. The system is efficient by structure.

Introducing the Term

The previous chapter deliberately did not use the term Entity-State Machine. This chapter has now introduced all the elements that term names.

The entity is the algebraic system S. It has identity. It contains the state machines that describe what S knows and how S changes.

The state machines are the variable naming machine, the value machines for each variable, and the relationship machines between variables.

Each state machine has valid states and valid transitions. Events drive transitions. Transitions that produce no change do not occur.

This is the Entity-State Machine. It is not a formal notation. It is the structure the previous chapters have been building, now named.

Every algebraic relation, every mathematical operation, every constant, and every constraint in the rest of this book fits inside this structure. Nothing requires a different model. Nothing requires a special case. The entity state machine is the complete foundation.

What Comes Next

Chapter 8 will complete Part 2 by addressing constants. Constants like e and pi appear in mathematics as fixed, magical values embedded in the universe. This chapter will show that they are not. They are variables. Variables with specific relationship state machines assigned as their definitions, expanded to whatever scope the current problem requires.

The factorial basis has a particular property that makes this concrete. Series with factorial denominators converge exactly in the factorial basis. Each term occupies exactly one position. For the constant e, this means the series definition and the factorial basis representation are the same thing. The definition is the number.

That equivalence is one of the clearest demonstrations that the algebraic system is not a different notation for conventional mathematics. It is a different foundation.

Chapter 8Constants Are Variables with Definitions

12 min read

There is a number that appears across virtually every part of mathematics. It governs how populations grow and how radioactive materials decay. It defines the shape of a bell curve. It appears in Euler’s identity, connecting five fundamental values in a single equation. Its decimal expansion begins 2.71828 and continues without end or repetition. Mathematicians call it e.

When a student encounters e for the first time, the typical presentation goes something like this: e is a special mathematical constant, like π. You should memorize its approximate value. Here are the situations where it appears. Now use it in these problems.

That presentation is not wrong. But it conceals a question that it never raises: where does e come from? Who put it there? Why does it have that particular value and not some other?

The answer is not mystical. e was not discovered engraved on a tablet. e was defined. Someone wrote down a rule and said: the variable e is the value that satisfies this rule. The rule is precise. The rule is mathematical. And the rule lives inside the algebraic system as a relationship state machine.

A Variable with a Definition

Return to the algebraic system built across the previous three chapters. The entity holds three state machines: x, y, and z. The relationship state machine that defines z says z equals x plus y. When x and y have values, z is determined. The relationship machine tracks this constraint.

Now add a fourth state machine to the entity. Call it e. The question is: what relationship state machine governs e?

The rule that defines e is an infinite series. Each term in the series is one divided by n factorial, for n starting at zero and continuing without bound. The terms are: one divided by one, one divided by one, one divided by two, one divided by six, one divided by twenty-four, one divided by one hundred twenty, and so on. Each successive term is smaller than the last, because n factorial grows rapidly. The sum of all terms converges to a fixed value. That value is e.

This is not a description from outside the algebraic system. It is a relationship state machine inside the entity. The relationship says: the state of the variable e is the state reached by summing all terms of this series within the current scope. The variable e is not imported from some external storehouse of mathematical constants. It is a state machine that receives the output of its defining relationship. Its value is the result of expanding that relationship to the required depth.

The word “constant” means only that the relationship assigned to e is never changed after it is defined, and so the resulting value never changes. A variable’s value changes when new events arrive and its relationships to other variables are updated. The variable e receives no new events after its relationship is set. So its value does not change. That stability is why it is called a constant. The mechanism, however, is no different from any other variable in the system.

Scope and Precision

The series for e is infinite. A finite algebraic system cannot expand an infinite series to all terms. So how does the system handle this?

The system expands e to the current fractional scope, which is distinct from the integer scope used for whole numbers. Each additional term evaluated corresponds to one additional fractional position becoming realized, the same way each additional integer position becomes realized as whole numbers grow. If the system has realized fractional positions negative one through negative three, three terms beyond the integer part have been added to e’s representation. Expanding the integer scope — adding position four, position five, and so on — does not by itself add any terms to e’s series; that capacity exists for whole-number magnitude, not for the precision of constants like e. The value of e at any given fractional scope is the exact partial sum of the defining series realized to that depth.

This is not an approximation in the conventional sense. At any fractional scope, the value is exact. The system carries no rounding error. When the fractional scope expands, the representation of e gains one additional digit, and that digit is exact. The system always knows how many terms it has realized, so it always knows the exact value of e at that depth.

Compare this to how a conventional computer stores π. A floating-point representation carries roughly sixteen significant digits. Those sixteen digits are a fixed-width approximation, and all precision beyond those digits is silently discarded. The system does not know what it has lost. It has no way to recover the discarded information. When calculations accumulate, the truncation propagates invisibly.

In the factorial basis, the situation is different. Every digit of e that is realized at the current fractional scope is present and exact. The system knows the depth. It knows how many terms of e it has realized. It knows that additional terms exist beyond the current depth. Nothing is silently discarded. The precision boundary is visible and explicit.

Why the Factorial Basis Is the Right Representation

Now the remarkable structure becomes visible, once integer and fractional positions are kept distinct. Look at the terms of the series for e again. The zeroth term is one divided by zero-factorial, which is one. The first term is one divided by one-factorial, which is also one. These two terms sum to two, and two is the integer part of e: in the factorial basis, two is the configuration with digit one at integer position two and digit zero at integer position one, [d2=1, d1=0].

The remaining terms are fractional. The n-th term, for n equal to two, three, four, and so on, is one divided by n-factorial. Recall from the fractional positions introduced for fractions: position negative j has weight one divided by (j+1)-factorial. Setting j equal to n minus one, position negative (n minus one) has weight one divided by n-factorial — exactly the weight of the n-th term. The n-th term of the series and the (n minus one)-th fractional position share the same weight; a term’s contribution of one divided by n-factorial is realized as a single digit of one at that fractional position, because position negative (n minus one) allows digits from zero up to (n minus one), and one is always within that range once n is at least two.

The conclusion follows directly, restricted correctly to the fractional part. Each term of the series for e, from the second term onward, maps to exactly one fractional digit position. The second term corresponds to fractional position negative one. The third term corresponds to fractional position negative two. And so on without exception. No term overlaps with any other. No term falls between positions.

When you write e in the factorial basis, the integer part is two, [d2=1, d1=0], and the fractional digit at every fractional position is one: position negative one holds one, position negative two holds one, position negative three holds one, and this pattern continues for every fractional position realized so far. The factorial basis representation of e is the integer configuration for two, followed by the fractional sequence one, one, one, one, extending as far as the current fractional scope allows.

The series definition and the fractional representation are the same thing. They are two ways of saying that e’s integer part accounts for the first two terms, and every term after that places exactly one unit at the next fractional position. One way says this as an algebraic sum. The other says it as a sequence of fractional digit values. Both descriptions are exact. Neither is an approximation of the other.

This is the factorial convergence advantage. For a series whose terms have factorial denominators and whose numerators are simple enough to normalize to a single digit at each position, each term maps exactly to one digit position. There is no rounding, no accumulation of error, no truncation, within the part of the series this correspondence covers.

Constants as Members of the System

The algebraic system entity now holds four named state machines. The variable x tracks one state. The variable y tracks another. The relationship machine z connects them by the rule z equals x plus y. The variable e holds the state reached by expanding its defining series to the current fractional scope.

All four are members of the same entity. All four follow the same rules. The no-change principle applies to e exactly as it applies to x and y, with the same scoping established in earlier chapters: if e already holds the configuration that adding zero or multiplying by one would require, no transition occurs; if some other relationship had previously left e in a different configuration, the relevant relationship machine would still need to drive it back, and that would be a real transition. For a constant whose defining relationship is never reassigned, this distinction rarely surfaces in practice, but the principle is the same one that governs every other variable.

The variable π follows the same pattern. It is a state machine assigned a geometric or series-based relationship. At any fractional scope, it holds the exact value of that relationship realized to that depth. The variable defined as the square root of two is a state machine assigned the constraint that its square equals two. The value it holds at any scope is the exact solution realized within that scope.

Every constant in mathematics is a variable with a definition. The definition is a relationship state machine. The variable is expanded to the required depth. The value is exact at that depth. Nothing is special. Nothing is imported from outside. The algebraic system entity contains constants the same way it contains every other state machine.

Convergence by Construction

The factorial convergence advantage for e extends to a specific, nameable class of series: those whose n-th term is bounded in magnitude by some fixed constant divided by n-factorial. For such a series, every term’s magnitude is at most that constant divided by n-factorial, and because the sum of one divided by n-factorial over all n converges to e itself, the sum of any series bounded this way converges as well, by direct comparison. This is a real guarantee, and it covers a useful range of series, including the series for e, for sine and cosine evaluated at a fixed value, and for many other factorial-denominator series with reasonably behaved numerators.

The guarantee is not unconditional. A series with factorial denominators does not converge merely because its denominators are factorials; the numerator matters. Consider a series whose n-th term is n-factorial divided by n-factorial. Every term equals exactly one, regardless of n, and a sum of infinitely many ones does not converge to any finite value. The factorial denominator alone did nothing to prevent this, because the numerator grew at exactly the same rate. The guarantee requires that the numerator stay bounded while the denominator grows; it is the relationship between the two that produces convergence, not the denominator in isolation.

This matters because the conventional framework requires proving convergence separately for every series, using tests such as the ratio test, the comparison test, or the root test, precisely because a series with a factorial-looking term is not automatically safe. The factorial basis simplifies this for the specific, bounded-numerator class described above: once a series is known to have a bounded numerator over a factorial denominator, convergence is guaranteed by comparison to e, without a separate test for that series. Series outside this class still require the same scrutiny conventional analysis has always applied.

When a numerator is not a simple bounded constant — when it is itself variable, signed, or larger than a position’s digit bound — the raw coefficient is not automatically a single valid digit at its corresponding position. Such a coefficient must be normalized across positions the same way an oversized integer digit is normalized by carrying, before the series can be read off as a clean sequence of position digits. The term-to-position correspondence described earlier in this chapter is cleanest exactly when each coefficient already fits its position’s digit bound without needing this additional normalization, as is the case for every term of e’s own series.

Finally, a finite partial sum realized at some fractional scope is an exact value at that scope, and it is a different thing from the infinite sum the series defines. The gap between the two — the sum of all terms beyond the current scope — is visible and boundable in the factorial basis, because the remaining terms are bounded by the same comparison to e used above. This is a meaningful advantage over a floating-point truncation, whose discarded remainder is invisible and unbounded from the representation alone. It is not the same as claiming the finite partial sum already equals the infinite value; it does not, except in the limit.

Closing Part 2

This chapter completes the second part of the book. The four chapters of Part 2 have built the algebraic system entity piece by piece. The simplest possible system held one variable and nothing else. A second variable was added, and a relationship between them was introduced. Now a constant has joined the entity as a variable with a fixed defining relationship.

The structure is now clear: an entity holds names, values state machines, relationship state machines, and constraint state machines. Variables, relationships, constants, and constraints are all instances of this structure. They behave differently only because different events have been applied and different relationship machines have been assigned. No special category exists. No primitive must be accepted without explanation.

Part 3 turns from structure to operation. What does it mean, inside this system, to add two values? What does it mean to subtract, to multiply, to divide? These are not external procedures applied to numbers from outside. They are relationship state machines that connect named state machines and specify what transitions must follow. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and more complex operations are all the same kind of thing. Part 3 builds each one from the same foundation that Part 2 established.

Part 3

Operations as Relationship State Machines

Chapter 9Addition as State Alignment

11 min read

Addition is taught as the first operation. Before subtraction, before multiplication, certainly before fractions or calculus, there is addition. This priority makes sense: it is the simplest operation to demonstrate, and it connects most directly to counting. When you have three apples and someone gives you two more, you now have five apples. The demonstration is tangible and convincing.

But the familiarity of addition is precisely what makes it worth examining carefully. Its apparent simplicity has concealed what it actually does. Addition is not a procedure performed on two separate numbers to produce a third. Addition is the alignment of two state machines within the same scope, followed by reading the combined configuration. The result is not a new number calculated from two inputs. It is the state that both machines occupy together.

This is not a trivial rephrasing. Understanding addition as state alignment reveals why carry behaves the way it does, why adding zero does nothing, and why certain additions require scope expansion before they can be completed.

Two State Machines, One Configuration

Return to the algebraic system holding the variables x, y, and z. The relationship state machine for z says z equals x plus y. This relationship is not a formula sitting in the margin. It is a constraint inside the entity saying: the combined configuration of x and y determines the state of z.

What does “combined configuration” mean? Variables are state machines occupying positions in the shared factorial-basis space. When x holds a value, x is in a particular state: its values state machine is at a specific position in the factorial-basis representation. When y holds a value, y is similarly positioned.

Adding x and y means asking: what state does the combined occupancy of both state machines represent? The answer is the state you reach by placing both configurations in the same space and reading the result. The two machines are not combined externally. They are aligned within the shared space the entity already maintains.

Consider x at state two and y at state three. Position 1 has weight 1! and holds digits zero or one. Position 2 has weight 2! and holds digits zero, one, or two. In the factorial basis, two is the configuration where position 2 holds one and position 1 holds zero: [d2=1, d1=0]. Three is the configuration where position 2 holds one and position 1 holds one: [d2=1, d1=1]. Adding them means placing both configurations in the same space and reading the combined occupancy at each position.

At position 1: x contributes zero; y contributes one. Combined occupancy is one.

At position 2: x contributes one; y contributes one. Combined occupancy is two.

Position 1 can hold zero or one, and the combined occupancy of one fits within that range. Position 2 can hold zero, one, or two, and the combined occupancy of two fits as well. No position’s maximum has been exceeded. The aligned configuration is [d2=2, d1=1], which represents the state five. Two plus three equals five, and this particular alignment required no carry at all, because neither position’s combined occupancy exceeded its maximum.

Carry as Scope Expansion

Not every alignment is this convenient. Consider adding three to itself. Three is [d2=1, d1=1]. Placing two copies of three in the same space gives a provisional, not-yet-normalized occupancy of two at position 1 and two at position 2: [d2=2, d1=2].

Position 1 can hold at most one. A combined occupancy of two exceeds that maximum by one unit. In conventional arithmetic, carry is presented as a procedure: if the digit exceeds the base, write the remainder and add one to the next column. The rule is correct but the explanation is mechanical. It does not say why the digit exceeded its limit or what the excess means.

In the algebraic system, carry is a normalization event grounded in the factorial weights themselves. Each digit position has a defined maximum occupancy. When combined occupancy at a position exceeds that maximum, the excess is exchanged for exactly one unit at the next position, because one unit at position i+1 is worth exactly i+1 units at position i: position i+1’s weight is (i+1)! = (i+1) × i!, which is i+1 times position i’s weight.

At position 1, the maximum is one. The combined occupancy of two exceeds the maximum by one unit. That one unit converts to one unit at position 2, because position 2’s weight (2!) is exactly 2 times position 1’s weight (1!). Position 1 returns to zero. Position 2’s occupancy becomes its original two plus the carried one, giving a provisional three: [d2=3, d1=0].

But position 2’s maximum is also exceeded: three is one more than its maximum of two. The same exchange happens again. One unit at position 2 converts to one unit at position 3, because position 3’s weight (3! = 6) is exactly 3 times position 2’s weight (2! = 2). Position 2 returns to zero. Position 3, which had held no digit before this addition, now holds one.

The fully normalized result is [d3=1, d2=0, d1=0], which represents the state six. Three plus three equals six, and reaching that result required two carry events in sequence, each one exchanging an overflowing position’s excess for a single unit at the next position.

This is not a coincidence, and it is not a rule imposed from outside. The structure of the factorial odometer ensures that when two states are aligned and carried correctly, the result is the state the odometer reaches after advancing by the sum of the two input values. The carry is not a correction procedure applied to a calculation that went wrong. Each carry is the natural behavior of a position whose combined occupancy became too large to hold directly; the excess is exchanged for a unit at the next position, and that position absorbs it.

In this example, the carry that reached position 3 activated a position that had held no digit before, which is a genuine case of scope expanding to a new dimension. But not every carry does this. Consider seven plus seven. Seven is [d3=1, d2=0, d1=1], and position 3 is already active before the addition. Adding seven to itself gives a provisional [d3=2, d2=0, d1=2]. Position 1 overflows and carries one unit into position 2, giving [d3=2, d2=1, d1=0]. Position 2’s new occupancy of one does not exceed its maximum of two, so no further carry occurs, and position 3’s occupancy of two does not exceed its maximum of three either. The result is [d3=2, d2=1, d1=0], which represents fourteen — and no new position was activated, because position 3 was already realized before this addition began. Carry is always a normalization exchange between adjacent positions; it is scope expansion only when the carry activates a position that had not previously held a digit. When the carry stays within already-active positions, it changes their digits without extending how many positions the variable occupies.

The Odometer Perspective

There is another way to see this. Adding three to two is the same as advancing the odometer three times from the state representing two.

Start the odometer at state two: [d2=1, d1=0]. Advance once: position 1 moves from zero to one, which is within its maximum. The odometer is at state three: [d2=1, d1=1]. Advance again: position 1 would move from one to two, but two exceeds position 1’s maximum of one. Position 1 resets to zero and the overflow carries into position 2. Position 2 was at one; it advances to two, which is within its maximum. The odometer is now at state four: [d2=2, d1=0]. Advance once more: position 1 moves from zero to one, within its maximum. The odometer is at state five: [d2=2, d1=1].

Two plus three equals five. But notice something the direct alignment calculation did not show: this odometer trace required one carry, during the second advance, when position 1 overflowed and position 2 absorbed the excess. The state-alignment calculation in the previous section reached the same result, [d2=2, d1=1], with no carry at all, because it combined both configurations’ digits directly rather than advancing one unit at a time. Both methods agree on the destination. They do not always take the same route to it. Advancing one unit at a time can pass through carries that a direct alignment of the two starting configurations never needs, because the direct alignment only normalizes the final combined occupancy, not every intermediate step along the way.

The carry events an odometer trace passes through are the same kind of event the odometer emits whenever a position fills during ordinary counting. Addition by direct alignment and addition by repeated single-unit advance always agree on the result; they can differ in how many carry events occur along the way.

Adding Zero

Now consider adding zero to x, where x is in the state representing five. The intention is to compute x plus zero.

Zero is the inferred default. Zero means no state machine has been activated for a variable. If no event has moved a variable, no values state machine has been realized for it. There is no second state machine to align with x.

The relationship state machine for z checks what the combined configuration of x and the zero variable looks like. The zero variable has no realized state machine. There is nothing to combine. The configuration of x is unchanged. The state machine for z must reflect the combined occupancy of x and the zero variable. The zero variable occupies no positions. The combined occupancy is the occupancy of x alone.

No transition has occurred. The values state machine for x has not moved. If z had no prior realized state, z’s first realized state is x’s configuration. If z already held some other value from a previous evaluation of this same relationship, the relationship machine would need to transition z to match x’s configuration; that would be a real transition in z, driven by the relationship, not by any change in x. But in the case considered here, nothing about x’s own configuration changed, so no scope expansion and no carry occurred in x. Nothing changed in x.

This is the no-change principle, applied directly to addition. A transition that produces no state change is indistinguishable from no transition at all. Adding zero is not an operation that happens to return the same value. Adding zero is not an operation on x. No state machine for x transitioned. The zero variable had no realized state machine, so there was nothing to align, and x’s own state remained exactly where it was.

This distinction matters for how the system is understood. If adding zero were an operation that returned the input unchanged, the system would need to register the attempt, perform the alignment, discover the zero, and confirm the result. That would require real processing. In the algebraic system, no such processing occurs. Zero has no realized state machine. The alignment step finds nothing to align. The existing state of x is already the result.

What Addition Actually Does

Looking at the structure so far: addition aligns two realized state machines in the shared factorial-basis space and reads the combined configuration. When combined occupancy at any position exceeds that position’s maximum, the system generates a carry event that normalizes the result; the carry is a genuine scope expansion only when it activates a position that previously held no digit. When one of the values is zero, no state machine exists to align, no transition occurs, and the no-change principle applies.

Addition is not defined as putting two numbers together and computing the result. Addition is the combined occupancy of two state machines in the shared space. The result is already present in the structure once both state machines are positioned. The carry is already determined by the positions’ maximum values. The structure encodes the answer; nothing is computed afterward.

This also clarifies the role of the relationship z = x + y as a relationship state machine inside the entity. The relationship machine does not perform a calculation when consulted. It maintains the constraint that z must always reflect the combined configuration of x and y. When x or y receives an event that changes its state, the relationship machine applies whatever scope expansion events are necessary and moves z to the new combined configuration. The constraint is active and continuous, not invoked only when a result is requested.

Part 3 Continues

Addition opened Part 3 because it is the operation closest to counting. Advancing the odometer is counting. Adding two values is advancing the odometer from one established state using a second established state as the count of steps. Carry is a normalization exchange between adjacent positions, and it is scope expansion specifically when it activates a position the odometer has not yet reached. Both appear during ordinary counting. The connection is complete.

The next chapter examines subtraction. Subtraction introduces one element not present in addition: direction. Moving a state machine backward through configurations requires tracking which way the machine is traveling. Negation is not a separate number type or an extension of the system. It is a relationship state machine expressing that transitions are moving in the reverse direction. The scope, the positions, and the factorial basis are unchanged. What changes is the orientation of the transitions.

Chapter 10Subtraction and Negation

12 min read

When students first encounter negative numbers, something in the presentation typically shifts. Up to that point, numbers had been concrete and countable: apples, steps, books. Then a teacher draws a number line extending in both directions, places zero in the middle, and says there are numbers to the left of zero. These are called negative. To subtract is to move left. To add is to move right.

The picture is memorable and it works for simple problems. But it quietly introduces a structural claim that the presentation never examines: that positive and negative numbers are two different kinds of numbers, living on opposite sides of a dividing point, with zero as the boundary between them. A student who later studies abstract algebra will discover this was a convenient simplification. A student who does not study abstract algebra will carry the picture for the rest of their life.

The algebraic system offers a different account. Subtraction is addition with a directional constraint. Negation is not a new number type. It is a relationship state machine expressing that a variable’s transitions are running in the reverse direction through the same states they would otherwise occupy. No new numbers are introduced. No extension of the system is required. The scope, the positions, and the factorial basis remain unchanged. What changes is the orientation of the transitions.

Direction as a Property of Transitions

The previous chapter established that addition aligns two state machines in the shared factorial-basis space and reads the combined configuration. The odometer advances forward: from any state, the next state is produced by incrementing the lowest position that has capacity remaining, carrying when a position fills, and expanding scope when every position in the current dimension is full.

Forward is the default. But the odometer can also run backward. From any state, the previous state is produced by decrementing the lowest position that holds a nonzero value, borrowing from the next position when a position would drop below zero. The sequence of configurations is the same sequence the odometer produces going forward; the direction of travel through that sequence is reversed.

The states themselves are unchanged by this reversal. State three is still the configuration it always was, regardless of whether the odometer reached it by advancing from state two or retreating from state four. The configuration belongs to the state. The direction belongs to the transition.

This distinction is the core of what negation means. A negative number is not a state with different properties from a positive number. It is a state in a values state machine whose transitions are oriented in the reverse direction. Negative five and positive five occupy the same state in the factorial-basis space. What differs is the orientation relationship attached to the variable.

Negation as a Relationship State Machine

The algebraic system represents negation by attaching an orientation relationship state machine to a variable. This machine has two states: forward and reverse. When orientation is forward, events that advance the variable move it toward larger configurations. When orientation is reverse, the same advancing events move it toward smaller configurations, and what would otherwise be a carry event becomes a borrow event.

Consider the variable x in the state representing five. The orientation machine for x is in the forward state. Apply a negation relationship: the orientation machine transitions from forward to reverse. The variable x remains in the configuration representing five. Nothing about the configuration has changed. But the meaning of future transitions has changed. Advances to x will now move it toward smaller states rather than larger ones. The variable x is now negative five.

Notice what did not happen. A new number called negative five was not created and placed on the left side of zero. The variable x did not travel across some boundary to a mirror-image region. The state machine for x is still in the same configuration. The orientation relationship machine changed state. That is all.

The conventional number line represents this as a point to the left of zero, and that representation is a spatial metaphor for the orientation relationship. The metaphor is useful. It is also misleading, because it suggests that five and negative five are two separate entities with zero between them, rather than one entity in two possible orientations. Students who struggle with the transition from positive to negative numbers are struggling, in part, because the conventional presentation offers them a picture that implies a discontinuity where there is none.

Subtraction as Addition with Orientation Set

With negation defined as an orientation relationship, subtraction follows without introducing any new mechanism. Subtracting y from x is adding x and y, with y’s orientation set to reverse.

The combined configuration is computed the same way as ordinary addition: align both state machines in the shared factorial-basis space and read the combined occupancy at each position. The difference is that y’s contributions run in the reverse direction. Where y’s forward contribution at some position would add to the combined occupancy, y’s reverse contribution subtracts from it.

When the combined occupancy at a position would drop below zero, a borrow event occurs. The next position lends one unit of its own occupancy to the current position, and because the next position’s weight is a whole multiple of the current position’s weight, that one unit converts into several units at the current, lower-weighted position. This is the symmetric counterpart of the carry event from addition: carry occurs when combined forward occupancy exceeds a position’s maximum, and the excess converts into a single unit at the next position; borrow occurs when combined occupancy drops below the position’s minimum, and a single unit from the next position converts into several units at the current position. As with carry, borrow is a genuine scope contraction specifically when it empties a position that had held a digit back to its default; when a borrow only redistributes digits among positions that remain active, it is normalization, not contraction.

Consider subtracting three from five. Five is [d2=2, d1=1]. Three is [d2=1, d1=1], with orientation set to reverse. At position 1: five contributes one; three in reverse contributes negative one. Combined occupancy is zero. At position 2: five contributes two; three in reverse contributes negative one. Combined occupancy is one. Neither position drops below its minimum, so no borrow is needed. The result is [d2=1, d1=0], which represents two. Five minus three equals two, and this alignment required no borrow, for the same reason the earlier addition of two and three required no carry: the combined occupancy at every position stayed within range.

Not every subtraction is this convenient. Consider subtracting seven from eighteen. Eighteen is [d3=3, d2=0, d1=0]. Seven is [d3=1, d2=0, d1=1], with orientation set to reverse. Before any borrowing, the combined occupancy is negative one at position 1 (eighteen contributes zero; seven in reverse contributes negative one), zero at position 2 (both contribute zero), and two at position 3 (eighteen contributes three; seven in reverse contributes negative one).

Position 1 holds negative one, below its minimum of zero. A borrow is needed. Position 2 lends one of its units to position 1; because position 2’s weight (2!) is exactly twice position 1’s weight (1!), that one unit becomes two units at position 1. Position 1 becomes negative one plus two, which is one. Position 2, having lent a unit, decreases by one, from zero to negative one.

Position 2 now holds negative one, below its own minimum. A further borrow is needed. Position 3 lends one of its units to position 2; because position 3’s weight (3! = 6) is exactly three times position 2’s weight (2! = 2), that one unit becomes three units at position 2. Position 2 becomes negative one plus three, which is two. Position 3, having lent a unit, decreases by one, from two to one.

The fully normalized result is [d3=1, d2=2, d1=1], which represents one times six plus two times two plus one times one, or six plus four plus one, which is eleven. Eighteen minus seven equals eleven, reached through a borrow that cascaded from position 1 through position 2 to position 3. This matches the worked example in Appendix B, section B.9, which carries the same two inputs through the identical borrow sequence.

Subtraction does not require a separate algorithm. It uses the same alignment process as addition, with the orientation relationship determining the direction of contribution at each position.

The Scope of the Result

One consequence of this structure is that subtraction can produce a result in a state where the orientation relationship is active on the result variable rather than on the inputs. When you subtract a larger value from a smaller one, the combined reverse occupancy exceeds the forward occupancy of the first variable. No configuration in the forward direction can represent the result.

The system does not treat this as an error. The result is a configuration in the same factorial-basis space with the orientation of the result variable set to reverse. Subtracting five from three gives the configuration representing two, with orientation set to reverse. That is negative two.

The result is exact and complete. The system knows the magnitude (the configuration representing two) and the orientation (reverse). Both are carried in the representation. When the result is used in a subsequent operation, the orientation relationship on the result variable participates in that operation’s alignment process. No special handling is required. No distinction between “positive arithmetic” and “negative arithmetic” exists. The orientation machine is part of the variable, and every operation treats it the same way.

Subtracting Zero

The previous chapter established that adding zero is not an operation, because zero has no realized state machine. Nothing exists to align with the other variable. The no-change principle applies: no state transition occurs.

Subtracting zero follows the same reasoning. To subtract zero from x, the system would set the orientation of the zero variable to reverse and align it with x. But the zero variable has no realized state machine. Setting orientation on an unrealized machine makes no difference; there is nothing to orient. The alignment step finds nothing to align. The configuration of x is unchanged.

Subtracting zero is not an operation that returns the input unchanged. Subtracting zero is not an operation. The no-change principle applies in exactly the same form it did for addition. The mechanism is identical; only the orientation setting differs, and that setting has no effect when the variable being oriented is unrealized.

What Negation Is Not

It is worth being direct about what this analysis rules out. Negation is not a separate dimension. Adding a negative number to a system does not expand the scope or add a new kind of position to the factorial basis. The same positions that represent positive states represent negative states; orientation determines the direction of traversal through those positions.

Negation is also not a new number type that requires extending the number system. The conventional story of mathematics is one of progressive extension: first the natural numbers, then the integers to include negatives, then the rationals to include fractions, then the reals, then the complex numbers. Each extension is presented as a response to an equation that the previous system could not solve. Each extension requires accepting a new kind of number.

In the algebraic system, none of these extensions involve new numbers. They involve new relationship state machines. Negation is an orientation relationship. Fractions are a scope-proportion relationship, which the next chapter examines. Complex numbers are a second orthogonal dimension in the values state machine, which a later chapter examines. In each case, the numbers are the same states they always were. The relationships between them are what changes.

This is a significant structural difference from the conventional account. It means that a student who understands positive states in the factorial basis already has everything needed to understand negative states, fractional states, and complex states. No new primitives are introduced. No new special cases are added. The system grows by acquiring new relationship state machines, not by expanding the inventory of number types.

The Relationship in the Running Example

Return to the algebraic system entity holding x, y, z, and e. The relationship machine for z says z equals x plus y. That relationship is directionally neutral: it combines the configurations of x and y with both in forward orientation.

To subtract y from x, the system creates a new relationship machine that specifies z equals x plus y with y’s orientation set to reverse. The relationship machine for this operation is a modified form of the addition relationship, carrying an orientation constraint on one of its inputs. The structure of the entity is the same. The relationship machine is more specific.

Nothing about x or y themselves changes. Neither variable acquires a permanent negation. The negation is a property of the relationship machine, specifying how y contributes to the combined configuration when computing z. If z were later defined by a different relationship, y would participate in that relationship without the reverse orientation.

This separation between the variable and the orientation of its contribution to a specific relationship is another instance of the general principle: properties belong to relationships, not to the entities those relationships connect.

Toward Fractions

Subtraction closes the discussion of directional operations. The next chapter examines fractions, which introduce a different kind of scope relationship. A fraction is not a number between two integers on the number line. It is a relationship expressing that one state is a constrained proportion of another, within a scope large enough to contain both. The structure that makes fractions natural in the algebraic system is the same structure that made carry and borrow natural: the factorial basis, where every position carries exact divisibility information from the moment the odometer generates the state.

Chapter 11Fractions as Scope Constraints

13 min read

Fractions are the first place where many students begin to lose confidence in mathematics. Up through addition and subtraction, numbers behave like things that can be counted and compared. Then fractions arrive, and suddenly numbers have parts. Three divided by four is written as a fraction, but it does not look like a number. It looks like a division problem that has not been finished. Students are told to treat it as a number anyway, and the rules for operating on fractions are presented as procedures to be memorized rather than consequences of a structure to be understood.

The difficulty is not with fractions themselves. The difficulty is with the conventional account of what a fraction is. A fraction is presented as a number between two integers, living in the spaces on the number line that integers leave empty. This account is not wrong, but it is structurally incomplete. It describes where fractions land on the number line without saying what they are.

In the algebraic system, a fraction is a relationship state machine. It expresses that one variable is a constrained proportion of another, within a scope large enough to hold both. No new kind of number is introduced. The scope expands to accommodate the relationship, and the fraction is exact within that scope.

What Division Is Asking

Before examining fractions, it helps to examine the question that division asks. Division is not the inverse of multiplication in some abstract algebraic sense. Division asks a specific question about the structure of the current state: which earlier state is the current state a multiple of?

The odometer generates states in sequence. Every state the odometer reaches has a position in that sequence. Some states are reachable by advancing from zero by the same amount multiple times: state six can be reached by three advances of two, or two advances of three, or six advances of one. The question division asks is: starting from zero, which uniform advance size would land exactly on this state?

When the advance size divides evenly into the current state, the answer is a whole number. When it does not divide evenly, something remains after the uniform advances are exhausted. That remainder is the residue, and it is already visible in the factorial basis representation of the current state.

This is the first important structural point. Division does not compute a relationship that was previously unknown. Division reads a relationship that the factorial basis already carries. The digit structure of any state encodes its divisibility relationships. To divide is to read those relationships from the representation, not to perform a fresh calculation.

The Residue Already Carried

Chapter 4 established that residues are properties carried in the factorial basis representation from the moment the odometer generates a state. Every digit position corresponds to a factorial boundary, and the presence or absence of a digit at that position carries direct divisibility information.

Now connect this to division. When you divide state twelve by four, you are asking whether four advances of a uniform size would land on twelve. Four divides evenly into twelve, so the answer is three. The relationship between twelve and four is already visible in the factorial basis representation of twelve, because twelve’s digits encode which multiples it contains.

When you divide a state whose divisibility is not exact, the residue is also visible in the representation. The factorial basis shows not only which divisors divide evenly but how much remains when they do not. No search is required. No repeated subtraction is needed. The structure reports the relationship directly.

This is why the factorial basis is the natural home for fractions. When a fraction’s denominator evenly divides a factorial boundary within the current scope, the fraction resolves exactly. The scope already contains the structure needed to express the relationship. No approximation is required, and no new digit positions are needed beyond those the scope already maintains.

Fractions as Scope-Proportion Relationships

A fraction one-third does not name a point between zero and one on some extended number line. It names a relationship: the variable that holds this value is in a state that stands in a one-to-three proportion to the full scope at its current dimension.

The factorial basis represents this proportion with a second sequence of positions, extending below the units position rather than above it. Each integer position i, for i equal to one, two, three, and so on, has weight i-factorial and digit range zero through i. Each fractional position, written as position negative j for j equal to one, two, three, and so on, has weight one divided by (j+1)-factorial and digit range zero through j. Position negative one has weight one-half and can hold zero or one. Position negative two has weight one-sixth and can hold zero, one, or two. Position negative three has weight one twenty-fourth and can hold zero, one, two, or three. A fractional value between zero and one is the sum of each fractional digit times its position’s weight, exactly as an integer value is the sum of each integer digit times its position’s weight.

One-half is the configuration with digit one at position negative one and zero at every position after it: one times one-half equals one-half. This resolves exactly at the first fractional position, the same way the number one resolves exactly at the first integer position.

One-third is the configuration with digit zero at position negative one and digit two at position negative two, with zero at every position after that: zero times one-half, plus two times one-sixth, equals two-sixths, which is one-third. This resolves exactly at the second fractional position. Two at position negative two is the maximum digit that position can hold, confirming that one-third needs the full capacity of that position and nothing beyond it.

Adding one-half and one-third means aligning their fractional digits the same way integer addition aligns integer digits. Position negative one: one-half contributes one; one-third contributes zero. Combined occupancy is one, within position negative one’s maximum of one. Position negative two: one-half contributes zero; one-third contributes two. Combined occupancy is two, within position negative two’s maximum of two. Neither position overflows, so no carry is needed. The result is digit one at position negative one and digit two at position negative two: one times one-half, plus two times one-sixth, equals one-half plus one-third, which is five-sixths. One-half plus one-third equals five-sixths, confirmed by the same alignment process Chapter 9 used for whole numbers, applied to fractional positions instead of integer ones.

Five-thirds is greater than one, so it has both an integer part and a fractional part: the integer part is one, represented at integer position one, and the fractional part is two-thirds, represented as digit one at fractional position negative one and digit one at fractional position negative two, since one-half plus one-sixth equals four-sixths, which is two-thirds. A variable’s full configuration spans both its integer positions and its fractional positions simultaneously; the two sequences meet at the units place and extend in opposite directions.

For this to be exact, the scope must extend far enough into the fractional positions to express the proportion completely. If the current fractional scope covers only position negative one, the fraction one-third cannot be expressed exactly; its full value requires position negative two as well. The fractional scope must expand the same way the integer scope does, one position at a time, and each new fractional position provides finer precision rather than greater range.

Fractions whose denominators evenly divide some (j+1)-factorial are always exactly representable once the fractional scope reaches position negative j. One-half is exactly representable at fractional scope one, because two divides two-factorial. One-third is exactly representable at fractional scope two, because three divides three-factorial, which equals six. One-sixth is already exactly representable at the same fractional scope, for the same reason.

This is why the factorial basis handles certain fractions with exceptional precision. The fractions whose denominators divide a small factorial resolve exactly within a few fractional positions, with no residue, no rounding, and no further scope expansion needed beyond that point. A fraction’s stored relationship — its numerator and denominator, or equivalently its exact finite digit sequence — is a different thing from a truncated digit sequence that stops before the exact point is reached; the factorial basis keeps the distinction visible, because the scope depth at which the digits terminate is explicit and known, not silently discarded.

Fractions That Do Not Resolve at Factorial Boundaries

Some fractions do not correspond to divisors of any small factorial. One-seventh, for example, requires fractional positions down to position negative six, because seven first divides a factorial at seven-factorial, which is five thousand forty, and position negative six carries weight one divided by seven-factorial. The fraction one-seventh is exactly representable once the fractional scope reaches that position, but the scope required is large compared to one-half or one-third.

For fractions of this kind, the algebraic system handles them the same way it handles the constant e: the scope expands to the required depth, and the value is exact within that scope. The relationship machine carries the numerator and denominator, and as the scope expands, the representation gains additional precision. At any scope, the representation is the exact value of the fraction within that scope, not a rounded approximation.

This differs structurally from floating-point arithmetic, where the representation is a fixed-width approximation and the loss of precision is invisible and irreversible. In the factorial basis, the scope is explicit, the precision is exact within the scope, and additional scope provides additional exact digits. The boundary between what is representable and what requires more scope is visible and known.

Division in the Running Example

Return to the algebraic system entity holding x, y, z, and e. The relationship machine for z has defined z as x plus y. Now consider a different relationship: z equals x divided by y.

This relationship machine specifies that z holds the state representing the proportion of x to y within the current scope. When x is in state six and y is in state three, z must be in the state representing two, because six contains three exactly twice. The relationship machine reads the divisibility information from the factorial basis representations of x and y and determines z’s state.

When x is in state five and y is in state three, z cannot be expressed as a whole-number state within the current integer scope. Five does not contain three exactly. The relationship machine expands z’s fractional scope to positions negative one and negative two, and z is assigned the exact configuration for five-thirds: integer digit one at position one, fractional digit one at position negative one, and fractional digit one at position negative two. Within that expanded scope, this value is exact.

The relationship machine for division is not an algorithm that searches for the right answer through trial and error. It reads the structure that the factorial basis already carries and performs whatever scope expansion is needed to express the result exactly. The divisibility information was already present in the representations of x and y. The relationship machine uses it directly.

Dividing by One

The previous two chapters examined adding zero and subtracting zero as cases where the no-change principle applies. Division by one deserves the same examination.

Dividing x by one asks: x stands in what proportion to a one-unit scope? The answer is immediate. One unit of a one-unit scope is the entire scope. The proportion is x to one, which is x itself. The required configuration for z is the same configuration x already holds.

Whether this produces a transition in z depends on what z held before, exactly as with the identity cases examined in multiplication. If z already held x’s configuration — because this is the first evaluation of the relationship, or because the previous divisor also produced this result — the relationship machine finds that the required state and the current state already agree, and no transition occurs: the no-change principle applies. If z held some other configuration, because the relationship had just been evaluated with a different divisor, the relationship machine still drives z to x’s configuration, and that is a real transition in z, even though x itself never moved.

Dividing by one, like multiplying by one, never forces the untouched input to move, and it leaves z unchanged exactly when z already matches x’s configuration. This is the same conclusion that applied to adding zero and subtracting zero, correctly scoped to the variable actually being written rather than to the operation as a whole.

What Fractions Are Not

The conventional account presents fractions as numbers filling in the gaps between integers. That account implies that the number system has gaps, that integers are the primary entities, and that fractions are secondary entities inserted to fill the holes. The presentation reinforces the idea that fractions require special procedures separate from integer arithmetic.

The algebraic system has no gaps to fill. The factorial-basis space is not a discrete set of points with empty regions between them. It is a structure of positions and occupancies, and the scope determines what states can be represented. Fractions are not interpolated between integers. They are states that require greater scope to represent, and the scope expands to accommodate them.

When the scope expands to represent one-third, no new kind of number has been added to the system. The same positions that represented integers now have finer resolution within the expanded scope. The integer states are still present; they now share space with additional states that the expanded scope makes distinguishable. The integers have not moved. The scope has grown, and more states are visible within it.

This also means that the rules for operating on fractions are not separate rules. They are the same addition and comparison operations applied to fractional positions instead of integer ones. Adding one-half and one-third is the same alignment process Chapter 9 used for whole numbers, applied once the fractional scope has expanded to position negative two, since three divides three-factorial, which equals six. Within that fractional scope, both fractions resolve exactly and their sum, five-sixths, is computed by the same state-alignment process as any other addition.

Into Multiplication

Fractions close the examination of proportion-based relationships in the algebraic system. The next chapter turns to multiplication. Multiplication might seem like it should have come before fractions, since it is typically taught earlier. But in the algebraic system, the structure of multiplication is most clearly visible after fractions have been established, because multiplication involves combining the dimensional structure of two states rather than reading their proportional relationship within a shared scope.

Multiplication creates a higher-dimensional configuration from two existing configurations. Understanding that fractions are scope-proportion relationships within a single shared space makes it easier to see what is different about multiplication: it crosses dimensions rather than working within one. That difference, and what it implies about multiplying by one and multiplying by zero, is what the next chapter examines.

Chapter 12Multiplication as Dimensional Expansion

12 min read

Students are taught that multiplication is repeated addition. Three times four is the same as adding three four times. That equivalence is arithmetically correct: both produce twelve. It works as a teaching bridge, because addition is already familiar and the shortcut is immediately useful.

But repeated addition and multiplication are not the same operation. They produce the same result for whole numbers, which is why the equivalence holds as far as the curriculum needs it to hold. The problems appear later: when multiplication is extended to fractions, to negative numbers, to complex numbers, and to dimensional objects like vectors and matrices, the “repeated addition” definition stops working. The teacher then introduces new rules for each extension, and students are left with a patchwork of special cases where a unified account would have served them better.

The algebraic system provides the unified account. Multiplication is not repeated addition. Multiplication combines the dimensional structure of two state machines to produce a higher-dimensional configuration. The result occupies a region of the state space that neither input could reach alone. This is not a metaphor. The factorial basis captures it directly, and the consequences follow without special cases.

What Dimension Means in Multiplication

Chapter 3 established that dimensions emerge from scope depth. Each time a position in the odometer fills and a new position opens, the system gains a dimension. The number line is a one-dimensional projection of a structure that is naturally multi-dimensional.

When two variables are added, their configurations are aligned within the same dimensional space. Both x and y occupy positions in the same factorial-basis representation. The carry events that occur during addition expand the scope within the existing dimensional framework: they push the combined configuration into higher positions, but within the same sequence of positions the odometer already maintains.

Multiplication is different. When two variables are multiplied, the result does not occupy a higher position in the same sequence. The result occupies a position in a space whose dimension is bounded by the sum of the dimensions of the two inputs — that sum is always enough room to hold the product, though the product’s actual dimension is often smaller. Multiplying a one-dimensional quantity by another one-dimensional quantity produces at most a two-dimensional quantity. Multiplying a two-dimensional quantity by a one-dimensional quantity produces at most a three-dimensional quantity.

This is not an abstract claim. It is visible in the arithmetic. When you multiply two-digit numbers, the result has more digits than either input. The extra digits are not just “more of the same.” They represent structure that belongs to the product of both inputs together, structure that neither input carried alone. The product occupies a dimensional region that required both inputs to generate.

The Factorial Basis Makes This Visible

In the factorial basis, the dimension of a number is determined by the highest position it occupies. A number whose highest occupied position is two occupies a two-dimensional scope. A number whose highest occupied position is three occupies a three-dimensional scope.

When two numbers are multiplied, the product’s highest occupied position is at most the sum of the highest positions of the two inputs, and reaching that sum is not guaranteed. Multiplying a number at scope two by a number at scope three produces a result whose occupied depth is no more than scope five, though it is often less. Allocating scope five in advance is always enough room for the product; the product does not always need all of it.

This is exactly what happens in familiar arithmetic. Multiplying a two-digit number by a three-digit number produces a number with up to five digits, but not always exactly five. Three and four, for instance, both have their highest occupied position at 2 in the factorial basis: three is [1, 1] and four is [2, 0]. Their product, twelve, is [2, 0, 0], with highest occupied position 3, not 2 + 2 = 4. The sum of the inputs’ occupied positions is a safe upper bound that guarantees enough room for the result; it is a structural ceiling, not the product’s actual dimension.

In the algebraic system, the relationship state machine for multiplication specifies this directly. Given two variables, each occupying a dimensional region of the factorial-basis space, the product variable occupies a dimensional region bounded by combining both, normalized to its actual required extent.
