The relationship machine for multiplication tracks this bound on its inputs and assigns the result to the appropriate scope.

Multiplying by One

The previous chapters established the no-change principle through three cases: adding zero, subtracting zero, and dividing by one. Multiplying by one is the fourth case, with one qualification that matters once a product variable already has a history of its own.

Multiplying x by one asks: what dimensional configuration is produced by combining x’s dimensional structure with one’s dimensional structure?

The number one occupies the lowest possible position in the factorial basis. It has no dimensional extent beyond the base position. Combining x’s dimensional structure with a structure of zero additional extent produces a result with x’s dimensional structure unchanged. No new dimensions are contributed. No new positions are occupied. The required configuration for the product is the same configuration x already holds.

Whether this produces a transition depends on what the product variable held before. If the product variable has no prior realized state, or if it already held x’s configuration, then the required result and the current result coincide, and no transition occurs: the no-change principle applies. But if the product variable previously held some other configuration — for instance, because the relationship had just been evaluated with a different second factor — the relationship machine must still drive the product variable to x’s configuration, and that is a genuine transition in the product variable, even though x itself never moved and even though the destination is the same configuration x already holds. The no-change principle describes what happens to a variable when the required state and the current state already agree; it does not claim that multiplying by one can never change any variable’s state.

This is now the fourth example of the no-change principle applied to arithmetic, correctly scoped: adding zero, subtracting zero, dividing by one, and multiplying by one never force an input variable to move, and they leave an output variable unchanged exactly when that output already matches the required result. When an output does not already match, the relationship machine still updates it, the same way it would for any other relationship evaluation.

Multiplying by Zero

Multiplying by zero is entirely different, and it is important to be precise about why.

The previous four non-operations all failed to produce a transition because the second input contributed nothing: no realized state machine for zero, no change in orientation for a proportion of one-to-one, no additional dimensional extent for the number one. In each case, the absence of a contribution meant the result state equaled the input state, and no transition occurred.

Multiplying by zero does not fit this pattern. The multiplication relationship machine given zero as a factor does not find an absent input. It finds a realized input: the zero state, which is the configuration of a variable that has been explicitly set to zero rather than never initialized. The distinction matters.

When a variable holds zero as an explicitly set value, the values state machine for that variable has been moved to the zero configuration by a real event. The event set the configuration to the base state. This is different from an unrealized variable, which has no state machine at all and contributes nothing to any alignment or combination.

When the multiplication relationship machine combines x’s dimensional structure with a zero-valued state machine, it asks: what higher-dimensional configuration is produced by combining x’s extent with the extent of a state machine whose entire dimensional occupancy is zero?

A state machine in the zero configuration occupies no positions. It has been returned to the inferred default. Combining any dimensional extent with zero dimensional occupancy produces zero dimensional occupancy. All of x’s digit positions, combined with the zero factor’s empty occupancy, contribute zero to every position of the product.

The result is that all of the values state machines for the product variable collapse to the inferred zero configuration: no positions occupied, with the zero state inferred rather than stored.

Whether this produces a transition depends, as with multiplying by one, on what the product variable held before. If the product variable held some other configuration — most commonly, if this is a relationship that previously had a different, nonzero result — the relationship machine drives it to the inferred zero state, and that is a real, generally irreversible transition: the prior configuration is no longer present in the system, and no later multiplication can recover it from the product variable alone. But if the product variable was already at the inferred zero state — because this is the first time the relationship has been evaluated, or because a previous factor was already zero — then the required result and the current result already agree, and no transition occurs, exactly as with any other case where a relationship machine confirms an already-correct state. Multiplying by zero is capable of producing a genuine, irreversible transition in a way that multiplying by one is not, but it does not guarantee one on every evaluation; it guarantees one only when the product variable’s prior state was something other than zero.

The Distinction That Matters

The distinction between multiplying by one and multiplying by zero is worth dwelling on, because it is the sharpest illustration of what the no-change principle actually means and where it stops applying.

Multiplying by one: the second factor contributes no additional dimensional extent. The required product configuration equals the first factor’s configuration. If the product variable already held that configuration, no transition occurs. If it held something else, the relationship machine updates it, and that update is a real transition in the product variable even though the first factor never moved.

Multiplying by zero: the second factor is a realized state machine in the zero configuration, with zero dimensional occupancy. The required product configuration is the inferred zero state. If the product variable already held that state, no transition occurs. If it held something else, the relationship machine drives it to the inferred zero state, and that transition is irreversible: no subsequent multiplication can recover the prior configuration from the product variable alone, because once it collapses to inferred zero, no trace of the earlier configuration remains in it.

The difference between the two cases is not that one always produces a transition and the other never does. Both are relationship evaluations that update the product variable only when the required state differs from its current state. The difference is in what a transition, when it happens, can be undone by. A transition to x’s configuration (multiplying by one) can be reversed by a later multiplication, because x’s configuration is still available elsewhere in the system. A transition to the inferred zero state (multiplying by zero) cannot be reversed by any later multiplication of the product variable, because the information that distinguished its prior state has been discarded, not merely overwritten with a recoverable value.

Multiplication in the Running Example

In the running example, the algebraic system entity holds x, y, z, and e. The relationship machine for z has been defined in various ways across these chapters: addition, subtraction, division. Now consider z defined as the product of x and y.

When x is in state three and y is in state four, the relationship machine for multiplication combines their dimensional structures and determines the product’s configuration. The result is twelve: the state the odometer reaches after twelve advances, occupying a dimensional region that neither three nor four individually requires.

When y transitions to state one, the relationship machine finds that the required product is now x’s own configuration, three, rather than twelve. Because z’s current state (twelve) differs from the required state (three), z transitions from twelve to three. This is a real transition in z, driven by the relationship, even though x itself never moved; what changed is y, and the relationship propagated that change to z. When y subsequently transitions to state zero (explicitly set, not unrealized), the relationship machine finds that y’s occupancy is zero, and the required product is the inferred zero state. Because z currently holds three, not zero, z transitions again, this time to the inferred zero state, and the configuration three is no longer recoverable from z.

The relationship machine does not behave differently depending on which factor changes. It monitors both x and y continuously, as all relationship machines do, and updates z whenever either input transitions.

Closing Part 3

This chapter closes the examination of operations as relationship state machines. Four chapters have covered addition, subtraction, fractions, and multiplication. In each case, the operation was shown to be a relationship state machine inside the algebraic system entity: a constraint that determines how one variable’s state must relate to others, updated continuously as the inputs change.

The no-change principle appeared in every chapter of Part 3, consistently, with a consistent scope: adding zero, subtracting zero, dividing by one, and multiplying by one never force the untouched input to move, and they leave the relationship’s output unchanged exactly when that output already holds the required result. Multiplying by zero can produce a genuine, irreversible transition in the output, but only when the output did not already hold the inferred zero state. In every case, whether a transition occurs depends on comparing the required state to the current state of the variable being written, not on which operation is being performed.

Part 3 has one more chapter before Part 4 begins. Complex numbers have been mentioned in passing as a second orthogonal dimension in the values state machine. The next chapter examines them directly, and shows that they require no new numbers, no special extension, and no apology. They follow from the dimensional structure that has been present throughout.

Chapter 13Complex Numbers as a Second Dimension

12 min read

The conventional introduction to complex numbers begins with an apology. There is no real number whose square is negative one. The square of any positive number is positive. The square of any negative number is also positive, because two negative signs cancel. Zero squared is zero. The equation x squared equals negative one has no solution anywhere on the number line.

At this point the presentation usually makes a move that generations of students have found unsatisfying. It says: let us simply define a new number, call it i, and declare that i squared equals negative one. Then define complex numbers as combinations of real numbers and multiples of i. Now the equation has a solution. Proceed.

The word “imaginary” was attached to these numbers centuries ago, and it stuck. The name is a confession embedded in the terminology: even the mathematicians who developed the theory felt they were inventing something that did not quite exist. Students who feel uneasy about accepting a number by declaration are responding accurately to the presentation they were given. The unease is not a sign of mathematical weakness. It is a sign that the conventional account of where complex numbers come from is genuinely incomplete.

The algebraic system offers the complete account. Complex numbers are not invented to solve an inconvenient equation. They are the natural result of adding a second orthogonal bounded dimension to the values state machine. The structure already supports this. Nothing new needs to be invented or declared.

What the Values State Machine Contains

Throughout Part 2 and Part 3, the values state machine for a variable has been described as a bounded state machine occupying positions in the factorial-basis space. Each position corresponds to a scope level. The variable advances through positions as events move it, carry events expand scope, and the current configuration represents the variable’s value.

This description has treated the values state machine as one-dimensional: a single sequence of positions, advancing in one direction. That one-dimensional treatment was sufficient for everything examined so far. But the structure of the values state machine does not require one dimension. A values state machine can contain multiple independent bounded sequences of positions, each advancing independently.

Chapter 3 introduced the idea that dimensions emerge from scope depth. When one position fills, the system adds another. The chapter focused on a single sequence growing longer. But the same logic that justifies adding a new position at the end of an existing sequence also justifies adding a new independent sequence. If the need to represent additional distinct states can drive scope expansion along one axis, it can equally drive the addition of a second independent axis.

A values state machine with two independent axes can represent states that no one-dimensional values state machine can represent. The first axis advances through states in one direction. The second axis advances through states in an orthogonal direction. The two axes are independent: a transition on one does not affect the other. The combined state is a pair of positions, one from each axis.

This is the complete structure of complex numbers. The first axis is the real component. The second axis is the imaginary component. The values state machine for a complex variable maintains two independent bounded sequences of positions. The variable is in a state described by two coordinates, one from each sequence.

Why This Dimension Is Orthogonal

The word “orthogonal” is important and worth being precise about. Two dimensions are orthogonal when movement in one dimension has no effect on position in the other. On a flat surface, moving north does not change how far east you are. The north-south axis and the east-west axis are orthogonal.

In the values state machine, the real and imaginary axes are orthogonal in the same sense. An event that advances the real component does not change the imaginary component. An event that advances the imaginary component does not change the real component. The carry events on one axis do not propagate to the other axis. The two sequences of positions advance, carry, and expand scope entirely independently of each other.

This independence is what makes the second axis genuinely a second dimension rather than just a second variable. Two variables x and y in the same algebraic system can be related to each other by relationship state machines. The real and imaginary components of a single complex variable are not related to each other by any relationship machine. They are simply two independent components of the same values state machine, occupying orthogonal axes of the same space.

The relationship between real and imaginary is structural, not relational. They are two independent tracking dimensions within one state machine, not two state machines connected by a rule.

The Equation x Squared Equals Negative One

With the second orthogonal dimension established, the equation x squared equals negative one can be examined without apology.

The variable x has a values state machine with two axes. The state of x is a pair: a position on the real axis and a position on the imaginary axis. The constraint state machine for x says that x squared must equal negative one.

Squaring a complex variable means applying the multiplication relationship machine to the variable and itself. Chapter 12 established that multiplication combines the dimensional structures of its inputs. When a complex variable is multiplied by itself, the multiplication relationship machine combines the two-dimensional structure of the variable with itself.

The multiplication of a complex variable with real component zero and imaginary component one by itself proceeds as follows. The real axis contribution combines as: zero times zero minus one times one, which is negative one. The imaginary axis contribution combines as: zero times one plus one times zero, which is zero. The result has real component negative one and imaginary component zero.

The result is negative one. The equation x squared equals negative one has a solution: the complex state with real component zero and imaginary component one. No new number was declared. The solution exists within the structure of a two-dimensional values state machine.

The conventional name for this state is i, and the declaration “i squared equals negative one” is not a definition of a new number. It is an observation about the behavior of the second axis when a multiplication relationship machine is applied. The observation is correct. The framing of i as an invented entity is what the algebraic system replaces.

No New Numbers Required

The broader implication is the same one drawn in Chapter 10 for negative numbers and Chapter 11 for fractions: complex numbers do not require extending the number system with a new type of entity.

The conventional account of mathematical history presents a sequence of extensions. Natural numbers were extended to integers to accommodate negatives. Integers were extended to rationals to accommodate fractions. Rationals were extended to reals to accommodate irrational quantities. Reals were extended to complex numbers to accommodate square roots of negatives. Each extension required accepting new entities whose existence was initially disputed and whose legitimacy was established only gradually.

The algebraic system collapses this sequence. Every entity in the sequence is already present in the structure of the values state machine at appropriate scope. Negative states require an orientation relationship machine, not new numbers. Fractional states require sufficient scope to express the proportion, not new numbers. Complex states require a second orthogonal axis in the values state machine, not new numbers.

The extensions were not discoveries of new mathematical objects. They were recognitions of structure that the values state machine already contained. Each “extension” corresponds to activating a structural feature that was always available: orientation, scope expansion, additional axes. The numbers did not grow. The descriptions of what the system could already do became more complete.

The Relationship to Chapter 3

Chapter 3 introduced dimensions as emerging from scope depth. When a position fills, a new dimension opens. That chapter focused on a single sequence of positions growing longer as counting advanced.

The second orthogonal axis in a complex variable’s values state machine is a different application of the same principle. Rather than growing the sequence longer when a position fills, a second independent sequence is added alongside the first. The first sequence tracks the real component. The second sequence tracks the imaginary component. Both grow independently according to the same factorial-basis rules. Both contribute to the complete state of the variable.

The simplex geometry mentioned in Chapter 3 applies here as well. A one-dimensional values state machine occupies a line in the state space. A two-dimensional values state machine occupies a plane. The real axis is one edge of the plane. The imaginary axis is another edge, perpendicular to the first. The complex state is a point in that plane. The factorial-basis structure of each axis determines the valid points in that plane and the transitions between them.

This connection to Chapter 3 is not decorative. It confirms that complex numbers were always part of the structure. Dimensions emerge from the need to represent more distinct states. A values state machine with one axis represents all the states reachable along that axis. A values state machine with two axes represents all the states reachable in the plane those axes define. The second axis was available from the beginning. Using it to track an independent component of a variable’s state is not an extension of mathematics. It is mathematics operating as it always could.

Complex Numbers in the Running Example

The algebraic system entity in the running example has held x, y, z, and e throughout Part 2 and Part 3. Each of these variables has used a one-dimensional values state machine. Their states are positions along a single real axis.

Adding a complex variable to the entity requires only that its values state machine be initialized with two independent axes rather than one. The variable is created the same way any variable is created: a named state machine is added to the entity. The difference is that the values state machine for this variable tracks two components independently.

Relationship state machines connecting a complex variable to other variables in the entity operate on both components. When a relationship machine involves multiplication of two complex variables, it applies the two-dimensional combination rule. When it involves addition, it aligns the real components independently of the imaginary components, exactly as the state-alignment process for addition was described in Chapter 9, applied separately to each axis.

No new rules are introduced. No special handling for complex arithmetic is required. The relationship machines that handle real-valued variables handle complex-valued variables by the same mechanisms, applied to the appropriate components.

What the Second Dimension Already Knows

One consequence of the second orthogonal dimension deserves direct attention, because it explains something the conventional curriculum treats as a collection of identities requiring memorization and proof.

Trigonometric functions — sine and cosine — describe how the two components of a unit state in two-dimensional space relate to each other. A unit state is a two-dimensional state where the total scope contribution from both axes combined is exactly one. As the angle from the first axis increases, the real component decreases and the imaginary component increases, but the total unit scope remains fixed. The sine of an angle names the imaginary component; the cosine names the real component.

The relationship between sine and cosine is therefore not something that requires establishing by proof. It is a structural consequence of both components belonging to the same unit state. When the real component and imaginary component are both drawn from a state whose combined scope is one, the sum of their squares must also be one. This is not a theorem about trigonometry. It is a description of what a unit state in a two-dimensional values state machine is. The identity holds not because someone proved it, but because the structure cannot be otherwise.

The same reasoning applies to every relationship between sine and cosine that the conventional curriculum lists as an identity. When two angles are combined — when the relationship machine for multiplication is applied to two unit states at different angles — the resulting components are determined entirely by how the two-dimensional multiplication relationship combines orientations. The formulas for the sine and cosine of a combined angle are not separate results requiring separate proofs. They are direct outputs of the multiplication relationship machine applied to two-dimensional states. The relationship machine was already specified in full when multiplication was defined. The angle addition formulas are already contained in that specification. They become visible when you ask how the machine behaves with unit states, not when someone derives them from a triangle.

This is what the second dimension already knows. Every trigonometric identity is a structural property of the two-dimensional values state machine and the relationship machines that operate on it. None of them need to be established independently.

Closing Part 3

This chapter closes Part 3. Five chapters have examined operations as relationship state machines: addition as state alignment, subtraction and negation as orientation relationships, fractions as scope-proportion relationships, multiplication as dimensional expansion, and complex numbers as a second orthogonal dimension. Every operation that the conventional account introduces as a new rule or a new number type has been shown to be a structural feature of the values state machine and the relationship machines that operate on it.

Part 4 returns to the factorial basis itself. The operations of Part 3 used residue structure and scope without examining that structure in detail. Part 4 examines factorial numbers as complete knowledge states, shows how residue properties are carried in the representation, and explores what those properties make possible for computation and analysis. The structure that was always present in the numbers now becomes the subject of direct examination.

Part 4

The Factorial Basis and Residue Properties

Chapter 14Factorial Numbers as Knowledge Checkpoints

9 min read

Factorial numbers appear throughout mathematics in places that seem unrelated. They count permutations and arrangements in combinatorics. They appear in the denominators of every term in Taylor and Maclaurin series. They define the convergence boundaries for infinite series. Chapter 8 showed that the series for e places exactly one unit at every factorial scope boundary. The probability of certain outcomes in statistics involves factorial denominators. Wherever deep structure is being counted or bounded, factorial numbers appear.

This ubiquity is not a coincidence. It is a consequence of what factorial numbers are. A factorial number is not merely a large number produced by multiplying all integers up to n. A factorial number is a complete knowledge state: the precise point at which the odometer has fully explored every divisibility relationship available at its current scope. Every state that could be reached by combining the dimensions up to that point has been reached. No structure within that scope is hidden.

Understanding why this is true turns factorial boundaries from numerical curiosities into structural landmarks. They are the checkpoints at which the system knows everything it can know at a given depth.

What “Complete” Means

The odometer generates states in sequence. Each state is a configuration of digit positions, and each digit position has a bounded range. The first position has range zero to one. The second position has range zero to two. The third position has range zero to three. And so on.

The odometer reaches a factorial boundary precisely when the positions below it have all simultaneously reached their maximum values. At that moment, every combination of values that the current set of positions can produce has been generated. The odometer has explored every configuration available within the current scope. The next advance requires opening a new position, expanding the scope.

At 2! which equals two, both values of the first position have been visited: zero and one. The configuration is complete within one dimension. At 3! which equals six, all combinations of the first and second positions have been visited. The first position has taken every value, the second position has taken every value, and every combination of the two has appeared exactly once. The configuration is complete within two dimensions.

At 4! which equals twenty-four, all combinations of the first, second, and third positions have been visited. At 5! which equals one hundred twenty, all combinations through the fourth position. At each factorial boundary, the odometer has exactly exhausted the configurations available within the current scope. No configuration has been missed. No configuration has been repeated.

This exhaustiveness is what makes factorial boundaries complete. They are not arbitrary milestones. They are the exact points at which the current scope is fully characterized.

Divisibility Is Fully Resolved at Factorial Boundaries

A consequence of this exhaustiveness is that divisibility relationships are fully resolved at factorial boundaries. Every number that could divide any state within the scope has had its divisibility tested against every state the odometer can represent at that scope. No divisibility question within the scope remains open.

At the boundary 2! equals two, the question of divisibility by two is fully resolved for all states the odometer has generated so far. State zero is divisible by two. State one is not. State two is, and two is the boundary itself. Within this scope, the divisibility pattern for two is completely known.

At the boundary 3! equals six, the questions of divisibility by two, three, and six are all fully resolved for all states up to six. State two is divisible by two but not three. State three is divisible by three but not two. State four is divisible by two but not three. State five is divisible by neither two nor three within this scope. State six is divisible by both.

At 4! equals twenty-four, divisibility by two, three, four, six, eight, twelve, and twenty-four is fully resolved for all states up to twenty-four. The factorial boundary carries complete divisibility knowledge for all the divisors that fit within its scope.

This is what “complete knowledge state” means. The factorial boundary is the first point at which nothing more can be known about divisibility within that scope. Every question that could be asked about divisibility of any number up to n! by any divisor up to n has already been answered by the structure. The answer is carried in the digit configurations of every number the odometer has generated.

Why This Matters for Computation

The significance of factorial boundaries as complete knowledge states extends beyond the theoretical. Any computation that needs divisibility information about numbers within a certain range can use the nearest factorial boundary as its reference point.

If the computation needs to know whether numbers up to one hundred are divisible by small primes, the relevant factorial boundary is 5! equals one hundred twenty. That boundary contains complete divisibility information for all divisors up to five. Every number up to one hundred twenty that is divisible by two, three, or five has its divisibility visible in its digit structure, without any additional computation.

Working from a factorial boundary means that the system has already done the work. The structure carries the answer. Reading divisibility from the representation is not computation; it is observation. The odometer generated the state, and in generating it, established all its divisibility relationships simultaneously.

This is the structural advantage that factorial boundaries provide for computation: they are the points at which the maximum amount of structure is available per unit of scope. Navigating to a factorial boundary and reading the structure costs less than computing divisibility from scratch for each number individually.

The Shape of the Space at a Factorial Boundary

Chapter 3 introduced simplex geometry as the natural shape for factorial-basis dimensions. The observation was that adding a new dimension to the odometer produces not a rectangular grid but a simplex: a structure where each new dimension has one more state than the previous.

At a factorial boundary, the full simplex for the current number of dimensions has been traversed. Every vertex of the simplex has been visited. Every edge has been traversed. The interior has been filled. The factorial boundary is the last state before the simplex at the current dimension count is complete and a new dimension must open.

Visualizing this concretely: at the boundary 2! equals two, the simplex in one dimension is a line segment with two endpoints and one interior state. At 3! equals six, the simplex in two dimensions has been fully explored. At 4! equals twenty-four, the three-dimensional simplex is complete. Each factorial boundary is the completion of a simplex, and each new dimension opens a new simplex of greater extent.

The completeness of the simplex at each factorial boundary is another way of seeing why factorial boundaries are knowledge checkpoints. A simplex that has been fully traversed contains no unexplored regions. The structure has been fully characterized.

Primes as Gaps in the Structure

The discussion of complete knowledge states creates the right context for introducing primes.

At any factorial boundary, the divisibility relationships for all numbers up to that boundary are resolved. But some numbers within the scope have no divisibility relationships with any smaller number other than one. The number five is not divisible by two, three, or four within the scope available at 4! equals twenty-four. The number seven is not divisible by two, three, four, five, or six within the scope available at 6! equals seven hundred twenty. Numbers like these are called primes.

The conventional account of primes says they are the fundamental building blocks of all integers. Every integer can be expressed as a product of primes in exactly one way. Primes are the atoms from which all other numbers are made.

That account is structurally backward. In the factorial algebraic system, the structure comes first and the divisibility relationships are visible within it. A prime is not a fundamental building block from which other numbers are assembled. A prime is a number that, at the current scope, has no divisibility events. No smaller number divides it evenly. Its digit structure in the factorial basis shows no relationship to any smaller factor.

This makes a prime not foundational but diagnostic. A prime is a signal that the current scope has not yet found the structure that would explain the number’s relationships. At scope 4!, the number five appears prime because the scope does not yet contain six factorial, which is the first factorial boundary at which the structure involving five becomes fully visible. When the scope expands to 5! equals one hundred twenty, the relationships involving five become explicit: twenty-five is five squared, thirty is five times six, and so on.

The primality of five is a property of the current scope, not an eternal property of five itself. As the scope expands, the relationships involving five become visible in the structure. Five’s apparent isolation at lower scope is a symptom of the scope’s limitation, not a fundamental attribute of the number.

What Primes Are Telling the System

Rather than being the foundation of arithmetic, primes serve as diagnostic markers. When the system encounters a prime within its current scope, the prime is reporting that no divisibility relationship has been found at the current depth. The scope needs to expand before those relationships become visible.

This has practical implications. A test for primality within the current scope is a test for the absence of divisibility events in the residue structure. It requires no special algorithm and no separate computation. The residue structure already carries divisibility information. Checking for primality is checking whether any divisibility event is present in the digit configuration of the number. If none is found within the current scope, the number is prime at that scope.

As the scope expands, numbers that appeared prime may acquire divisibility relationships. In the factorial basis, this corresponds to new digit positions opening up and the number’s configuration extending into dimensions where its relationships become visible. A prime at scope n is a number that has not yet encountered its first divisibility relationship. The scope boundary is the limiting factor, not the number itself.

Part 4 Continues

This chapter established factorial boundaries as complete knowledge states and introduced primes as structural gaps rather than foundational atoms. The next chapter builds directly on this foundation. If factorial boundaries carry complete divisibility information, then the residues of all numbers near a factorial boundary can be read directly from the structure. The chapter after that shows how factorial boundaries serve as navigation landmarks, making it possible to jump to a known-complete state and work backward rather than always counting forward from zero.

The structure that makes these operations possible is already in the representation. Part 4 is the examination of what that structure says.

Chapter 15Residues of Factorial Basis Numbers

10 min read

Most people learned a handful of divisibility rules in school. A number is divisible by two if its last digit is even. A number is divisible by three if its digits sum to a multiple of three. A number is divisible by five if its last digit is zero or five. A number is divisible by nine if its digits sum to a multiple of nine. These rules were presented as tricks for mental arithmetic, useful but somewhat arbitrary, requiring memorization without explanation.

The rules are not arbitrary. They are observations about the decimal representation reading structure that the number itself carries. Because the decimal basis uses powers of ten, and because ten shares factors with two and five, certain divisibility relationships become visible in specific digit positions. The rules work because of the alignment between the decimal basis and the divisors being tested.

In the factorial basis, this alignment is total rather than partial. The factorial basis was built to carry divisibility relationships in its structure, not as a coincidental side effect. Every position in the factorial basis corresponds to a factorial boundary. Every factorial boundary, as Chapter 14 established, is a complete knowledge state for all divisibility within its scope. Reading divisibility from the factorial basis is not applying a trick. It is reading the structure directly.

What a Residue Is

When the odometer advances through states, it generates configurations. Some configurations are divisible by a given number; some are not. The remainder when a state is divided by a given divisor is that state’s residue with respect to that divisor.

State six divided by four gives quotient one and remainder two. The residue of state six with respect to four is two. State seven divided by four gives quotient one and remainder three. The residue of seven with respect to four is three. State eight divided by four gives quotient two and remainder zero. State eight is divisible by four exactly; its residue with respect to four is zero.

In the factorial basis, the residue of any state with respect to any divisor is carried in the digit configuration from the moment the odometer generates that state. No division is required to find the residue. The digit configuration reports it directly once the relevant positions are known.

Reading Divisibility by Two

The first position in the factorial basis has range zero to one, corresponding to a weight of one factorial, which is one. The second position has range zero to two, corresponding to two factorial, which is two. Every state whose second position holds a value contributes a multiple of two to the total. Every state whose second position holds zero contributes nothing from that position.

Now consider any state and ask whether it is divisible by two. The weight of every position beyond the second is a multiple of two: three factorial is six, four factorial is twenty-four, five factorial is one hundred twenty. All are divisible by two. The only position whose weight is not a multiple of two is the first position, which has weight one factorial equals one.

Therefore, the divisibility of any state by two depends entirely on the value of the first digit position. If the first position holds zero, the state is divisible by two, because all other contributions to the total are multiples of two. If the first position holds one, the state has a residue of one with respect to two.

Reading divisibility by two from the factorial basis is reading the first digit position. If it is zero, the number is even. If it is one, the number is odd. No computation is required. The digit is the answer.

Reading Divisibility by Three

The weight of the third position is three factorial equals six, which is divisible by three. The weight of every position beyond the third is a multiple of six and therefore a multiple of three. The weight of the second position is two factorial equals two, which is not divisible by three. The weight of the first position is one factorial equals one, which is not divisible by three.

Therefore, the divisibility of any state by three depends on the combined values of the first and second digit positions. The contribution from all positions beyond the second is divisible by three and contributes zero residue. The first position contributes its value directly, and the second position contributes twice its value. The residue of the entire state with respect to three equals the residue of the first digit plus twice the second digit with respect to three.

To check whether a state is divisible by three: take the first digit, add twice the second digit, and check whether the result is divisible by three. If it is, the entire state is divisible by three. If not, the remainder is the residue.

This is not a separate computation applied after finding the number. The first and second digits are present in the representation. The answer is already there; it only needs to be read.

Reading Divisibility by Six

Divisibility by six requires divisibility by both two and three simultaneously. The first digit determines divisibility by two. The first and second digits together determine divisibility by three. A state is divisible by six when both conditions are satisfied: the first digit is zero, and the first digit plus twice the second digit is divisible by three.

When the first digit is zero, divisibility by three reduces to checking whether twice the second digit is divisible by three, which reduces to checking whether the second digit is divisible by three. The second digit ranges from zero to two. Of those values, zero is divisible by three and three would be divisible by three but exceeds the range. So the second digit must be zero.

A state is divisible by six exactly when both the first digit and the second digit are zero. Both the position corresponding to weight one and the position corresponding to weight two are unoccupied. The state’s entire value comes from positions with weights that are multiples of six.

Reading this from the factorial basis: if the first two digit positions are both zero, the number is divisible by six. If either holds a nonzero value, the residue with respect to six is visible in those positions.

Reading Divisibility by Five

Five requires a different approach, because five does not divide any factorial boundary below five factorial equals one hundred twenty. Below that boundary, no position weight is a multiple of five. The first five positions have weights one, one, two, six, and twenty-four. None of these is divisible by five.

Beginning at the sixth position, with weight five factorial equals one hundred twenty, every subsequent position weight is a multiple of one hundred twenty and therefore a multiple of five. Below the fifth factorial boundary, divisibility by five is determined entirely by the combined contribution of the first five positions.

For states below one hundred twenty, checking divisibility by five requires examining the combined value of the first four positions. For states near or above the fifth factorial boundary, the contribution from positions at and beyond the fifth is automatically divisible by five, and the first four positions determine the residue.

This illustrates an important structural property: the depth of positions required to read a particular residue depends on the position of the relevant divisor relative to the factorial boundary structure. Divisors that appear early in the factorial sequence (two, three, six) are readable from early positions. Divisors that appear late (five, seven, eleven) require examining more positions before the carrying structure takes over.

The Residue at Any State Comes From a Bounded Window

The pattern established across these examples generalizes. For any divisor d, there exists a factorial boundary n! such that n! is divisible by d. Beyond that boundary, all position weights are multiples of d and contribute zero residue. The residue of any state with respect to d is determined entirely by the digit positions below the boundary n!.

This means that for any divisor, there is a bounded window of digit positions that carries the complete residue information. The window has a fixed size, determined by the smallest factorial boundary divisible by d. Reading the residue requires examining only the positions within that window.

For divisors that divide small factorial boundaries, the window is small. Divisibility by two requires examining one position. Divisibility by three requires examining two positions. Divisibility by six requires examining two positions. For divisors that divide only large factorial boundaries, the window is larger, but it remains finite and known.

This bounded window property is what makes the factorial basis computationally efficient for residue calculations. The structure carries the information in a known location. No search is required. No repeated division is needed. The positions within the window are read, and the residue is present.

Residues of Nearby Numbers

Chapter 14 established that factorial boundaries are complete knowledge states. This chapter has shown how the residue of any state is carried in its digit positions. These two facts combine to make residues of nearby numbers directly accessible.

Consider any state near a factorial boundary. The boundary itself has residue zero with respect to every divisor within its scope, because the boundary is the product of all integers up to that scope level. States near the boundary differ from the boundary by small amounts, and those differences are visible in the low-order digit positions.

A state that is one less than a factorial boundary has a configuration where all low-order positions are at their maximum values. A state that is two less than a factorial boundary has a configuration where the lowest position has dropped from its maximum by one and the next position may have adjusted. The residue of each state near the boundary is visible in the low-order positions.

Working near factorial boundaries is therefore computationally natural for residue analysis. The boundary provides a known reference point with residue zero. Every state near the boundary differs from the boundary by an amount that is directly readable from the low-order digit positions, and the residue of the nearby state is the same as the residue of that difference.

This is not an optimization applied after the fact. It is the structure itself providing the information. The odometer generated the state, the factorial basis encodes the residue in the digit configuration, and the system reads the residue by examining the relevant positions. The three steps are not three operations on a number. They are three descriptions of the same thing.

What the Rules Were Teaching

Returning to the divisibility rules learned in school: those rules were teaching a simplified version of what the factorial basis carries directly. The rule for divisibility by three in decimal, checking whether the sum of digits is divisible by three, works because the decimal basis uses powers of ten and ten has a residue of one with respect to three. The rule compensates for the mismatch between the decimal basis and the divisor.

In the factorial basis, no compensation is needed. The basis was built around the same factorial boundaries that define divisibility relationships. The rules are not tricks layered over an incompatible representation. The rules are direct readings of the structure the basis carries.

The implication for understanding mathematics is significant. Students who memorize divisibility rules and feel they are using tricks rather than understanding something real are correct in their assessment of the decimal presentation. In the factorial basis, they would not need to memorize rules. They would observe structure. The observation would be sufficient because the structure is the answer.

Part 4 Continues

The next chapter examines what factorial boundaries as navigation landmarks make possible for computation. If the residue of any state is readable from its digit positions, and if factorial boundaries are complete knowledge states with residue zero for every divisor within their scope, then it is possible to jump to a factorial boundary and work backward to a target rather than always advancing forward from zero. The efficiency of this approach, and its connection to how the system naturally works, is what Chapter 16 examines.

Chapter 16Skipping Ahead and Working Back

9 min read

When navigating an unfamiliar city, people rarely count blocks from the origin. They identify a known landmark near the destination and navigate from the landmark. The landmark need not be the destination. It needs to be close enough that the remaining distance is manageable, and known well enough that the navigator can establish position relative to it without uncertainty.

The factorial basis provides landmarks of exactly this kind. Factorial boundaries are known precisely. Their digit configurations are simple: at n!, the position corresponding to n! holds one and all lower positions hold zero. Their divisibility properties are completely known from their structure. Their distance from any nearby state is readable directly from the low-order digit positions of that state.

Most computational approaches to number-theoretic problems advance forward from zero, testing each state along the way. This is natural when zero is the only known reference point. But the factorial basis provides reference points throughout the number line, at intervals defined by the factorial sequence. Using these reference points changes the character of computation: instead of searching forward into unknown territory, the system jumps to a known state and reads the short distance to the target from the structure that is already there.

What It Means to Work Backward

The odometer advances forward. Given any state, the next state is produced by incrementing the lowest position with remaining capacity, carrying as needed. This forward direction is how counting works, and it is the direction the odometer naturally travels.

But the odometer can also be consulted in reverse. Given any state, the previous state is produced by decrementing the lowest nonzero position, borrowing as needed. And given a known reference state and a target state, the difference between them is readable from the digit positions where they differ. Working backward from a factorial boundary to a target is the same as reading that difference.

Suppose the target state is one hundred seventeen and the nearest factorial boundary above the target is five factorial, which equals one hundred twenty. The difference is three. In the factorial basis, three is represented as a configuration in the low-order positions. The state one hundred seventeen is the state reached from the boundary one hundred twenty by subtracting three, which means applying the reverse direction for three steps.

The digit configuration of one hundred seventeen relative to the boundary one hundred twenty is exactly the digit configuration of three, expressed as a subtraction from the boundary. This is not a separate computation. The low-order positions of one hundred seventeen already carry the information. They report that the state is three units below the nearest factorial boundary. Reading those positions is reading that fact directly.

The Digit Configuration of States Near a Boundary

Chapter 15 established that the residue of any state with respect to any divisor is carried in the low-order digit positions up to the relevant factorial boundary. The same positional structure also carries the distance from the nearest factorial boundary.

A state at exactly a factorial boundary has all low-order positions holding zero and the boundary position holding one. As the odometer advances beyond the boundary, the low-order positions fill in sequence, exactly as they did at the beginning of the counting process. Position one fills first, then position two, and so on until all low-order positions reach their maxima and the next factorial boundary is reached.

This means the low-order digit positions of any state record two things simultaneously. They record the distance of that state from the most recent factorial boundary below it, counting forward. They also record the distance from the next factorial boundary above it, counting backward, because the remaining capacity in the low-order positions tells how many more advances are needed to reach the boundary.

Both distances are carried in the same digit positions. Reading the current values gives the distance from the lower boundary. Reading the remaining capacity (each position’s maximum minus its current value, accumulated) gives the distance to the upper boundary. No computation is needed for either. The structure reports both distances as soon as the digit positions are examined.

Jumping to a Boundary

For many computations, the most efficient approach is not to advance from zero or from any arbitrary starting state, but to identify the relevant factorial boundary and jump to it directly.

Jumping to a factorial boundary does not require traversing the intervening states. The factorial boundary’s digit configuration is known by definition: the boundary position holds one, all lower positions hold zero. The system can establish this configuration directly, treating the boundary as a known state rather than as a state that must be reached by advancing the odometer.

This is computationally justified because the factorial boundary is fully characterized. Its residues are known. Its divisibility relationships are known. Its position in the factorial-basis sequence is known. No information is lost by jumping to it rather than advancing to it, because all the information the intermediate states carry is also available at the boundary and in the low-order positions of states near it.

Jumping to a boundary and working backward is the natural approach when the target is known to be near a factorial boundary. The jump establishes the reference point. The backward reading establishes the distance. The target state’s configuration is the boundary configuration modified by the low-order positions that represent the distance.

The Connection to Residue Analysis

Chapter 15 showed that the residue of any state with respect to a divisor is readable from the low-order positions. Chapter 14 showed that the boundary itself has residue zero for every divisor within its scope. Together, these facts make residue analysis near a boundary especially efficient.

When the target state is near a factorial boundary, its residue with respect to any divisor within the boundary’s scope is the same as the residue of its distance from the boundary. The boundary contributes zero residue. The distance from the boundary contributes the full residue of the target.

Computing the residue of one hundred seventeen with respect to three: the nearest factorial boundary is one hundred twenty, which has residue zero with respect to three. The distance from the boundary is three. The residue of three with respect to three is zero. Therefore the residue of one hundred seventeen with respect to three is zero. One hundred seventeen is divisible by three.

This conclusion was reached by identifying the boundary, reading the distance, and checking the residue of the distance. No division of one hundred seventeen was performed. The structure provided the answer through reference-point navigation.

For states further from any factorial boundary, the approach still applies but may require examining more low-order positions. The efficiency advantage is greatest when the target is close to a factorial boundary, and the factorial boundaries become more densely spaced relative to the numbers they contain as the scope increases.

What the State Machine Prefers

The broader principle behind this approach is that state machines are most efficient when they work within an already-established scope. The factorial odometer has already generated every state from zero to the current position. The structure of all those states is already determined by the odometer’s construction. No additional computation established that structure; the odometer generated it as a consequence of advancing.

A state machine operating within an established scope does not need to rediscover the structure of that scope. The structure is already present. Operations on states within the scope read the existing structure rather than computing new structure. This is cheaper in every sense: fewer transitions, fewer scope expansions, and no redundant work.

Jumping to a factorial boundary and working backward is the most scope-efficient approach to many problems because the factorial boundary is a state the odometer has already established. The system knows this state fully. Working from the boundary back to the target state is working within the scope that has already been characterized, reading the structure the odometer already generated.

This contrasts with advancing forward from an arbitrary starting point, which may require generating new states and new scope before reaching the target. When the target is already within the established scope, generating new states is unnecessary. The work has been done. The structure is there to be read.

Previewing Calculus

The logic of working from a known reference state to a target by reading a short distance is the same logic that governs calculus behavior at boundaries.

In calculus, the derivative of a function at a point measures how quickly the function’s value changes as the input approaches that point. Near a boundary of the valid scope, the rate of change is large: small advances in the input produce large changes in the output. Approaching a scope boundary from within is exactly the situation where the remaining capacity in the low-order positions decreases rapidly, and the distance to the boundary shrinks to zero.

The integral of a function over a range measures the total accumulated value of the function across that range. Accumulating states from one factorial boundary to another is the same as summing the contributions of all digit configurations between the two boundaries. The factorial basis provides natural start and end points for this accumulation.

Both of these observations will be developed in Part 5. The point here is that the navigation logic of Part 4, jumping to a known boundary and reading the distance, is the same structural logic that underlies the calculus operations of Part 5. The behavior of derivatives near scope boundaries and the behavior of integrals between factorial boundaries are applications of the same principle: factorial boundaries are known complete states, and proximity to them is readable from the structure.

Part 4 Closes in the Next Chapter

Chapter 17 completes Part 4 by returning to primes with the full context now established. Chapter 14 introduced primes as structural absences within the current scope. Chapters 15 and 16 have shown how the factorial basis carries residue information and how factorial boundaries serve as navigation landmarks. With this context, the role of primes as diagnostic signals rather than foundational atoms can be examined in full.

A prime is a state whose low-order positions carry no divisibility events for any divisor within the current scope. The factorial basis reports this absence directly. The prime is not special in its structure; it is notable for what its structure lacks at the current depth. What that absence means, and what it tells the system about the current scope’s limitations, is the subject of the next chapter.

Chapter 17Primes as Diagnostic, Not Foundation

12 min read

Prime numbers occupy a special place in the cultural imagination of mathematics. They appear on the covers of popular science books. They are the subject of one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics, the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of primes among the integers. They are the foundation of modern cryptography: the security of encrypted communications depends on the practical difficulty of factoring large numbers into their prime constituents. Primes feel fundamental in a way that other numbers do not.

The conventional account reinforces this feeling. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic states that every positive integer greater than one can be expressed as a product of primes in exactly one way. This theorem is taken to mean that primes are the atoms of arithmetic: the irreducible elements from which all other numbers are assembled. The structure of the integers is understood as arising from combinations of primes. Start with the primes, multiply them together in various combinations, and you produce all the other numbers.

The factorial algebraic system reframes this picture rather than inverting it outright. Primes are not assembled from smaller pieces: the odometer generates every number, prime or composite, by the same single mechanism, and a prime’s relationship to every other number is settled the moment it exists, not constructed afterward by combination. What does shift with scope is something narrower and more precise: how directly a number’s divisibility relationships can be read from its digit positions using a short combination rule, rather than by testing divisors one at a time. For divisors that divide some small factorial — two, three, four, six — that short rule exists from the moment the relevant factorial boundary is reached. For a prime that divides no small factorial, no comparably short rule exists until the scope reaches a factorial boundary built from a multiple of that prime. The number itself is prime or composite independent of scope; the ease of seeing why is not.

The Inversion

To see this clearly, return to how the odometer generates numbers. The odometer begins at zero and advances through configurations. It does not begin with primes and combine them. It generates every state in sequence: one, two, three, four, five, six, and so on. Every state is generated by the same mechanism. No state has priority over any other. The odometer does not know or care which states will later be identified as prime.

As the odometer advances, every state it generates carries divisibility information in its digit configuration. State six carries information about divisibility by two, three, and six, directly readable from its low-order positions. State twelve carries information about divisibility by two, three, four, and six the same way. These states are not assembled from primes. They are generated by the odometer, and these particular divisibility relationships are visible in their digit configurations from the moment of generation.

State five, when the odometer reaches it, is prime: it has no divisor other than one and itself, and this is true regardless of scope. Its digit configuration shows no non-trivial divisor readable by the two, three, four, or six rules, because none of those divisors evenly divide five. This is consistent with five being prime, but it is not the same claim as “five is prime because the scope has not yet reached far enough” — five would remain prime at any scope, including scopes far beyond five factorial.

What does change with scope is whether multiples of five have appeared yet in the sequence the odometer has generated, and whether a short positional rule for recognizing them exists. Twenty-five is five times five. Thirty is five times six. Fifty-five is five times eleven. These composite numbers do not exist “yet” in any scope-dependent sense — thirty is composite whether or not the odometer has reached it — but a short rule for reading “is this number a multiple of five” directly from its digits only becomes available once the scope reaches one hundred twenty, which is five factorial, the first factorial boundary that five evenly divides. Below that scope, recognizing a multiple of five still requires an ordinary check; above it, a positional shortcut becomes available, the same way the two, three, four, and six rules became available at their own boundaries.

Primality as a Scope Readout

Chapter 14 introduced this idea briefly: how directly a number’s relationships can be read from the structure depends on scope, even though the number’s own primality does not. Chapter 15 showed how residues are carried in the low-order digit positions. Chapter 16 showed how factorial boundaries serve as reference points for reading those residues. Now all three observations combine, with the distinction kept explicit.

At scope n, the low-order positions directly expose divisibility by every integer that evenly divides some factorial at or below n. A state whose digits show no such divisor is not yet confirmed composite by the positional rules available at that scope — but it may still be composite, if its smallest prime factor is larger than what those rules can detect. True primality testing in general still requires checking for divisors up to the square root of the number’s value; the factorial-basis positions shortcut this check only for the divisors that are themselves tied to small factorials.

Primality testing in the factorial basis is partly a side effect of maintaining residue state and partly ordinary work. The residue information for two, three, four, and six is already present in the digit positions and requires no separate computation. Testing whether a larger prime, such as five, seven, or eleven, divides a given number still requires either an ordinary check or a scope large enough to reach a factorial boundary built from a multiple of that prime. The factorial basis removes the computation for a specific, useful set of divisors; it does not remove the need for trial division in general.

This also clarifies the computational cost of primality testing. The cost is proportional to the number of positions that must be examined, which is bounded by the factorial boundary relevant to the divisors being tested. For a state near the factorial boundary n!, testing primality requires examining positions up to the boundary that contains divisors up to the square root of the state’s value. This is a bounded operation whose cost is determined by the structure of the factorial basis, not by the magnitude of the number being tested.

The Fundamental Theorem Revisited

The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says that every integer greater than one has a unique prime factorization. In the conventional account, this theorem is foundational: it establishes primes as the atoms from which all integers are built, and it asserts that the decomposition into atoms is unique.

In the factorial algebraic system, the same fact holds, but the interpretation is different. Every state above the boundary n! can be expressed in terms of the primes below n! and the states generated by combining them. This is true. But the expression in terms of primes is not a construction. It is a decomposition.

The state already exists. The odometer generated it. Its digit configuration already carries all its structural properties. Decomposing it into prime factors is a way of reading a particular aspect of that structure: which primes, at the current scope, are visible as divisors of the state. The decomposition is a description of what the state contains, not a recipe for how to build it.

Consider the difference between these two framings. In the construction framing, integers are assembled from primes, and primes are the necessary starting material. In the description framing, every integer is a state generated by the odometer, and the prime factorization is one way of describing the divisibility structure that the integer carries. The construction framing implies that primes come first and composites are derived. The description framing implies that all states are generated equally and the prime factorization describes a property of each state after the fact.

The factorial basis supports the description framing directly. Every state is generated by the odometer. The divisibility structure is carried in the digit configuration. Reading the prime factorization is reading those digits. No state is more primary than any other. The distinction between prime and composite is a distinction about what the residue structure at the current scope looks like, not a distinction about what kind of thing the state fundamentally is.

What the Structure Does and Does Not Tell the System

If positional divisibility rules are a diagnostic rather than a definition of primality, what exactly are they diagnosing?

At scope n, a state whose digits show no divisor readable by the rules for two, three, four, and six, and for any other divisor of a factorial at or below n, has not been shown composite by those rules. This tells the system something specific and limited: no short positional check available at this scope has found a factor. It does not tell the system that the state is prime, only that the available short checks did not find a divisor. Confirming primality in general still requires checking candidate divisors up to the square root of the state’s value, exactly as conventional arithmetic does; the factorial basis shortens this check only for the specific divisors tied to small factorials.

This is useful information, but it should not be overstated. When a computation encounters a state with no factorial-tied divisor visible, it knows only that the cheap checks were inconclusive, not that the state is confirmed prime and not that enlarging scope will necessarily resolve the question soon. A true prime whose smallest nontrivial potential divisor is itself a large prime, such as thirty-five, which is five times seven, will not get a positional confirmation of compositeness until the scope reaches a factorial boundary built from a multiple of five or of seven — one hundred twenty at the earliest — even though thirty-five is a small number. The representational shortcut and the actual density of primes among the integers are two different things, and the factorial basis speeds up one narrow kind of check without changing the other.

The distribution of true primes among the integers, and the precise questions the Riemann hypothesis asks about that distribution, are facts about the integers themselves. They do not depend on which representation is used to write the integers down, and the factorial basis’s positional shortcuts for divisors of small factorials do not constitute an explanation of the prime number theorem or a restatement of the Riemann hypothesis. What the factorial basis does offer is a genuine computational convenience for a specific, useful set of divisors, and an honest account of which divisors that set includes and which it does not.

The Role of Primes in Cryptography

Modern cryptographic systems depend on the practical difficulty of factoring large numbers into their prime constituents. The security of RSA encryption, for example, relies on the fact that multiplying two large primes together is fast, while factoring the product back into the original primes is computationally expensive. This asymmetry is the foundation of the security.

In the factorial algebraic system, this asymmetry has a structural explanation. Multiplying two states is a dimensional expansion: it combines the digit structures of two numbers into a higher-dimensional configuration. The product’s digit structure contains both inputs’ structures in combined form. Reading the product’s digit structure gives the combined structure directly.

Factoring the product means recovering the two separate inputs from the combined structure. This is a decomposition operation: finding which two configurations, when combined by multiplication, produce the observed product. The factorial basis carries the product’s structure, and that structure contains the information needed for factoring. But extracting it requires examining positions across the scope of the product, which grows with the size of the factors.

The cryptographic asymmetry is a consequence of the dimensional structure of multiplication. Combining dimensions is local: it takes the structures of two inputs and produces the structure of the product in one operation. Separating dimensions is non-local: it requires examining the product’s structure across its full scope to determine which factors could have produced it. The factorial basis makes this asymmetry visible as a property of dimensional combination, not as an arbitrary fact about arithmetic.

Closing Part 4

This chapter closes Part 4. Four chapters have examined the factorial basis and residue properties. Factorial boundaries are the states where a new position activates. Residues for divisors tied to small factorials are carried in digit positions and readable without division. Navigation can proceed from factorial boundaries backward to targets rather than always advancing from zero. Primes are not assembled from smaller pieces, and the ease of reading a number’s divisibility relationships from its digits is scope-dependent even though the number’s own primality is not.

The picture of arithmetic that emerges from Part 4 is one where structure carries real, useful information, without carrying all of it equally cheaply. The structure of the factorial basis determines which relationships are visible without computation at each scope, for the specific divisors tied to small factorials. The facts of divisibility, primality, and residue for those divisors follow from the structure directly. For divisors not tied to any small factorial, the structure still carries the information, but reading it requires either ordinary computation or a much larger scope.

Part 5 turns from arithmetic to calculus. Calculus has the reputation of being the hardest subject in the standard mathematics curriculum. Part 5 will argue that this difficulty comes entirely from the conventional presentation, which introduces calculus as a theory of infinitely small numbers requiring careful limiting arguments. In the algebraic system, calculus is boundary behavior: what happens when a state approaches the edge of its valid scope. The derivative measures proximity to a scope boundary. The integral measures accumulated state occupancy within a bounded region. No infinitesimals are needed. No limiting arguments are required. The structure that Part 4 established is exactly the structure that Part 5 will use.

Part 5

Calculus Without Limits

Chapter 18What Calculus Is Actually Asking

11 min read

Calculus arrives in the curriculum as if it requires a kind of number that does not quite exist. The original presentations by Newton and Leibniz used infinitely small quantities: numbers smaller than any positive number but not equal to zero. These infinitesimals made the calculations work, but they also made mathematicians uncomfortable. Something that is smaller than any positive number but still positive seemed to violate the basic properties of arithmetic. For two centuries, infinitesimals were used because they produced correct results while being treated with formal suspicion.

The resolution, developed in the nineteenth century, replaced infinitesimals with limits. The limit definition of the derivative avoids infinitesimals by describing the behavior of a ratio as the denominator approaches zero without ever reaching it. This resolved the logical problem but introduced a new pedagogical one. Students who grasped the informal infinitesimal argument suddenly needed to learn a formal machinery of epsilons and deltas that handled the same ideas with more caution and considerably more complexity. Calculus became technically rigorous and pedagogically difficult at the same time.

The difficulty is not intrinsic to calculus. It is a consequence of using the number line, a one-dimensional representation, to describe behavior that is fundamentally about the structure of a space near its boundaries. The number line cannot directly express what calculus is trying to say, so calculus invented workarounds. The algebraic system does not need workarounds. The structure that calculus is describing is exactly the boundary structure of the factorial-basis state space, which is present in the system from the beginning.

This chapter does not develop the specific mathematical claims about derivatives and integrals. Those are for the chapters that follow. This chapter reframes the question: what is calculus actually looking at?

The Shape of a Valid Region

Every variable in the algebraic system occupies a state within a bounded region of the state space. The region is bounded because the values state machine has a finite scope at any given time. Within the scope, the variable can occupy any valid state. Outside the scope, the variable cannot be represented.

The relationship state machines impose additional constraints. The variable z in the running example must satisfy the constraint z equals x plus y. The valid states for z are those consistent with the current states of x and y. If x is in state three and y is in state four, z must be in state seven. The valid region for z is determined by both its own scope and by the constraints imposed by its relationship machines.

The constraints and the scope together define a region in the state space where the algebraic system’s description is valid. Within that region, every state is reachable, every constraint is satisfiable, and every relationship machine operates normally. The system is well-behaved throughout the interior of this region.

Near the boundary of the region, the behavior changes. As a state approaches the edge of the valid scope, the constraints become harder to satisfy simultaneously. As the scope is approached from within, the remaining capacity in the digit positions decreases. The low-order positions approach their maxima. Carry events become more frequent. The system is using all of its available scope to represent the current state.

At the boundary itself, the scope is exhausted. The state machine is at the last configuration available before scope expansion is required. Beyond the boundary, no valid state exists in the current scope. The system either expands to a larger scope or the state is not representable.

What “Near a Boundary” Means

Chapter 16 showed that the distance from any state to the nearest factorial boundary is carried in the low-order digit positions. The remaining capacity in those positions tells how many more advances are possible before the boundary is reached. States near a factorial boundary have small remaining capacity. States far from a factorial boundary have large remaining capacity.
