It is tempting to conclude from this that proximity to a capacity boundary, by itself, makes a relationship machine’s output change rapidly. That conclusion does not hold in general, and it is worth being precise about why before going further. A capacity boundary is a property of the representation: how much room is left in the currently allocated integer positions before a new position must activate. Whether crossing that boundary produces a large or small change in a relationship machine’s output depends entirely on the relationship machine, not on the boundary itself. Consider the relationship machine that simply copies its input: the output equals the input, unchanged. As the input advances from twenty-three, [3, 2, 1], to twenty-four, [1, 0, 0, 0], every low-order position resets and a new position activates — a full capacity-boundary crossing — but the output advances from twenty-three to twenty-four as well, a change of exactly one, the same as the input change. The representation reorganized itself completely; the scalar relationship between input change and output change did not become large at all. Similarly, a relationship machine with a constant output produces no output change whatsoever, regardless of how many capacity boundaries the input crosses while reaching it.

What does make a relationship machine’s output change rapidly near a particular input value is a property of the relationship machine’s own definition: how fast its output’s rate of change grows as the input approaches that value. This is exactly what the conventional derivative measures, and the factorial-basis representation does not substitute for defining it. A capacity boundary is relevant to this question only indirectly, through a different route explored next: the finest available input step, which does depend on scope, but on the scope of the fractional positions, not on how close the input is to its next integer capacity boundary.

What “Approaching Zero” Means

The limit definition of the derivative in conventional calculus takes the ratio of output change to input change as the input change approaches zero. This is the source of the infinitesimal problem: zero input change means no change, which makes the ratio undefined, so the limit must approach zero without reaching it.

In the algebraic system, the question is not about changes approaching zero in the abstract. The question is about the smallest input change the system can currently represent, and that smallest change is governed by the fractional positions introduced for fractions, not by the integer positions that govern magnitude. At fractional scope depth f — meaning fractional positions negative one through negative f are realized — the finest available input step is the weight of the deepest realized fractional position, which is one divided by (f+1)-factorial. This quantity decreases toward zero as f increases: one-half at f equal to one, one-sixth at f equal to two, one twenty-fourth at f equal to three, and so on without bound. This is the algebraic system’s direct counterpart to Δx approaching zero: the finest representable step shrinks as fractional scope deepens, and unlike a limit, each step along the way is an exact, nameable value, not an approach to an unreachable target.

Given a relationship machine and an input value x, the finite difference quotient at fractional scope depth f is the output change when x advances by one divided by (f+1)-factorial, divided by that same step size. This quotient is a specific, computable number at every finite f; no limit is required to compute it at any given depth. Whether this sequence of finite quotients converges to the conventional derivative as f grows, and how quickly, depends on the relationship machine’s own behavior near x, exactly as it does in conventional numerical analysis: for a relationship machine whose output changes smoothly and predictably near x, the finite quotients approach the conventional derivative, with an error that shrinks as the step size shrinks; for a relationship machine with a genuine discontinuity or an undefined output near x, the finite quotients may fail to settle on any single value no matter how small the step becomes. The factorial basis makes the step size and the resulting quotient exact and visible at every depth. It does not, by itself, guarantee that the sequence of quotients converges; that still depends on the relationship machine being differentiable at the point in question, the same requirement conventional calculus imposes.

The conventional limit is a way of expressing the target this sequence of finite quotients approaches, when it does approach one, while avoiding the formal problem of infinitesimals. The algebraic system makes each term in that sequence an exact, computable value at a named fractional scope depth, and the question of convergence to a single limiting value is a genuine mathematical question about the relationship machine, not something the representation settles automatically.

What Calculus Is Looking At

With this reframing in place, the two central operations of calculus become describable in structural terms.

The derivative is a measure of how sensitive the output state of a relationship machine is to changes in the input state, evaluated at a specific location in the state space, computed as the limit of finite quotients at increasing fractional scope depth, when that limit exists. A relationship machine can be highly sensitive, mildly sensitive, or constant near a given input value; which of these holds is a property of the relationship machine’s own definition, not of how close the input happens to be to an integer capacity boundary. At a location where the relationship machine’s defining constraint cannot produce any valid output state at all — such as a division relationship machine whose divisor is zero — no finite quotient can be formed, and sensitivity is undefined there, which means the relationship machine does not apply at that location.

The integral is a measure of the total output of a relationship machine accumulated over a region of the input’s state space, as a weighted sum of exact finite samples taken at some fractional scope, converging to a single value as the scope deepens and the samples grow finer and more numerous. Chapter 20 defines the sample weighting precisely; the summary here is that the integral accumulates output across a region rather than describing output at a single point, the way the derivative does.

Both operations describe properties of the relationship between a relationship state machine and the region of the state space where it operates. The derivative describes local sensitivity. The integral describes global accumulation. Neither requires infinitely small numbers. Neither requires limiting arguments as a foundational justification. Both require only the structure of the state space and the relationship machines that operate within it.

Why Calculus Has Always Worked

The conventional calculus, with its limits and infinitesimals and epsilon-delta definitions, has always worked. It has produced correct results for three hundred years of applied mathematics, engineering, physics, and economics. The question is not whether conventional calculus works. The question is why it works, and whether the explanation is the simplest one available.

The explanation that the algebraic system provides is that conventional calculus is an accurate description of local sensitivity and global accumulation among relationship machines, expressed in a notation that must use limiting arguments because the number line cannot directly represent a sequence of exact finite quotients at increasing precision. The limits and the infinitesimals are workarounds for the gap between the one-dimensional representation and the sequence of exact fractional-scope quotients being described. They are not the thing itself. They are the shadows the thing casts on a line.

When the full structure is available, the shadows are no longer needed. The derivative is the limit of a sequence of exact finite quotients at increasing fractional scope. The integral is an accumulation of exact finite samples, weighted appropriately, at increasing fractional scope. The fundamental theorem connecting them is a structural consequence of how accumulation and local rate of change relate, developed carefully in Chapter 20. No infinitesimal is required at any step. What is required is the same convergence reasoning conventional analysis has always used, now applied to an exact, nameable sequence instead of an abstract limiting process.

The Chapters That Follow

Chapter 19 develops the derivative in concrete terms. It examines familiar calculus results, shows what each one’s sequence of finite quotients looks like at increasing fractional scope, and is explicit about which results follow directly from the factorial-basis representation and which still require the same differentiability reasoning conventional calculus uses.

Chapter 20 develops the integral as a weighted accumulation of finite samples. It connects integration to the infinite series discussion from Chapter 8, shows how integrating a series-defined function accumulates its relationship machine’s terms, and works through the fundamental theorem of calculus as a finite telescoping identity whose correspondence to the continuous case requires the same hypotheses conventional analysis requires.

Chapter 21 looks back at the conventional calculus curriculum and identifies precisely which steps become unnecessary once the structural picture is in place. The difficulty of calculus as it is taught is real. Its source is the mismatch between the representation and the thing being represented. Removing the mismatch removes the difficulty.

Chapter 19Derivatives as Boundary Proximity

11 min read

The standard introduction to derivatives begins with a picture. Draw a curve. Pick a point on the curve. Draw a line that touches the curve at exactly that point without crossing it. The slope of that line is the derivative. This is the tangent line definition, and it is geometrically intuitive enough that most students grasp it quickly.

The definition works as a visual entry point, but it describes a construction rather than a meaning. Slope is rise over run: the ratio of vertical change to horizontal change. Saying the derivative is slope says how to compute it geometrically, not what the result is telling the system. Students who push past the computation and ask what a derivative is measuring typically receive an answer involving rates of change, instantaneous velocity, or the limit of a difference quotient. All of these are correct, and none of them fully satisfies the question.

The algebraic system provides a concrete alternative. The derivative of a relationship machine’s output with respect to its input, evaluated at a particular input value, is the limit of a sequence of exact finite quotients computed at increasing fractional scope depth: at depth f, advance the input by the finest representable step, one divided by (f+1)-factorial, and divide the resulting output change by that same step. Each term in this sequence is an exact, computable number. Whether the sequence converges to a single value, and what that value is, depends on the relationship machine’s own behavior near the input in question — exactly the dependency conventional calculus expresses through differentiability, not a property that the factorial-basis representation supplies on its own.

Every result in calculus that involves derivatives can still be understood through this sequence of finite quotients. The chapter works through the principal cases, including one worked numerically in full.

Constant Output: Zero Derivative

The simplest relationship machine assigns the output a fixed value regardless of the input. Whatever state the input variable occupies, the output variable remains in the same state. The output does not respond to input changes.

At every fractional scope depth, advancing the input by the finest representable step produces no change in the output at all, because the output never changes. The finite quotient at every depth is therefore zero divided by the step size, which is zero. The sequence of finite quotients is constant at zero, so its limit is zero.

The derivative is zero. This matches the conventional result for any constant function, and it follows directly from the output genuinely not responding to the input, not from any claim about scope boundaries.

Linear Output: Constant Derivative

A linear relationship machine assigns the output a state that advances at a fixed rate as the input advances. Each unit advance in the input produces a fixed advance in the output. The ratio of output change to input change is constant everywhere in the valid region.

At fractional scope depth f, advancing the input by the step one divided by (f+1)-factorial produces an output change of that same fixed rate times the step. Dividing by the step recovers the fixed rate exactly, at every depth. The sequence of finite quotients is constant at the fixed rate, so its limit is that same rate, with no need to let the depth grow at all.

The derivative of a linear relationship is constant. This matches the conventional result: the derivative of a straight line is its slope, the same at every point, because the finite quotient already equals that slope exactly at every finite scope depth.

A Worked Example: The Quadratic Case

A quadratic relationship machine assigns the output the square of the input. Unlike the constant and linear cases, the finite quotient for a quadratic relationship machine is not the same at every scope depth; it changes as the depth increases, and tracking how it changes is instructive.

Take the input value two. The output at two is four. Compute the finite quotient at increasing fractional scope depth, using the step one divided by (f+1)-factorial at each depth f:

At depth one, the step is one-half. The input advances to two and one-half. The output becomes six and one-quarter. The output change is two and one-quarter. Dividing by the step of one-half gives four and one-half.

At depth two, the step is one-sixth. The input advances to two and one-sixth. The output becomes approximately four point six nine four. The output change is approximately zero point six nine four. Dividing by the step of one-sixth gives approximately four point one six seven, or exactly twenty-five sixths.

At depth three, the step is one twenty-fourth. The finite quotient works out to exactly ninety-seven twenty-fourths, approximately four point zero four two.

At depth four, the step is one one-hundred-twentieth. The finite quotient works out to exactly four hundred eighty-one one-hundred-twentieths, approximately four point zero zero eight.

The sequence of finite quotients, four and one-half, then twenty-five sixths, then ninety-seven twenty-fourths, then four hundred eighty-one one-hundred-twentieths, is approaching four, and it keeps getting closer as the fractional scope deepens. This matches the conventional result: the derivative of the square of x is two times x, which at x equals two is four. The algebraic system reaches this value as the limit of an exact, computable sequence, with every term in the sequence an honest finite quotient rather than an approximation whose error is hidden.

This is the behavior of any polynomial with a positive leading term: the finite-quotient sequence at a given input value converges to the conventional derivative at that value, and the convergence can be verified term by term rather than asserted.

The Reciprocal: A Genuine Analytic Blow-Up

Consider a relationship machine whose output is the reciprocal of the input: the output is one divided by the input. As the input approaches zero from positive values, the output grows without bound, and the conventional derivative, negative one divided by the input squared, also grows without bound in magnitude. This growth is a real analytic fact about the reciprocal relationship near zero; it holds regardless of how the input and output are represented, and the sequence of finite quotients at increasing fractional scope depth, evaluated at inputs approaching zero, reflects this genuine blow-up rather than any artifact of the factorial-basis representation.

At exactly zero input, the relationship machine itself has no valid output: dividing by zero produces the DivisionUndefined outcome described in Appendix A, not a number. No finite quotient can be formed there, because there is no output value to take a difference of. The derivative is undefined at zero for the ordinary reason that the function itself is undefined there, not because any representational scope boundary has been reached.

The Square Root: Derivative Grows Large Near Zero

The square root relationship machine assigns the output a state whose square equals the input. At input zero, the output is zero. As the input grows, the output grows more slowly: the derivative decreases.

The derivative of the square root at input zero is a specific case that conventional calculus describes as tending toward infinity as the input approaches zero from positive values: the derivative of the square root of x is one divided by twice the square root of x, and as x approaches zero from above, this quantity grows without bound. This is a genuine analytic fact about the square root relationship near zero, confirmed by the sequence of finite quotients at inputs close to zero and increasing fractional scope depth: each quotient is large, and the quotients grow larger as the input moves closer to zero. The growth is a property of the square root relationship itself, not an artifact of how input and output are represented.

As the input grows larger, the derivative decreases, matching the same formula: one divided by twice the square root of x shrinks as x grows. Far from zero, the square root function has a small, slowly changing derivative.

At zero, the behavior depends on the direction of approach. Approaching from positive values, the output is real and the derivative grows without bound, as described. Approaching from negative values, no real output state exists at all: the square root of a negative number has no state in a one-dimensional values state machine, so no finite quotient can even be formed, and the derivative is undefined from that direction for the same reason the reciprocal’s derivative is undefined at zero — the function itself has no value there to form a quotient from.

Chapter 13 showed that complex numbers resolve the missing-output problem by adding a second orthogonal axis: with that axis available, the square root of a negative real input has a well-defined output state on the imaginary axis, so the relationship machine is no longer undefined for negative inputs. This does not, however, make the derivative at zero itself finite. Zero remains a genuine singular point of the square root relationship even with the complex axis available, in the same sense that a branch point in complex analysis is a real feature of the function, not an artifact of restricting to one dimension. What the second axis resolves is the domain of the relationship machine; what it does not resolve is the behavior of the derivative exactly at the one point where the relationship is singular.

What Each Derivative Result Is Reporting

The pattern across these cases is consistent, once stated in terms of the finite-quotient sequence rather than boundary distance. A zero derivative reports that the output genuinely does not respond to small input changes near that point. A constant nonzero derivative reports a uniform rate of response, the same at every input value. A derivative that grows with the input, as in the quadratic case, reports a rate of response that itself depends on where the input is. A derivative that grows without bound as the input approaches a specific value, as in the reciprocal and square root cases, reports a genuine analytic singularity in the relationship machine at that value. An undefined derivative reports that the relationship machine has no valid output at the input in question, so no finite quotient can be formed there at all.

These are four different readings of the same underlying computation: the limit, when it exists, of a sequence of exact finite quotients taken at increasing fractional scope depth. The factorial basis makes every term in that sequence exact and visible. It does not, by itself, change what the limit is or whether it exists; that is a property of the relationship machine being evaluated, exactly as it is in conventional calculus. What changes is that the sequence of approximations leading to the limit is no longer hidden inside a single symbolic limiting argument — each one is a specific, checkable number at a named scope depth.

This account is more concrete than the conventional symbolic rules, without claiming to replace the underlying mathematics. A student who computes several terms of the finite-quotient sequence by hand, as in the quadratic example above, sees the convergence directly rather than taking it on the authority of a differentiation rule. That transparency is the genuine advantage; it is not a claim that convergence happens automatically or that every relationship machine’s derivative is somehow already known from the representation alone.

Derivatives in the Running Example

The algebraic system entity holds x, y, z, and e, with the relationship machine for z defining z as a function of x and y. Consider a modification: define z as the square of x plus one, divided by x. This relationship machine is undefined at x equal to zero, because the division relationship machine has no valid output there, and it has a well-behaved derivative for every nonzero input state, diverging as x approaches zero from either direction, in the same manner as the plain reciprocal relationship examined earlier in this chapter.

The relationship machine monitors x continuously. When x is in a state far from zero, the output z changes moderately in response to small changes in x, and the finite-quotient sequence at such an input converges to a finite value. As x approaches zero, the finite-quotient sequence, evaluated at inputs near zero, grows without bound, matching the analytic fact that one minus one divided by x squared diverges as x approaches zero. At x equal to zero itself, no finite quotient can be formed, because the relationship machine has no output there at all.

The derivative is not something computed separately from the relationship machine. It is the limit, when one exists, of the finite-quotient sequence taken at the relationship machine’s output, evaluated at a specified input value and increasing fractional scope depth. Computing the derivative means computing enough terms of that sequence to see what it is converging toward, or to see that it is diverging, as in this example near zero.

Into Integration

The next chapter examines integration, which accumulates the output of a relationship machine across a region of the input state space. Where the derivative describes the relationship machine’s local behavior at a single point, the integral describes the relationship machine’s global behavior across an entire region.

The connection between the two is developed carefully in the next chapter rather than assumed here. The derivative measures a local rate of change, as the limit of a finite-quotient sequence. The integral accumulates output across a region, as the limit of a weighted sum of finite samples. That accumulating a rate of change recovers total change is the content of the fundamental theorem of calculus, and Chapter 20 derives it as a finite telescoping identity before discussing what must hold for that identity to carry over to the continuous case.

Chapter 20Integration as State Accumulation

13 min read

The standard introduction to integration presents it as the area under a curve. Given a function and two boundary values on the horizontal axis, the integral is the area of the region bounded above by the curve, below by the axis, and on the sides by vertical lines at the two boundary values. The picture is geometric and accessible. Students can see what is being measured.

Then the calculation method arrives, and the picture recedes. Computing the area requires the Riemann sum construction: divide the region into thin vertical strips, compute the area of each strip by multiplying its width by the function’s value at some point within the strip, sum all the strips, and then take the limit as the strip width approaches zero. This limiting process is the same machinery that appeared in the derivative definition, and it carries the same formal weight. The area picture promised intuition; the Riemann sum delivers rigor at the cost of complexity.

The algebraic system does not need the Riemann sum construction in the same form, but it does need the same idea the Riemann sum captures: accumulation is a sum of output values weighted by the step size, not a bare sum of output values. Integration is weighted state accumulation: at a given fractional scope depth, the input advances in steps of size one divided by (f+1)-factorial, and at each step the relationship machine’s output is multiplied by that step size before being added to a running total. The weighting matters, and the next section works through why.

What Accumulation Means

Throughout this book, state machines have been described as occupying positions. A variable is in a state. The state is a position in the factorial-basis space. The variable’s value is its current position.

Consider why the weighting is necessary before defining accumulation formally. Take a relationship machine whose output is always one, regardless of input, and accumulate it over the interval from zero to one. At fractional scope depth two, the step size is one-sixth, and there are six steps across the interval. If each step contributed its raw output value of one, unweighted, the total would be six — growing without bound as scope deepens and the step count increases, even though the region being measured has not changed. This cannot be what the integral of a constant function over a fixed interval is reporting; the conventional integral of the constant one from zero to one is one, not something that grows with precision.

Weighting each step’s contribution by the step size resolves this. At fractional scope depth two, each of the six steps contributes one times one-sixth, and the six contributions sum to exactly one. At fractional scope depth three, the step size is one twenty-fourth, there are twenty-four steps, and each contributes one times one twenty-fourth, summing to exactly one again. The weighted total correctly stays at one regardless of scope depth, for the constant function, which is what a correct notion of accumulation over a fixed region must do.

Accumulation, defined correctly, is the process of advancing the input through a bounded region in steps of size one divided by (f+1)-factorial, recording the relationship machine’s output at each step, multiplying that output by the step size, and summing these weighted contributions. This is precisely what an integral approximates. The integral of a relationship machine’s output from input state a to input state b is the limit of this weighted sum as the fractional scope depth f grows without bound, when that limit exists.

No infinitesimal is invoked at any finite depth: every weighted sum at a given depth is a finite sum of exact values, computed from a finite number of exact steps. What requires the same care conventional analysis always has is whether the sequence of weighted sums, taken at increasing depth, converges to a single value — this depends on the relationship machine’s behavior across the region, exactly as Riemann integrability does in the conventional setting.

The Connection to Scope

The description above assumes the input advances in steps of size one divided by (f+1)-factorial, which shrinks as the fractional scope depth f increases. At a low fractional scope, each step is comparatively large and the weighted sum uses few samples. At a higher fractional scope, each step is smaller, more samples fit within the same region, and the weighted sum uses more of them.

As the fractional scope deepens, the weighted sum typically becomes a better approximation to the integral the relationship machine defines over that region, for the same reason a Riemann sum with thinner strips typically approximates an integral more closely. Both the weighted factorial-basis sum and the Riemann sum are sequences of exact finite values indexed by a shrinking step size; whether either sequence converges, and to what value, is a property of the function being accumulated.

This is the algebraic system’s version of what the Riemann sum construction achieves. The Riemann sum makes the strips thinner and thinner to approach the exact area, taking a limit as strip width approaches zero. The algebraic system deepens the fractional scope, making the input steps finer and finer, with the weighted sum approaching the same limiting value under the same convergence conditions. The two constructions are the same idea, expressed with an exact, nameable step size at every stage rather than an abstract limiting variable.

The result at any finite fractional scope is not an approximation in the sense of being imprecise; it is an exact weighted sum of exact values, computed at that scope’s step size. Whether it equals the integral depends on how far from the limit that particular depth happens to be; the gap is visible and, for well-behaved functions, shrinks as the depth increases, the same way the finite-quotient sequence’s gap to the true derivative shrinks in Chapter 19.

A Worked Example: Constant and Linear Accumulation

Take the interval from zero to one, and a relationship machine whose output is always one, regardless of input. At fractional scope depth two, the step size is one-sixth, so the interval contains exactly six steps. Each step contributes its output, one, times the step size, one-sixth, giving one-sixth per step. Summing six contributions of one-sixth each gives exactly one. At fractional scope depth three, the step size is one twenty-fourth, the interval contains twenty-four steps, and each contributes one twenty-fourth; summing twenty-four of them again gives exactly one. The weighted accumulation of the constant function one, over the unit interval, is exactly one at every fractional scope depth checked, matching the conventional integral of one from zero to one.

Now take a relationship machine whose output equals its input, over the same interval from zero to one, using the left endpoint of each step to evaluate the output. At fractional scope depth one, the step size is one-half, there are two steps, and the weighted sum is one-quarter. At fractional scope depth two, the step size is one-sixth, there are six steps, and the weighted sum is five-twelfths, which is approximately zero point four one seven. At fractional scope depth three, the step size is one twenty-fourth, there are twenty-four steps, and the weighted sum is twenty-three forty-eighths, approximately zero point four seven nine. The sequence one-quarter, five-twelfths, twenty-three forty-eighths is approaching one-half, matching the conventional integral of x from zero to one, which is one-half. The left-endpoint convention used here systematically underestimates a function that is increasing across the interval, which is why each term in the sequence falls just below one-half rather than oscillating around it; a right-endpoint or midpoint convention converges to the same limit from a different side.

This establishes, for these two simple cases, that state accumulation and Riemann summation are the same process in different notation: both produce a sequence of exact, finite, weighted sums that converge to the conventional integral as the step size shrinks, under the same conditions on the function being integrated.

Integration of Series-Defined Functions

Chapter 8 introduced constants as variables with definitions, subject to a bounded-coefficient condition that guarantees convergence. The variable e is defined by the series whose n-th term is one divided by n-factorial, and this series meets that condition.

Now consider integrating a series-defined relationship machine whose terms meet the same bounded-coefficient condition. The relationship machine’s output at any input state is the sum of the series’ terms up to the current fractional scope. Integrating this relationship machine across a region, using the weighted accumulation defined above, accumulates each realized term’s contribution across the region.

When the series meets the bounded-coefficient condition, each term’s accumulation converges on its own, and the accumulated total is the sum of these term-by-term accumulations, by the same comparison argument used in Chapter 8 to establish the series’ own convergence. This holds at every fractional scope depth realized so far, with the gap to the full infinite accumulation bounded the same way the gap in a partial sum is bounded.

This is a genuine advantage over an unweighted or informal termwise approach: because the bounded-coefficient condition is checked once, up front, the term-by-term accumulation is justified without needing to separately verify convergence for the integrated series — a real simplification, though it follows from the bounded-coefficient condition established in Chapter 8, not from the digit positions alone.

The Fundamental Theorem

The fundamental theorem of calculus states that differentiation and integration are inverse operations. The derivative of the integral of a function is the function itself, and the integral of the derivative of a function gives back the function’s values at the boundary points. This theorem is presented in conventional calculus as a deep and surprising connection between two separately defined operations.

In the algebraic system, a finite version of this connection is an exact identity, true at every fractional scope depth with no approximation at all, and it is worth stating that identity before discussing what it takes to extend it to the continuous case.

Fix a fractional scope depth f, with step size h equal to one divided by (f+1)-factorial, and suppose the region from a to b contains exactly N such steps, so that b equals a plus N times h. At each step i, from zero to N minus one, define the finite quotient at that step as the output change over that single step, f of (a plus (i+1) times h) minus f of (a plus i times h), divided by h. Multiplying this finite quotient by h, to accumulate it the way the previous sections accumulate any output, gives back exactly f of (a plus (i+1) times h) minus f of (a plus i times h) — the step’s own output change, with nothing lost and nothing added, because the division and multiplication by h exactly cancel.

Summing this quantity across all N steps from i equal zero to i equal N minus one telescopes: every interior value of f appears once with a plus sign, from the end of one step, and once with a minus sign, from the start of the next step, and cancels. What remains is f at b minus f at a. This is the statement: accumulating the finite-quotient sequence across a region, at any fixed fractional scope depth, exactly recovers the total output change across that region. This identity holds at every finite depth, for any relationship machine, with no convergence argument needed, because it is pure algebraic cancellation, not a limiting statement.

Extending this finite, exact identity to the familiar continuous statement of the fundamental theorem — that accumulating the true derivative recovers the total change — requires two further things that conventional analysis has always required: that the finite-quotient sequence at each point actually converges to a single derivative value as the fractional scope deepens, established point by point the way Chapter 19 established it for several cases, and that the resulting limiting derivative function is itself well-behaved enough that the accumulation process continues to converge to the exact total change as scope deepens, rather than to some other value. When both hold, the finite identity above converges, term by term, to the familiar continuous fundamental theorem. The factorial basis does not remove the need for these two conditions; it makes the finite, unconditional part of the argument — the telescoping identity itself — visible and exact at every step, separate from the convergence questions that remain genuine mathematical content.

Indefinite Integration as Reverse Navigation

The indefinite integral asks: given a relationship machine for the derivative, what relationship machine for the output would produce that derivative? This is the reverse navigation problem from Chapter 16, applied to relationship machines rather than to individual states.

Chapter 16 showed that factorial boundaries are navigation landmarks: given the boundary and the distance from it, the target state is fully determined. Given the accumulated total at each point along the way and the accumulated total at the starting point, the intermediate states are fully determined.

Indefinite integration is finding the relationship machine that, when its finite-quotient derivative is taken, matches the specified derivative machine. This is a well-posed problem whenever the specified derivative values are consistent with some accumulation: given the derivative values at every input state in a region, the weighted accumulation from any fixed starting point determines the output at every other point in that region, by the finite telescoping identity established above. The indefinite integral is the accumulation from the starting point.

The constant of integration, which appears in every indefinite integral in conventional calculus, corresponds to the choice of starting point in the accumulation. Different starting points produce different totals at the same input state, differing by a constant offset. The constant of integration is not an arbitrary mathematical convention. It is the starting state of the accumulation, which the indefinite integral problem leaves unspecified until boundary conditions are provided.

What Integration Is Not Requiring

The preceding account of integration required no infinitely small quantities. No limit of strip widths was taken in the construction of the weighted sum at any single fractional scope depth. The accumulation was a finite, weighted sum at every depth. The scope could be deepened to approach the limiting value more closely, but at any depth the weighted sum itself was exact.

The Riemann sum construction is a correct method for computing integrals, and the comparison here is not that the factorial basis replaces it but that the two constructions are the same idea in different notation: both build a sequence of exact finite weighted sums indexed by a shrinking step size, and both require the same convergence conditions on the function being integrated for that sequence to settle on a single value. The factorial basis makes each term in the sequence a named, exact value at a named depth, which the Riemann sum’s language of strip width approaching zero does not emphasize as clearly, but the underlying mathematical content — a sequence of finite sums converging under suitable hypotheses — is the same in both.

A student who learns integration through weighted state accumulation in the factorial basis will see each partial sum as an honest, exact value at a named step size, not as a hidden approximation. The student still needs the same convergence reasoning conventional analysis requires to conclude what the sequence of partial sums is approaching, but every term along the way is transparent and checkable, rather than folded into a single symbolic limiting expression.

Closing Part 5 in the Next Chapter

Chapter 21 looks back at the conventional calculus curriculum with the structural picture now complete. The difficulty of calculus is real. Students who struggle with it are not failing to understand something that should be easy. They are struggling with a presentation that requires careful management of objects that cannot be directly expressed in the number-line model. Chapter 21 names the specific points where the conventional presentation introduces this complexity, and shows what each of those points looks like when the structural account is available instead.

Chapter 21Why Calculus Felt Hard

10 min read

Students who struggled with calculus were often told that the subject requires a special kind of mathematical maturity. The informal explanations are intuitive enough, but when it comes time to work with the formal definitions, many students find that intuition stops helping. The gap between understanding what a derivative means informally and being able to work with the epsilon-delta definition of a limit is, for many people, where calculus becomes genuinely difficult.

The conventional response is to attribute the difficulty to the abstraction level required. Limits, continuity, and the formal definition of the derivative demand comfort with quantified statements and with reasoning about behavior “as something approaches something else.” This is held to be inherently harder than the concrete arithmetic and algebra that precede calculus in the curriculum.

That explanation is wrong. The difficulty does not come from the abstraction level. It comes from a specific structural mismatch: the number line cannot directly represent the concepts that calculus needs to express, so calculus invented workarounds for the mismatch. The workarounds are what students find hard. The concepts themselves, expressed in the algebraic system, are straightforward. Looking back across the three calculus chapters, the sources of difficulty can be named precisely and traced to their structural origin.

The Infinitesimal Problem

The original inventors of calculus used infinitely small quantities. Newton’s fluxions and Leibniz’s differentials both relied on quantities that were small enough to be negligible when added to ordinary numbers but large enough to serve as denominators. This is logically incoherent on the number line: no positive number can be both nonzero and smaller than every positive number.

The workaround was to treat infinitesimals as a useful fiction: employ them in calculations, obtain correct results, and accept that the formal justification would come later. The formal justification, when it arrived in the nineteenth century, replaced infinitesimals with limits. This resolved the logical problem by changing the question. Instead of asking about infinitely small quantities, limits ask about the behavior of a ratio as its denominator approaches zero. The denominator never actually reaches zero, so the division-by-zero problem never arises formally.

In the algebraic system, there is no infinitesimal problem. The minimum advance available to the input at any scope is the unit of that scope’s lowest position. As the scope expands, that unit becomes smaller, providing finer resolution. The process of expanding scope and recomputing is what the limit is approximating. The algebraic system does this directly by expanding scope, without needing to describe a ratio approaching a value it never reaches. The concept that limits were designed to express is naturally available in the algebraic system as scope expansion.

The Epsilon-Delta Definition

The formal definition of a limit states that a function approaches a value L as the input approaches a point c if, for every positive number epsilon, there exists a positive number delta such that whenever the input is within delta of c but not equal to c, the output is within epsilon of L.

This definition is logically precise and pedagogically impenetrable. Students who understand what a limit is intuitively rarely find the epsilon-delta definition illuminating. It reads as a formal restatement of “getting close” using quantifiers that require careful parsing. Most students learn to use the definition for simple proofs without acquiring a structural understanding of why the definition has that specific form.

In the algebraic system, the concept the epsilon-delta definition is capturing is direct. Epsilon is the precision required in the output. Delta is the scope within which the input must remain to guarantee that output precision. The definition is saying: for any required output precision, there is a scope of input precision that achieves it. This is the statement that the relationship machine is well-behaved at the point c, meaning the scope of the output at any depth is determined by the scope of the input at that depth. The epsilon-delta definition is formalizing scope-to-scope correspondence between input and output in the number-line language. In the algebraic system, this is the normal behavior of a continuous relationship machine.

Continuity and Its Definition

A function is continuous at a point if its limit at that point exists and equals the function’s value at that point. A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point in the interval. The definition is a composition of the limit definition, and it inherits all of the limit definition’s complexity.

In the algebraic system, continuity is the property of a relationship machine that is valid throughout its scope. A continuous relationship machine produces a valid output state for every input state within the valid region, with no gaps, no jumps, and no scope boundaries cutting through the interior of the region. The machine transitions smoothly from one output state to the next as the input advances, because scope expansion and carry events within the relationship machine are handled gracefully.

A discontinuity in the algebraic system is a location where the relationship machine either has no valid output (undefined derivative, as in Chapter 19) or jumps to a different output region without a continuous path. The jump corresponds to a scope boundary in the relationship between input and output: the relationship machine changes behavior sharply at the boundary, and the output state is in a different region after the boundary than before it.

Continuity is a structural property of the relationship machine, not a separately defined property requiring its own limiting arguments. The algebraic system either has a valid state at each input or it does not. When it does, throughout a region, the relationship machine is continuous. The concept does not require the apparatus of limits to state.

The Area Interpretation and Its Complications

The area interpretation of integration is genuinely useful. Representing the integral as the area under a curve gives a geometric picture that helps students verify results and develop intuition. The problem is not the area picture itself. The problem is what the area picture requires to be made rigorous.

The Riemann sum construction divides the region into strips, computes the area of each strip approximately, and then takes the limit as the strips become infinitely thin. Every step in this construction requires justification. Why does the approximation converge? Why is the limit independent of how the strips are chosen within each subdivision? Why do left-endpoint and right-endpoint sums converge to the same value? These questions require real analysis to answer fully, and most calculus students never see the answers.

In the algebraic system, none of these questions arise. The accumulation is exact at every scope. The states being accumulated are discrete and countable. No strip width is being varied. No approximation is being refined. The accumulated total at scope n is the exact integral at that scope’s resolution, and expanded scope gives a more precise exact result. There is no gap between the approximation and the exact value, because there is no approximation.

The Fundamental Theorem as Surprise

In the conventional presentation, the fundamental theorem of calculus is a surprising and profound result. The derivative and the integral were defined independently, each through a separate limiting process, and the theorem reveals that they are inverse operations. This feels like a deep discovery.

The feeling of surprise is produced by the independent definitions. When derivative and integral are both defined through limiting processes that look different from each other, their connection is not visible in the definitions. The proof of the fundamental theorem must work to establish the connection.

In the algebraic system, the connection is immediate from the structural definitions. The derivative at each input state is the rate at which the output advances per unit of input advance. The integral from a to b is the total output advance from a to b. Summing the rates of output advance at each step from a to b gives the total output advance from a to b. This is an arithmetic observation, not a deep theorem. The fundamental theorem is surprising only when derivative and integral are defined in ways that conceal their structural relationship.

Indeterminate Forms

Calculus courses include a collection of techniques for handling expressions that appear to be zero divided by zero or infinity divided by infinity at particular input values. These are called indeterminate forms. L’Hopital’s rule provides a method for evaluating them by replacing the original ratio with the ratio of derivatives.

These cases are instances of two relationship machines simultaneously reaching scope boundaries at the same input value. At the boundary point, both the numerator and denominator are at the edge of their valid scopes. Both are zero (or both are expanding scope simultaneously). The ratio at the boundary is structurally a question about the relative rates of boundary approach of the numerator and denominator as the input approaches the boundary point.

L’Hopital’s rule says that the ratio of the two original functions near the boundary equals the ratio of their derivatives near the boundary. In the algebraic system, this is a statement about relative boundary approach rates. The numerator’s rate of approach to its boundary, compared to the denominator’s rate of approach to its boundary, determines the ratio at the boundary. The derivatives measure those approach rates. The rule is structurally transparent once boundary proximity is understood as the meaning of the derivative.

The mystery of indeterminate forms disappears when boundaries are structural events rather than paradoxical values. Zero divided by zero is not an algebraic disaster. It is two relationship machines that both reach scope boundaries at the same input state. The ratio of their boundary approach rates is well-defined even when both rates individually produce boundary events.

What the Workarounds Were Protecting Against

Looking back across all of the workarounds, a pattern is visible. Every piece of difficult machinery in conventional calculus was protecting against the same underlying problem: the number line has no way to represent boundaries directly.

On the number line, boundaries appear as paradoxical values. Zero is a point that cannot be divided by. Infinity is a value that cannot be reached. The square root of a negative number is a value that does not exist. These are boundaries, but the number line can only represent them as locations where something breaks rather than as structural events that the system handles naturally.

Limits, epsilon-delta definitions, infinitesimals, and the Riemann sum construction are all ways of discussing behavior near boundaries without directly representing the boundaries. They are accurate descriptions of what happens near the boundaries. They are also complex and require careful formal handling because the representation underlying them cannot directly say what they are trying to say.

The algebraic system can say it directly. Boundaries are scope events. Reaching a boundary means expanding scope. Approaching a boundary means moving through states with decreasing remaining capacity in the low-order positions. The boundary is a structural feature of the state space, not a paradox. Once it is described structurally, all the workarounds become unnecessary.

Closing Part 5

Calculus is not an inherently difficult subject. The concepts it contains are natural consequences of the boundary structure of the factorial-basis state space. What is difficult is the conventional presentation, which requires workarounds for a representation mismatch that does not exist in the algebraic system.

Students who found calculus hard were not lacking mathematical maturity. They were responding accurately to a presentation that required accepting objects whose existence the model could not fully justify and learning rules whose structural basis the model could not fully reveal. The difficulty was in the presentation. The mathematics was always coherent.

Part 6 turns from examining individual mathematical topics to the larger question of what this system makes possible. The algebraic system is not a new notation for existing mathematics. It is the structure that existing mathematics was always describing, made directly accessible. Part 6 examines three consequences: what the algebraic system means for computation, what it means for geometry, and what it means for how mathematics can and should be taught.

Part 6

What Becomes Possible

Chapter 22The Algebraic System as Computation

9 min read

There is a gap in the conventional picture of mathematics and computing. Mathematics describes relationships between quantities. Computing implements procedures that transform inputs into outputs. The two disciplines feel like different activities: mathematics is declarative, describing what is true; computing is imperative, specifying what to do. To use mathematics in a program, a developer translates mathematical relationships into computational steps. The relationship z equals x plus y becomes an assignment statement. The derivative of a function becomes a numerical approximation computed by a loop. The mathematical description and the computational implementation are treated as separate things connected by a translation step.

The algebraic system built across this book does not require that translation step. The system is not a description of mathematics that must then be implemented. The system is already computation. The state machines are executable. The events that drive transitions are the inputs the system receives. The transitions are the operations the system performs. The resulting states are the outputs the system produces. The algebraic system and a running computer program are the same kind of thing.

What Makes the System Executable

A system is executable when its description specifies, without ambiguity, what happens next in response to any event. Given the current state and an incoming event, the system’s next state is determined. No additional interpretation is needed. No translation is required. The specification is the execution.

The factorial algebraic system meets this criterion directly. Each state machine has a defined set of valid states and a defined set of valid transitions. An event arrives. The event either matches a defined transition or it does not. If it matches, the state machine transitions to the new state. If it does not match, the state machine remains in its current state. The no-match case is not an error. It is the system reporting that the event does not apply to this machine at this time.

Relationship machines participate in execution in the same way. When an input state machine transitions, the relationship machines that reference it are evaluated. The relationship machine determines whether the output state must change to remain consistent with the new input state. If it must change, the output state machine transitions. If it must not change, the no-change principle applies. No polling is required. No reconstruction is required. The transition of any input immediately drives evaluation of all relationship machines that reference it.

This is constraint propagation as computation. The algebraic system does not wait to be queried. It maintains its state continuously, and when any state changes, the implications of that change propagate through the relationship machines to all affected outputs. The system is always consistent, because the relationship machines enforce consistency as part of the transition mechanism.

The Representation Carries What the System Knows

In a conventional program, the data that a program has computed is stored in variables. When the program needs a value, it reads the variable. If the variable has not been set, the program reads an uninitialized value, which is either a default or an error depending on the language.

The factorial algebraic system handles this differently. The representation carries what the system knows, and it distinguishes between states that have been established by events and states that are inferred defaults. A variable that has never received an event is in the zero state by default, and that zero is not stored. It is inferred. A variable that has received an event is in whatever state that event produced, and that state is carried in the digit configuration of the values state machine.

This distinction is not merely descriptive. It is computationally significant. Inferred zero means the system has not processed any information about this variable yet. No event has arrived that bears on it. Explicit nonzero means the system has processed events and these specific transitions occurred. The representation tells the consuming code not just what the value is but whether the value reflects actual input or a default in the absence of input.

In conventional programs, the difference between “this value is zero because I calculated it” and “this value is zero because nothing happened yet” is invisible in the representation. Both are stored as zero. Distinguishing them requires additional flags, sentinel values, or documentation conventions, all of which are workarounds for a representation that does not carry this information natively.

The factorial algebraic system carries it natively. The inferred zero is structurally different from an explicit zero established by an event, in the same way that an unoccupied digit position is structurally different from an occupied digit position. The representation encodes the computational history of the variable, not just its current value.

Events as Input, States as Output

Every computation receives input and produces output. In the algebraic system, inputs are events. An event is a signal that something has changed: a value has been provided, a condition has been met, a time has elapsed, a user has acted. Events drive transitions. The state machine receives the event, matches it against its defined transitions, and either transitions to a new state or remains in the current state.

Outputs are states. The current state of every state machine in the system is the output available to any other machine that references it. States are not pushed to outputs explicitly. They are maintained continuously by the relationship machines, and any part of the system that needs to read a value reads the current state of the relevant state machine.

This input-output model is more natural for most problem domains than the conventional procedure model. Most real systems respond to events: a payment arrives, a sensor triggers, a request is submitted. The response to an event is a set of state transitions across the system, not a linear sequence of procedure calls from a main function.

In the conventional programming model, responding to events requires queuing systems, callback handlers, polling loops, or reactive frameworks. These are all mechanisms for working around the mismatch between the event-driven nature of the problem and the procedure-driven execution model of the language. The algebraic system does not have this mismatch. Events are the primitive input. State transitions are the primitive response. The model aligns with the problem from the start.

The Algebraic System and the Logical Computer

The algebraic system is one application of the Entity-State Machine structure. An entity holds named state machines. Events drive transitions. Relationship machines propagate changes. The representation carries what the system knows.

The same structure, applied to computing systems rather than mathematical quantities, is the logical computer described in the companion volume, From Numbers to Systems. A logical computer is a computing system modeled as an entity containing state machines for all the information it manages, with events driving transitions and relationship machines enforcing the rules of the domain.

The algebraic system built across this book and the logical computer built in that book are the same idea applied to different problem domains. The algebraic system’s variables are the logical computer’s data elements. The algebraic system’s relationship machines are the logical computer’s business rules. The algebraic system’s constraint propagation is the logical computer’s rule enforcement. The algebraic system’s scope expansion is the logical computer’s capacity growth.

This is not an analogy. The mathematical structure and the computational structure are identical because they are both applications of the Entity-State Machine model. Mathematics is what the model does when its entities represent quantities and its relationship machines represent mathematical constraints. Computing is what the model does when its entities represent information and its relationship machines represent domain rules. The model is the same. The domain is what differs.

A reader who has worked through this book and understands the algebraic system already understands the logical computer’s structure. Applying that understanding to computing systems is the work of From Numbers to Systems. The mathematical and computational domains reinforce each other, because they share the same foundation.

What This Means for Mathematics Software

Conventional mathematics software translates mathematical expressions into computation. A symbolic algebra system parses an expression, builds an internal representation, applies transformation rules, and produces output. The mathematical structure and the computational structure are different. The translation layer between them is a significant source of complexity.

A system built on the factorial algebraic system does not translate. The mathematical structure is the computational structure. Adding the relationship machine z equals x plus y to the entity is the same as implementing the constraint that z must equal x plus y in the running system. The constraint is active from the moment it is added. No translation is needed. No separate enforcement mechanism is needed. The state machine transitions enforce the constraint as a consequence of how state machines work.

This applies at every level of mathematical complexity. The relationship machine for the integral of a series-defined function, when added to the entity, immediately begins accumulating the function’s output as the input advances. The system does not need a numerical integration subroutine. The accumulation is what the relationship machine does. The mathematical definition and the computational behavior are the same description.

Computation Without Polling

One specific consequence worth noting is the elimination of polling. Conventional programs often poll: they periodically check whether a value has changed and act when it has. Polling is a workaround for the lack of a native event-and-transition model. When the program needs to know whether something changed, it asks repeatedly rather than being told once.

The algebraic system is event-driven by construction. When a state changes, every relationship machine that references that state is evaluated immediately. No polling is needed. The state change drives evaluation, and the results propagate through the relationship machines until every dependent state has been updated. The system is always consistent without any mechanism to check for consistency.

This is computationally efficient. Instead of checking all values on every cycle to find the ones that changed, the system processes only the transitions that actually occur. The cost of maintaining consistency is proportional to the number of events that arrive and the number of relationship machines they trigger, not proportional to the size of the entire state space.

For the kinds of systems described in Fixing Fragile Software, this efficiency advantage is significant. Large enterprise systems contain thousands of data elements and hundreds of business rules. Polling all of them continuously is expensive. An event-driven system that propagates only actual changes is efficient by construction.

Closing Part 6 Continues

Chapter 23 extends the algebraic system to geometry, showing how the dimensional structure of the factorial basis generates spatial relationships without requiring distance as a primitive. Chapter 24 returns to the curriculum argument: now that the full system has been presented, the specific curriculum discontinuities from conventional mathematics education can be traced to their source and resolved. Chapter 25 closes the book.

The algebraic system is mathematics as computation and computation as mathematics. The apparent gap between the declarative description of relationships and the imperative execution of procedures closes when both are understood as the same Entity-State Machine structure operating in different domains.

Chapter 23Geometry Without Distance

11 min read

Ask anyone what geometry is about and they will say space. Lines, angles, triangles, circles. The picture that comes to mind is drawn on a flat surface: a white page with pencil marks, a blackboard with chalk figures, a coordinate grid with labeled axes. Geometry feels like the study of shape in space, and space feels like the most primitive thing there is. Space is just there. It is the background against which everything else occurs.

This intuition is wrong in a specific and correctable way. Space is not primitive. Distance is not primitive. Shape is not primitive. All of these are derived from something simpler: the configurations that a system of constraints permits. Geometry is the study of valid state configurations, and valid configurations emerge from the same structure that generates numbers. Space, distance, and shape all follow from the algebraic system’s relationship machines. Nothing additional is required.

Where Dimensions Actually Come From

Chapter 3 established that dimensions emerge from scope depth, not from spatial intuition. The factorial odometer’s first position fills at state 1, and the advance to state 2 forces a second position into existence. The second position is not added to a pre-existing space. It is generated because the system must produce a new distinguishable state and the current structure cannot. The dimension exists because distinguishability requires it.

Two independent factorial odometers — one for each axis — generate a two-dimensional state space. A point in that space is a pair of states: one from each odometer. The two odometers do not interact. No carry crosses from one to the other. This independence is what orthogonality means in the algebraic system: two dimensions are orthogonal when they share no transitions. Movement in one dimension produces no transition in the other. This is not a geometric claim about perpendicular lines drawn at right angles on paper. It is a structural claim about the independence of state machines.

Three independent odometers generate a three-dimensional state space. Four generate a four-dimensional one. The dimensionality of the space is simply the number of independent factorial odometers in the system. No intuition about spatial extent is required, and no visualization of higher dimensions is needed. Four dimensions is four independent odometers. One hundred dimensions is one hundred independent odometers. The structural definition scales without difficulty.

Shape as Relationship Constraint

A line in conventional geometry is defined as an infinite set of points satisfying a linear equation. In the algebraic system, a line is a relationship state machine: a constraint that specifies which combinations of two variables’ states are valid. The relationship y equals mx plus b is a relationship machine that says: for every state of x, the valid state of y is mx plus b. Every state pair that satisfies this constraint is on the line. Every state pair that does not satisfy it is not on the line.

This is more natural than the conventional definition for a concrete reason. The conventional definition begins with points and then asks which points satisfy an equation. The algebraic system begins with the constraint and asks which configurations the constraint permits. The constraint is the definition. The set of valid points is a consequence, not the starting place.

A circle is a relationship machine that constrains two variables such that the sum of their squared distances from a central configuration remains constant. The circle is not the set of all points equidistant from the center. The circle is the constraint. Points satisfying the constraint are valid states. Points not satisfying it fall outside the circle’s valid region.

Curves, surfaces, and higher-dimensional shapes are all relationship state machines that constrain which combinations of variable states are permitted. The shape is the constraint. The geometric figure is the set of configurations that the constraint allows.

Distance as Derived, Not Primitive

Conventional geometry begins with distance. The Euclidean distance between two points is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences. This formula is introduced early and treated as fundamental. Geometry is then built on top of it.

In the factorial algebraic system, distance is a derived quantity. It is the output of a relationship state machine, not an input to the geometry. Two points exist as pairs of states in the two-dimensional state space. A relationship machine that computes the scope difference between them produces a number. That number can be called the distance between the points. But distance is the result of applying a relationship machine to two configurations. It is not the foundation of the geometry.

This distinction matters because it reveals which geometric structures are primitive and which are derived. In conventional geometry, a shape is defined by the distances between its points. An equilateral triangle is a triangle all of whose sides have equal length. In the algebraic system, an equilateral triangle is a set of three configurations related by a constraint that holds the scope differences between each pair equal. The distance equality is a property of the relationship machine, not the starting definition.

Removing distance from the foundations does not weaken geometry. It strengthens it, because the geometry that results is valid for any metric — any definition of distance — and the choice of metric is a choice of relationship machine. Euclidean geometry, Manhattan-distance geometry, and spherical geometry are all the same structural system with different relationship machines defining what “scope difference” means. The framework holds all of them. No separate theory is needed for each.

Local Consistency and Non-Euclidean Geometry

The key insight that unlocks non-Euclidean geometry is recognizing that the constraints in a geometric system need not hold uniformly across the entire state space. They need only hold locally. A set of relationship machines defines what is valid at each configuration. The relationships that hold at one configuration may differ from those at another.

Euclidean geometry is the case where the local constraints are the same everywhere. The parallel postulate — through any point not on a given line, exactly one line exists that does not intersect the given line — holds at every configuration in the Euclidean plane. The relationship machine expressing this constraint has constant parameters across the whole state space.

Spherical geometry replaces this with a different local constraint. On the surface of a sphere, every pair of great circles intersects. No non-intersecting lines exist through any point. The relationship machine for spherical geometry does not permit the parallel case. This is not an exception or a special case. It is a different relationship machine. The geometry follows from the constraint, not from a modification of some presumed universal spatial truth.

Hyperbolic geometry goes in the opposite direction: through any point not on a given line, infinitely many non-intersecting lines exist. Again, a different relationship machine. The geometry follows.

All three geometries are valid. All three are systems of relationship state machines applied to configurations in a multi-dimensional state space. The transition from Euclidean to non-Euclidean geometry is a change of relationship machine, not a discovery that space has a different shape. Space does not have a shape until a relationship machine gives it one.

Geodesics as Sequences of Valid Transitions

A geodesic is the path between two configurations that is locally consistent at every step. In Euclidean space, geodesics are straight lines. In spherical geometry, geodesics are great circles. In hyperbolic geometry, geodesics have a different form. The question “what is the geodesic between two points?” is the question “what sequence of state transitions, each satisfying the local constraint, connects these two configurations?”

The algebraic system answers this naturally. At each configuration, the relationship machine specifies which transitions are valid. The geodesic is the sequence of configurations reachable by valid transitions, where each step stays as close as possible to the direct path. The notion of “direct” is defined by the relationship machine’s local constraint, not by a prior notion of straightness.

This treatment makes geodesics structurally clear. A geodesic is not special because it is straight. It is special because it is the sequence of valid transitions that minimizes the number of steps. Minimizing steps is minimizing the scope of the transitions required to move from one configuration to another. The relationship machine defines the step cost, and the geodesic is the path that minimizes total cost.

Curvature as Rate of Constraint Change

Curvature, in conventional geometry, is defined as a measure of how much a curve deviates from a straight line, or how much a surface deviates from a flat plane. In the algebraic system, curvature has a simpler description: it is the rate of change of the local constraint across state transitions.

A flat plane has constant local constraints. Moving from one configuration to a neighboring one changes the configuration but does not change the relationship machine that applies locally. The local constraint is the same everywhere. Curvature is zero.

A sphere has non-constant local constraints. Moving from one configuration to a neighboring one changes not only the configuration but also the local relationship machine slightly. The amount of change per step is the curvature. A sphere of larger radius has smaller curvature because the local constraint changes more slowly across equivalent steps. A sphere of smaller radius has larger curvature.

The curvature of a surface, in this treatment, is the derivative of the local relationship machine with respect to position. Chapter 19 established derivatives as boundary proximity measures. The curvature derivative is measuring how quickly the constraint boundary changes as the system moves through state space. Curvature and derivative are both instances of the same structural measurement applied to different aspects of the system.

The Simplex and the Natural Geometry of Scope

Chapter 3 introduced simplex geometry as the natural visual for factorial-basis dimensions. The simplex is worth revisiting here, because it connects the algebraic system’s dimensional structure directly to geometry.

A zero-dimensional simplex is a point: a single configuration. A one-dimensional simplex is a line segment: two configurations connected by a transition. A two-dimensional simplex is a triangle: three configurations, each connected to the other two by transitions. A three-dimensional simplex is a tetrahedron: four configurations, each connected to all three others.

At each step, adding a new dimension adds exactly one new vertex and connects it to all existing vertices. The simplex captures the fact that a new dimension is not added to space but added to the structure of reachable configurations. Each new vertex is a new configuration that is distinguishable from all existing configurations and related to them by the same transition structure.

The simplex is the geometry of scope expansion. Each time the factorial odometer fills its current scope and expands, a new vertex is added to the simplex. The geometry of the algebraic system grows with scope. This growth is not spatial in the sense of occupying more room. It is structural in the sense of generating more distinguishable configurations. The simplex tracks which configurations exist and how they are related. Distance within the simplex is the number of transitions required to move between two configurations, which is exactly the scope-difference measure described earlier.

Where This Leads

The algebraic system’s treatment of geometry has consequences beyond the classical geometric figures. Physics describes the universe using geometry: space, time, mass, and energy are related through geometric constraints in Einstein’s general relativity. In that theory, massive objects curve space-time, and the curvature of space-time determines the paths that objects follow.

Translating this into the algebraic system’s language: massive objects change the parameters of the local relationship machines that govern valid transitions in space-time. The geodesics through a region of curved space-time are the sequences of valid state transitions under those relationship machines. The curvature is the rate of change of those parameters across configurations. General relativity, at this level of description, is a system of relationship state machines whose parameters vary across state space. No geometric intuition about bent space is required. The constraint structure is sufficient.

This does not mean the algebraic system supplants the mathematics of general relativity. The mathematical machinery of tensor calculus and differential geometry describes the same structure in detail. What the algebraic system contributes is a clear account of what that machinery is doing: maintaining a system of relationship state machines whose parameters vary by configuration and computing the valid transitions under those constraints. The geometry follows from the constraint structure, just as it has in every example in this chapter.

The Geometry Already Present

The preceding chapters established arithmetic, algebra, and calculus on the factorial algebraic system.
