Each operation arrived as a natural consequence of the system’s structure: addition as state alignment, multiplication as dimensional expansion, derivatives as boundary proximity, integration as state accumulation.

Geometry arrives the same way. Points are configurations. Lines and curves are relationship machines. Distance is a derived scope measurement. Curvature is the rate of change of local constraints. Non-Euclidean geometry is geometry with different relationship machines. Geodesics are sequences of valid transitions.

None of this requires a separate foundation. Space does not have to be assumed. Distance does not have to be taken as primitive. The geometry grows from the same system that generated counting, arithmetic, and calculus. The algebraic system always contained geometry. Building it out was a matter of recognizing the relationship machines that were already present.

Chapter 24What This Means for How We Teach Mathematics

12 min read

Most students who struggle with mathematics believe the fault is theirs. They tried, they followed the procedures, and at some point something stopped making sense and never started again. The explanations teachers gave were clear enough — the steps were demonstrable, the rules were memorable — but the underlying logic never clicked. Eventually the student concluded that mathematics required a particular kind of mind, and they did not have it.

This diagnosis is wrong. The students who struggle with mathematics are not failing because of a deficit in their thinking. They are failing because the model they were given is broken. The model makes promises it later withdraws. It builds intuitions it later dismantles. It asks students to trust a framework and then informs them, repeatedly, that the framework they trusted was only a simplified version of something more complicated. Students who struggle with mathematics are often the ones who took the framework seriously. Their trust was the problem.

The Seven Discontinuities

A conventional mathematics education contains at least seven moments where students are told that what they learned before was incomplete or wrong. These are not rare edge cases. They are structural features of the conventional model, built into the curriculum at every level.

The first discontinuity occurs in early arithmetic. Students are taught that you cannot subtract a larger number from a smaller one. Four minus seven has no answer. This is stated as a fact. Later, the curriculum introduces negative numbers and informs students that four minus seven equals negative three. The earlier statement was not just incomplete; it was a barrier, a rule that must now be dismantled. Students who built the rule carefully into their understanding of subtraction must now unlearn it.

The second discontinuity occurs when division is introduced. Students learn that division must come out evenly. Twenty divided by four equals five. Twenty divided by three has no clean answer, or produces a remainder that is set aside. Later, fractions arrive and the earlier restriction is lifted: twenty divided by three equals six and two thirds. The division that was formerly inadmissible is now routine. The restriction was never mathematically necessary. It was a limitation of the integer model that the curriculum presented as a general truth.

The third discontinuity is more conceptual. Multiplication is taught as repeated addition. Three times four means adding three groups of four, or four groups of three. This definition works for integers. When the curriculum reaches irrational numbers, this definition stops working. Multiplying the square root of two by the square root of three cannot be understood as repeated addition of any number of groups. When students reach matrices, the repeated-addition model fails entirely: matrix multiplication follows different rules. The intuition built on repeated addition must be replaced with a more abstract definition. For many students, this replacement never fully takes hold, and multiplication of non-integers remains procedural rather than understood.

The fourth discontinuity involves variables. Early algebra teaches that a variable holds an unknown value. The problem says “let x equal the number of apples” and the student solves for x. This framing works for simple equations. When the curriculum advances to functions, variables change role entirely. x is no longer an unknown value to be found. x is the input to a function, ranging across all valid inputs. f(x) is the output corresponding to each input. Students who built a careful model of variables as unknown fixed quantities must now rebuild their understanding of what a variable is. Some never complete this rebuild, and functions remain opaque.

The fifth discontinuity involves negative numbers under square roots. Students are taught that you cannot take the square root of a negative number. The square root of negative one does not exist. This is presented as a mathematical impossibility, not a model limitation. Later, complex numbers arrive and the square root of negative one is assigned the name i. The impossible thing is now possible, with a new name. Students are not wrong to feel that the rules have changed, because the rules have changed. The model that declared the square root of negative one impossible has been replaced with a model that accommodates it, and the earlier declaration is quietly forgotten.

The sixth discontinuity occurs in precalculus. Slopes are introduced as the measure of how a function changes: rise over run, a ratio of two finite differences. This intuition carries students through linear functions and basic rate problems. When calculus arrives, slopes are replaced by derivatives, and derivatives require limits. The finite differences of slope calculations are replaced by infinitesimal increments that are not actually zero but behave as zero in the limit. The slope intuition, carefully built, is now a useful approximation of a more technical concept. Students who took the slope definition at face value must now accept that the definition they understood was a simplification.

The seventh discontinuity is the largest. Calculus is introduced as working because of infinitely small quantities. Infinitesimals are described as numbers so small they can be treated as zero when added to ordinary numbers. This is how the derivative is motivated and how integration is explained. Later, in real analysis, students learn that infinitesimals are not real numbers at all. The calculus they learned was correct in its results but not in its foundations. The limiting process that makes calculus rigorous is technically different from the infinitesimal intuition that made calculus accessible. Students who found calculus intuitive through infinitesimals may find real analysis bewildering, because the intuition they relied on is being replaced rather than extended.

What Each Discontinuity Costs

At every transition, a student must do two things simultaneously. The first is learning the new model: negative numbers, fractions, complex numbers, limits. The second is dismantling the intuitions built with the old model: the restriction against subtracting larger from smaller, the requirement that division come out evenly, the impossibility of the square root of negative one. These are not the same task, and doing them at the same time is harder than either task alone.

Students who succeed at these transitions are students who can hold an old model loosely, not building too much on its specific restrictions. They treat the rules as provisional. When the rule changes, they update the rule and continue. This is an adaptive cognitive strategy, but it is not the strategy the curriculum invites. The curriculum presents its rules as facts. Students who believe facts are stable and that mathematics is a domain of permanent truths are not making an error. They are being accurate about mathematics in general while being misled about the specific model they have been given.

The students who struggle most at discontinuities are often the most careful thinkers. They built the rule against subtracting larger from smaller into their understanding because they were told it was true and they take truths seriously. When the rule is later contradicted, the problem is not just that they must learn a new rule. The problem is that their trust in the model was violated. If this rule was provisional, every rule might be provisional. Mathematics, which should be the domain of certainty, has become unreliable. At that point, many students stop building on mathematical intuition because they have learned that the intuition will eventually be dismantled.

The Factorial Algebraic System Has None of These Discontinuities

Every one of the seven discontinuities arises from the conventional model’s choice of starting primitives: integers first, then extensions to cover cases the integers cannot handle. Each extension requires modifying or abandoning a rule that the integer model established. The discontinuity is not a pedagogical failure. It is a mathematical consequence of starting from the wrong foundation.

The factorial algebraic system starts from the right foundation, and none of these discontinuities occur within it.

Subtraction without restriction works immediately. The orientation relationship state machine handles subtraction of a larger value from a smaller one from the first moment subtraction is introduced. There is no stage at which the rule is “subtraction requires the first number to be larger.” The orientation relationship simply exists, and when subtracting a larger from a smaller, the orientation reverses. A student who learns subtraction through the algebraic system learns it correctly and completely in one pass.

Fractions work from the beginning as scope-proportion relationships. There is no stage at which division is restricted to even division. The relationship machine that handles twenty divided by four also handles twenty divided by three. Scope expansion provides the precision that the restricted integer division lacked. A student who learns division through the algebraic system does not encounter a barrier that is later removed.

Multiplication is dimensional expansion, not repeated addition. This definition works for integers, for irrationals, and for matrices because all of these are cases of combining the dimensional structures of two state machines into a higher-dimensional configuration. The definition does not change as the domain expands. The same relationship machine handles all cases. No replacement of the multiplication model is ever required.

Variables are state machines from the beginning. A variable is not an unknown value to be found. It is a state machine that may be in any valid state and can be constrained by relationship machines. This understanding of a variable is correct for simple equation-solving, for functions, for parameterized curves, and for any other use the curriculum introduces. A student who learns variables as state machines will find functions to be exactly what they expect: relationship machines connecting the state of one variable to the state of another.

The square root of negative one is handled by the second orthogonal dimension of the values state machine. This is introduced in Chapter 13 as a natural extension of the same dimensional structure that generates all numbers. There is no stage at which complex numbers are impossible. There is only the question of whether the system has a second dimension, and the answer is always yes. A student who learns the values state machine as two-dimensional from the beginning will not encounter a prohibition that must later be lifted.

Derivatives do not require limits or infinitesimals. The derivative is the boundary proximity measure: the rate at which the output state changes per unit of input state change as the input approaches a scope boundary. This definition is exact, not approximate. It does not rely on infinitesimals, and it does not require the slope intuition to be replaced. A student who learns derivatives as boundary proximity measures learns the correct concept immediately and will find real analysis to be a confirmation of what they understood, not a revision of it.

Calculus requires no infinitesimals and no limits. Integration is finite state accumulation at every scope. The fundamental theorem is an arithmetic observation about how accumulation and boundary proximity relate. These are exact statements, not approximations that must be formalized later. A student who learns calculus through the algebraic system will find real analysis’s rigorous definitions to be formal statements of what they already know, not corrections to an earlier hand-wave.

Intuition That Compounds Rather Than Collapses

The most important consequence of a foundation without discontinuities is that intuition compounds rather than collapses.

In the conventional model, mathematical intuition is repeatedly reset. A student builds careful intuitions at each level, and those intuitions are then partially dismantled at the next level. The student learns not to build too deeply on any particular mathematical concept, because the concept may be revised. This learned shallowness is often described as mathematical maturity: the experienced student holds mathematical rules lightly and accepts extensions and modifications readily. But mathematical maturity, defined this way, is a coping strategy for a broken model. It is not what mathematical thinking should be.

In the factorial algebraic system, every concept introduced at an early level is the correct concept. The orientation relationship that handles the sign of a number in third-grade arithmetic is the same orientation relationship that handles complex conjugates in university mathematics. The scope-proportion relationship that handles fractions in fourth grade handles rational functions in precalculus and, at a deeper structural level, the p-adic numbers in advanced number theory. The dimensional expansion that handles multiplication of integers handles multiplication of matrices. The boundary proximity measure that handles the derivative of a simple function handles the derivative of any function in any valid region of state space.

A student who builds careful intuitions about the algebraic system at an early age does not need to revise those intuitions as the mathematics advances. The intuitions grow. Each new level of mathematics is a deeper application of the same structure. The kindergartener’s odometer and the doctoral student’s research are the same machine operating at different scope depths. The student who understood the odometer deeply has a head start at every subsequent level, because the structure is always the same structure.

This is not a small difference. A curriculum built on the factorial algebraic system would produce students who are permanently accumulating mathematical understanding, rather than periodically having it reset. The students who currently succeed despite the discontinuities are those who tolerate disruption well. A curriculum without discontinuities would allow students who think carefully and build deep intuitions to succeed because of those qualities, not despite them.

A Note on What Would Be Required

Rebuilding a mathematics curriculum on the factorial algebraic system is not a small project. The curriculum exists as it does for reasons that include teacher training, standardized testing, textbook production, and a century of accumulated pedagogical convention. These are real constraints. They do not change the analysis, but they do mean that the argument in this chapter is a long-term claim about what is possible rather than a short-term prescription for what to do next.

What is achievable sooner is introducing the factorial algebraic system as a supplementary framework for students who encounter the discontinuities and feel, correctly, that something is wrong with the conventional model. A student who has just been told that the square root of negative one now exists, after being told it was impossible, deserves a better explanation than “mathematics is sometimes surprising.” The algebraic system provides one. The second orthogonal dimension was always there. The conventional model simply did not show it.

The curriculum problem is real and solvable. Its solution runs through the same structure that this book has been building since Chapter 1.

Chapter 25The Other Side of Math

10 min read

When a photograph is taken of a sculpture, the photograph is not wrong. It shows exactly what the sculpture looks like from one angle, in one light, at one moment. Every measurement taken from the photograph is accurate. Every proportion is correct for the visible face. A student who studies the photograph can learn a great deal about the sculpture. But the photograph is not the sculpture. It has two dimensions where the sculpture has three. It has no back, no underside, no interior. All of that structure exists; the photograph simply cannot show it. Working from the photograph alone, a student would eventually encounter confusions that feel like properties of the sculpture but are actually artifacts of the projection.

This is the situation with conventional mathematics. The number line is a photograph of the algebraic system. It is accurate as far as it goes. Every calculation performed on the number line produces a correct answer. Every procedure the curriculum teaches produces the right result. The projection is not wrong. But it is a projection, and the confusions that students encounter are not properties of mathematics. They are artifacts of the projection.

What the Projection Discards

When the algebraic system is projected onto the number line, several things are lost.

The first is dimensional structure. The factorial odometer generates states across multiple independent dimensions. A number in the algebraic system occupies a position in a multi-dimensional state space, and its position carries information about its relationships to every nearby number. When that number is projected onto the number line, it becomes a single point. Its dimensional address collapses to a scalar. The information about which dimension each digit occupies, and what that means for divisibility and scope, is no longer visible. What remains is the number’s position on the line, which is enough for arithmetic but not enough to see the structure.

The second is residue information. Every number generated by the factorial odometer carries its divisibility relationships in its digit configuration. The structure of those digits tells, immediately and without calculation, which numbers divide it, which do not, and what remains when they do not divide evenly. Projecting onto the number line removes the digit structure and retains only the resulting scalar. Divisibility must then be recalculated from the scalar, which is why divisibility tests exist: they are reconstruction attempts, working backward from the projection to recover structure the projection discarded.

The third is the distinction between inferred and established states. In the algebraic system, a variable that has never received an event is in the inferred zero state, which is structurally different from a variable that received an event whose result was zero. The projection onto the number line collapses both to zero. The number line cannot distinguish between “no event occurred” and “an event occurred whose result is zero.” Additional tracking mechanisms must be added to recover this distinction when it matters.

The fourth is the nature of operations. In the algebraic system, addition is state alignment, subtraction is orientation reversal, multiplication is dimensional expansion, and division is residue reading. Each operation has a structural description that explains why it works and what it means. When projected onto the number line, these operations become procedures: rules for transforming one set of symbols into another. The procedures produce correct answers, but they no longer explain themselves. The student who asks why multiplication distributes over addition receives a proof, not an explanation, because the number-line projection does not carry the structural reason. The reason is visible in the algebraic system’s dimensional structure, but the projection has discarded it.

The fifth is the nature of boundaries. In the algebraic system, scope boundaries are structural events: places where the current structure reaches its limit and expansion is required. Calculus, as Chapters 18 through 21 showed, is entirely about the behavior of the system near these boundaries. When projected onto the number line, boundaries become paradoxical values: infinities, undefined expressions, limits that are approached but never reached. The calculus that follows from this projection is accurate in its results but forced to work around its own representation through limits, epsilon-delta arguments, and careful avoidance of the boundary itself. None of these workarounds are needed in the algebraic system.

What the Projection Preserves

Losing dimensional structure, residue information, state provenance, operational meaning, and boundary accessibility is a significant loss. But the projection has served well for a very long time, and it deserves credit for what it preserves.

The number line preserves scalar arithmetic. Any calculation that produces a scalar answer — add these, subtract those, multiply by this, find the square root of that — is correctly handled by the number line model. The procedures are reliable. The answers are right. For the majority of mathematical work done over centuries, scalar arithmetic was sufficient, and the number line was an adequate representation.

The number line also preserves order. Numbers on the line have a clear relationship to one another: each is greater than all numbers to its left and less than all numbers to its right. This ordering supports comparison, sorting, and ranking, which are important operations in both pure mathematics and practical application. The algebraic system has order too, expressed in terms of scope depth and state advancement. But the number line makes order visually immediate in a way that is genuinely useful.

The number line preserves continuity intuition. The line extends infinitely in both directions with no gaps, and this conveys something true about the density of real numbers. Every pair of distinct points has a third point between them. This property, real and important, is accessible to intuition through the line metaphor in a way that might take longer to appreciate through the algebraic system’s state generator.

The conventional account of real numbers requires a construction — Dedekind cuts or an equivalent — to fill the gaps that irrational values leave in the rational number line. This construction is mathematically careful and historically important. But it exists because the rational number line genuinely has gaps, and those gaps need filling. In the algebraic system, the same values that require Dedekind cuts on the number line are simply variables with defining relationships. The square root of two is the state that satisfies the constraint that its square equals two. Pi is the state defined by its geometric relationship to a circle. Each of these is a variable in the algebraic system, expanded to whatever scope the problem requires. There are no gaps to fill, because the values are not points on a pre-existing line. They are configurations reachable through scope expansion of their defining relationships. Completeness is a consequence of how the system represents values, not a property that requires a separate construction to achieve.

The projection is lossy but not arbitrary. The structure that survives is real structure. The structure that is lost is the structure the curriculum never shows.

The Other Side

The title of this chapter refers to what is on the other side of the projection: the full algebraic system that the number line is projecting from.

That system has been built across this book. It begins with the factorial odometer generating distinguishable states, one at a time, each preserving all prior structure. It assigns names to those states and calls them numbers. It defines variables as state machines occupying positions in that structure. It constructs arithmetic operations as relationship state machines that constrain how variables’ states may change in relation to one another. It handles constants as variables with infinite-series or geometric definitions, expanded to whatever scope the problem requires. It frames calculus as boundary behavior: derivatives as proximity to scope boundaries, integrals as accumulated occupancy across bounded regions. It extends to geometry by treating shapes as relationship constraints on multi-dimensional configurations, and distance as a derived scope measurement rather than a foundation.

At every step, the system was not introducing new primitives. It was showing that the primitives the conventional model required are derived quantities in a simpler system. Numbers are not primitive. Operations are not primitive. Distance is not primitive. Infinitesimals are not primitive. The odometer’s state generator is the only primitive required. Everything else is relationship machines operating on states.

The reader who has followed this argument is now in possession of both the projection and the system it projects from. The number-line model is still available and still correct for what it covers. The algebraic system is now also available for the cases where the projection’s limitations cause confusion or force workarounds. Having both is not contradiction. It is clarity: understanding what the simpler model is a projection of, and therefore understanding why the simpler model’s workarounds take the form they do.

The Mathematics That Was Always There

The algebraic system is not a new mathematics. Nothing in this book is a new discovery. The factorial odometer is a way of describing number generation that mathematicians have understood for a long time. Residue arithmetic is classical number theory. Entity-state machines have been used in computer science for decades. Relationship propagation is a well-established concept in constraint programming. The idea that derivatives measure boundary proximity and integrals measure accumulated occupancy is expressed formally in the standard mathematics of real analysis, even if that mathematics uses different language.

What is new in this book is the assembly: the decision to start from the right primitive and build every subsequent concept from it without exception. Most mathematics education starts from the number-line model and then adds corrections as the curriculum advances. This book starts from the state generator and derives the number-line model as a projection. That reversal changes what needs to be explained and what counts as an obvious consequence.

The result is that every concept the conventional curriculum introduces as a new and potentially difficult extension turns out to be a natural consequence of the structure already in place. Negative numbers follow from orientation relationships. Fractions follow from scope-proportion relationships. Complex numbers follow from the second orthogonal dimension. Calculus follows from boundary behavior. None of these required new foundations. They were all already present in the state generator and the relationship machines.

A reader who first encountered mathematics through the conventional model and now understands the algebraic system is not switching to a different mathematics. They are seeing the mathematics they were always doing from a different vantage point. Every calculation they have ever performed on the number line was a projection of an operation that the algebraic system describes structurally. The algebraic system was there all along. The conventional model was a useful photograph of it.

An Invitation

The factorial odometer began with a single position, a single digit, a single distinguishable state. It advanced to the second state, then the third, carrying the full structure of what it had already generated at each step. The scope expanded when it had to, not before. Each new dimension was required, not assumed. Every number that emerged carried, in its digit configuration, everything the system knew about its relationships to every other number.

That is how this book has proceeded as well. Each concept arrived when it was needed. Each relationship machine was introduced by showing what problem it resolved. Each extension was shown to be present in the existing structure rather than added as a new case. The argument carried its full structure at every step.

The reader who counted on the odometer in Chapter 2 and followed the structure through to the geometry of Chapter 23 has not learned a theory. They have built a machine. The machine generates numbers, performs operations, handles calculus, and produces geometry. It handles every level of the curriculum from counting to graduate mathematics using the same moving parts at different scope depths.

The other side of math is not a complicated place. It is, if anything, simpler than the conventional model. It has fewer primitives, fewer special cases, fewer workarounds. Its apparent complexity comes entirely from the scope depth at which questions are asked, not from the structure itself. The structure is the odometer, advancing one state at a time, carrying everything it knows, expanding its scope only when required.

That structure was always there. This book was a way of seeing it.

Appendix A: The ESM Specification for a Factorial Algebraic System

19 min read

This appendix provides a formal specification of the Entity-State Machine structure underlying the factorial algebraic system described in this book. The chapters build this structure incrementally through examples and argument. This appendix collects the definitions in a single organized reference for technical readers who want precise definitions, and it notes explicitly, at each place one exists, where a further contract (such as the native multiplication rule in A.5, RelSM evaluation ordering in A.7, or ConSM conflict resolution in A.6) remains to be specified before an implementation could be built from this appendix alone.

The specification uses the Entity-State Machine (ESM) model, in which a system is described as an entity containing named state machines. Each state machine has a defined set of valid states and a defined set of valid transitions between states. Events drive transitions. Relationship machines are state machines whose states are derived from the states of other machines. The representation carries what the system knows; inferred states are not stored.

A.1 The Entity

A factorial algebraic system is an entity. An entity is a named thing with persistent identity. It contains state machines, and the collection of current states across all its state machines constitutes the entity’s current configuration.

Definition (Entity): An entity E is a tuple (Name, SM) where Name is a unique identifier and SM is a set of state machines. The current configuration of E is the set of current states across all members of SM.

A factorial algebraic system is an entity whose state machines are classified into four types: the Variables State Machine, the Values State Machines, the Relationship State Machines, and the Constraint State Machines.

A.2 The Variables State Machine

The Variables State Machine (VSM) maintains the set of named variables defined in the system. A variable is registered in the VSM when it is introduced into the system. Removing a variable removes it from the VSM and dissolves all Values and Relationship State Machines associated with it.

Definition (Variables State Machine): The VSM is a state machine whose states are sets of variable names. The initial state is the empty set. The valid transitions are:

  • AddVariable(v): transitions from state S to state S ∪ {v}, provided v is not already in S.
  • RemoveVariable(v): transitions from state S to state S  {v}, provided v is in S.

The VSM has no inferred state. If no variables have been added, the VSM is in the empty-set state, which is explicit.

A.3 Values State Machines

For each variable v registered in the VSM, the system contains a Values State Machine (ValSM) that carries the current value of v. The state space of the ValSM is structured by the factorial basis.

Definition (Factorial Basis State Space): The factorial basis state space of integer scope depth d and fractional scope depth f is the set of all digit configurations (c_1, c_2, …, c_d ; c_{-1}, c_{-2}, …, c_{-f}) where each integer digit c_i, for i from 1 to d, satisfies 0 ≤ c_i ≤ i, and each fractional digit c_{-j}, for j from 1 to f, satisfies 0 ≤ c_{-j} ≤ j. Position i has weight i! for integer positions and 1/(j+1)! for fractional position −j. The scalar value corresponding to a configuration is Σ c_i × i! for i from 1 to d, plus Σ c_{-j} / (j+1)! for j from 1 to f. Integer scope depth governs the largest representable magnitude; fractional scope depth governs the finest representable step. The two are independent: increasing d does not add fractional precision, and increasing f does not add integer range.

Definition (Values State Machine): The ValSM for variable v is a state machine with:

  • State space: the factorial basis state space at the current integer and fractional scope depths, extended with an orientation bit (positive or negative) and, optionally, a second orthogonal axis for complex-valued variables.
  • Initial state: the inferred zero state, which is not stored. If no event has moved the ValSM, its state is inferred to be zero on the primary axis with positive orientation, at integer and fractional scope depth zero.
  • Valid transitions: any transition to a different valid state within the current scope, a scope expansion transition that increases d by one (integer) or f by one (fractional) and maps the current configuration into the larger state space, or a normalization transition that redistributes digit values among positions already within the current scope depth without changing d or f.

Definition (Inferred State): A ValSM is inferred if no event has ever driven a transition in it. An inferred ValSM does not require storage. Its value is defined to be zero. An inferred ValSM becomes realized the moment any event drives a transition in it, and it remains realized afterward even if a later transition returns its scalar value to zero; a realized ValSM reading zero and an inferred ValSM are structurally distinct states, though both report the same scalar value.

Definition (Scope Expansion vs. Normalization): A carry or borrow event at position i that would require a digit value outside position i’s valid range redistributes the excess or deficit to position i+1. If position i+1 was previously inferred (never realized) and the event realizes it for the first time, this is a scope expansion event, and the integer or fractional scope depth increases by one. If position i+1 was already realized before the event, the redistribution is a normalization event: the digit values at already-realized positions change, but the scope depth does not. Scope expansion is a genuine, representation-level event, distinct from normalization, which is ordinary digit adjustment within already-allocated capacity.

Definition (Orientation): The orientation bit of a ValSM is either positive or negative. The initial orientation is positive. An orientation relationship machine may set the orientation to negative, which represents a value in the opposite direction from zero without changing the digit configuration. Subtraction is addition with the orientation of the subtracted operand reversed before alignment.

Definition (Second Axis): A ValSM may carry a second orthogonal factorial basis state space, independent of the primary axis, with its own digit configuration, orientation, and scope depth. No carry crosses between the two axes. A state on the second axis is designated by a distinct axis identifier. The combination of primary-axis state and second-axis state constitutes the full state of the ValSM for a complex-valued variable.

A.4 Relationship State Machines

A Relationship State Machine (RelSM) defines a constraint between two or more variables’ ValSMs. The RelSM does not hold an independent value. Its state is the current set of input ValSM states together with the constraint expression that governs the output ValSM’s required state.

Definition (Relationship State Machine): A RelSM is a state machine with:

  • Input references: one or more named variables whose ValSMs drive transitions in the RelSM.
  • Output reference: one named variable whose ValSM is governed by the RelSM.
  • Constraint expression: a mathematical relationship that specifies the required output state as a function of the input states.
  • Evaluation rule: whenever any input ValSM transitions, the RelSM evaluates the constraint expression against the new input states and, if the required output state differs from the current output state, drives a transition in the output ValSM to the required state.

Definition (Consistency): The system is consistent when every RelSM’s constraint expression is satisfied by the current states of its input and output ValSMs. The system maintains consistency continuously: every RelSM evaluation either confirms consistency or drives the output ValSM to restore it.

Definition (No-Change Principle): A transition that produces no state change is indistinguishable from no transition. If a RelSM evaluates its constraint expression and determines that the required output state equals the current output state, no transition occurs in the output ValSM. This is not an error; it is the system confirming that the current state already satisfies the constraint. The principle is a statement about the output ValSM’s current state versus its required state; it does not depend on which operation produced the requirement.

The no-change principle governs the four identity operations, with the scope of each guarantee stated precisely:

  • Adding zero: the zero operand is inferred (no realized ValSM exists), so the input being added contributes nothing, and the non-zero input’s own ValSM never transitions. Whether the output ValSM (if distinct from the non-zero input) transitions depends on whether it already held that input’s configuration; if it did not, the RelSM still drives it to match, which is a transition in the output, not in the untouched input.
  • Subtracting zero: the same guarantee as adding zero, with orientation reversal applied to an inferred zero, which produces no orientation change. The input being subtracted from never transitions.
  • Dividing by one: the required output state equals the dividend’s configuration. If the output ValSM already holds that configuration, no transition occurs. If it holds a different configuration — left over from a previous evaluation with a different divisor — the RelSM drives it to match, which is a transition in the output.
  • Multiplying by one: the required output state equals the non-identity factor’s configuration. The same conditional applies: no transition if the output already matches, a transition if it does not.

Multiplying by zero is handled differently: the required output state is always the inferred zero state regardless of the other factor’s configuration. If the output ValSM already holds the inferred zero state, no transition occurs, by the same general principle above. If the output ValSM holds any other configuration, multiplying by zero drives a transition to the inferred zero state, and this transition is irreversible: no subsequent RelSM evaluation can recover the discarded configuration from the output ValSM alone, because the inferred zero state carries no record of what preceded it.

A.5 Arithmetic Relationship Machines

The four arithmetic operations correspond to specific RelSM configurations.

Addition RelSM: Takes two input ValSMs (v_1 and v_2) and one output ValSM (v_out). The constraint is: v_out = state_alignment(v_1, v_2), where state alignment combines the factorial-basis digit configurations of v_1 and v_2 with carry propagation across shared digit positions. A carry that redistributes digits among positions already realized in v_out is a normalization transition; a carry that realizes a previously inferred position for the first time is a scope expansion transition. Both are driven by the same carry rule; they differ only in whether the position receiving the carry was already realized.

Subtraction RelSM: Equivalent to the Addition RelSM with the orientation of v_2 reversed before alignment. Borrow events follow the same normalization-versus-contraction distinction as carry events, applied in reverse.

Multiplication RelSM: Takes two input ValSMs (v_1 and v_2) and one output ValSM (v_out). The constraint is: v_out = dimensional_expansion(v_1, v_2), where dimensional expansion produces a configuration whose occupied scope depth is bounded above by the sum of the occupied scope depths of v_1 and v_2. This bound is a safe allocation ceiling, not a guarantee of equality: for example, v_1 at occupied depth 2 (three) and v_2 at occupied depth 2 (four) produce a product at occupied depth 3 (twelve), not depth 4. The native digit-by-digit multiplication and normalization rule that computes dimensional_expansion directly in factorial basis, without bridging through scalar values, is not yet specified in this appendix; Appendix B’s worked example uses a scalar bridge as a verification method pending that specification.

Division RelSM: Takes two input ValSMs (v_dividend and v_divisor) and one output ValSM (v_quotient), with an optional remainder ValSM. The constraint reads the residue of v_dividend relative to v_divisor from the factorial-basis digit positions of v_dividend when v_divisor’s value divides a small factorial, using the position-combination rules given in Appendix B section B.7; for divisors without such a rule, the residue is read by ordinary division. If v_dividend is exactly divisible by v_divisor within the current scope, the quotient is exact. If not, the quotient is expressed using the fractional positions defined in A.3, extended to whatever fractional scope depth is needed to express the result exactly or to the precision the current fractional scope allows.

A.6 Constraint State Machines

A Constraint State Machine (ConSM) binds multiple RelSMs into a coherent system constraint. A ConSM specifies which configurations across all ValSMs in the entity constitute valid states of the system as a whole.

Definition (Constraint State Machine): A ConSM is a state machine with:

  • Scope reference: the set of ValSMs and RelSMs it governs.
  • Validity expression: a predicate over the current states of all referenced ValSMs that evaluates to valid or invalid.
  • Response rule: when the validity expression evaluates to invalid, the ConSM drives events to the relevant RelSMs to restore a valid configuration, or signals that no valid configuration is reachable at the current scope.

ConSMs are used to enforce multi-variable constraints beyond binary relationships, such as the constraint that three variables satisfy a trigonometric identity, or that all variables in a geometric system satisfy consistent curvature constraints.

This specification does not yet define a general resolution procedure for two ConSMs that impose incompatible requirements on the same ValSM, for a cycle of RelSMs whose required outputs depend on each other circularly, or for a RelSM network with more than one valid configuration satisfying every constraint simultaneously. A deployed system needs one of: a declared evaluation order, a declared conflict-resolution rule, or an explicit signal (see A.7) reporting that the current constraint set does not resolve to a single configuration. Until such a rule is declared, “the system maintains consistency continuously” describes the goal of ConSM evaluation, not a guarantee that every constraint network the specification permits will converge to one answer on its own.

A.7 Event Model

All transitions in the factorial algebraic system are driven by events. An event is a named signal with optional parameters that arrives at the entity and is dispatched to the state machines that define transitions for it.

Definition (Event): An event is a tuple (Name, Parameters) where Name identifies the transition to invoke and Parameters carry any values required by the transition.

The standard events in the factorial algebraic system are:

  • SetValue(v, config, orientation): drives a transition in the ValSM for v to the specified digit configuration and orientation.
  • Align(v_1, v_2, v_out): drives the Addition RelSM for the specified variables.
  • Expand(v): drives a scope expansion event in the ValSM for v.
  • AddVariable(v): drives a transition in the VSM.
  • RemoveVariable(v): drives a transition in the VSM and dissolves all associated machines.

Definition (Event Dispatch Order): When an event arrives, it is dispatched first to the ValSM or VSM transition it directly names. Any RelSM whose input references include the ValSM that just transitioned is then evaluated, in an order this specification does not yet fix when more than one RelSM shares an input; a deployed system must declare a specific order (such as declaration order or a dependency-sorted order) to be deterministic when multiple RelSMs could be affected by a single event. A RelSM evaluation that changes an output ValSM is itself treated as the input to any further RelSM that references that output, so a single incoming event can propagate through a chain of RelSM evaluations before the system settles.

Definition (Failure and Boundary Outcomes): The following conditions do not raise exceptions, because logical cells do not fail by definition; instead, each produces a specific, named outcome that other state machines can observe and react to:

  • SetValue with a digit outside its position’s valid range: rejected; the event is not processed, and the ValSM’s prior state is unchanged. This is a “no match” outcome, consistent with the ESM principle that an event with no matching valid transition simply does not occur.
  • Division where the divisor’s ValSM is the inferred or realized zero state: the Division RelSM produces no valid quotient state; the quotient ValSM is left at its prior state (or inferred, if it had none), and a DivisionUndefined(v_dividend, v_divisor) signal is raised rather than any SetValue transition on the quotient.
  • A relationship requiring more fractional or integer scope than the system is configured to allocate: an InsufficientScope(v, requested_depth) signal is raised, and the affected ValSM remains at its last valid state until an Expand event provides the needed depth.
  • A ConSM validity expression that cannot be satisfied by any reachable configuration of its referenced ValSMs: an Unsatisfiable(ConSM_id) signal is raised, consistent with A.6’s note that this specification does not yet define automatic resolution for such cases.

These signals are raised events in the sense used elsewhere in this book’s ESM model: they may be handled synchronously by another state machine in the same entity, passed to a parent logical cell asynchronously, or left unhandled, in which case the system remains in its last valid state with the signal available for external inspection.

A.8 Series-Defined Variables

A variable may be defined by an infinite series relationship rather than by a direct SetValue event. This is the mechanism for mathematical constants such as e and π.

Definition (Series RelSM): A Series RelSM is a RelSM whose constraint expression is an infinite series with a bounded-coefficient guarantee: the magnitude of the n-th term is at most some fixed constant divided by n-factorial. (A series without such a bound on its coefficients is not guaranteed to converge merely because its denominators are factorials — the series whose n-th term is n-factorial divided by n-factorial is a standing counterexample, since every term equals one and the sum diverges.) The series defines the variable’s value as the sum of its terms realized so far. Terms whose index corresponds to an integer position (the zeroth and first terms, of weight one each) contribute to the variable’s integer part. Terms of index two and higher, each of weight one divided by n-factorial, correspond one-to-one with fractional position negative (n minus one), as defined in A.3. As the fractional scope expands, additional terms are evaluated and realized at the next fractional position.

For a series whose every term-coefficient, once reduced to the weight of its corresponding position, is a digit within that position’s valid range — as is the case for e’s own series, where each coefficient is exactly one — the series is exact at every fractional scope depth realized so far, with no approximation involved. The variable’s value at fractional scope depth f is the integer part plus the first f fractional terms, represented exactly in the factorial basis. A coefficient outside its position’s valid digit range must first be normalized across positions, the same way an oversized integer digit is normalized by carrying, before this one-to-one correspondence applies.

For a series meeting the bounded-coefficient guarantee but without integer-valued coefficients at each position — such as the series for sine or cosine evaluated at a general input — the representation is exact at the fractional scope realized so far, and the gap to the infinite sum is bounded by the same comparison argument that establishes convergence, even though individual digits are not simply one at each position. Scope expansion provides additional exact digits, not a rounded decimal; the distinction between a finite exact partial sum at the current scope and the infinite value the series defines remains meaningful and should not be collapsed, since the partial sum equals the infinite value only in the limit.

A.9 System Lifecycle

A factorial algebraic system begins in the empty configuration: the VSM in its initial empty-set state and no ValSMs, RelSMs, or ConSMs realized. Reaching the configuration used throughout this book’s running example — an entity already holding named variables x, y, z, and e, with RelSMs already defined for z and e — requires two kinds of events, and the distinction matters for what “has received no events” means:

  • Structural events (AddVariable, and the configuration of a RelSM’s or ConSM’s constraint expression) establish which variables, relationships, and constraints exist. These are what populate the VSM’s name set and attach RelSMs to variables.
  • Value events (SetValue, Align, and the other events in A.7) move a ValSM away from its inferred default.

A system can have received structural events without having received any value events: the VSM holds a populated name set, RelSMs are attached and ready to evaluate, and every ValSM is still inferred at zero, because no value event has yet moved any of them. This is the state this book’s running example starts from in each chapter: the names x, y, z, and e exist, but no values have been set. “No events at all” describes a stricter, earlier state in which even the VSM is empty; “no value events yet” describes the state where variables and relationships are defined but every value is still inferred. Both states require no ValSM storage, but only the first requires no VSM storage either.

Variables are added through AddVariable events, creating ValSMs in their inferred initial states. Relationships are defined through RelSM configurations, which immediately begin evaluating consistency. Events arrive and drive transitions. Scope expands as required. The system maintains consistency continuously through RelSM evaluation, subject to the conflict-resolution and ordering caveats noted in A.6 and A.7.

A system with defined variables and relationships but no value events yet is in its locally inferred state for every ValSM: all ValSMs inferred at zero, no RelSM has yet evaluated a non-default result, and the VSM holds the defined variable names. This state requires storage only for the VSM’s name set and the RelSM and ConSM definitions themselves, not for any ValSM.

A system after receiving value events carries exactly the information those events established, in the digit configurations of its realized ValSMs and the evaluation states of its RelSMs. It carries nothing more.

A.10 Relationship to the Logical Computer

The factorial algebraic system is one application of the Entity-State Machine model. The same model, applied to computing systems, is the logical computer described in From Numbers to Systems. The correspondence is direct:

Factorial Algebraic System Logical Computer
Variable Data element
Values State Machine Data element state machine
Relationship State Machine Business rule
Constraint State Machine Multi-rule constraint
Event Business event
Scope expansion Capacity growth
Inferred zero Uninitialized element
Consistency maintenance Rule enforcement

The mathematical and computational applications of the ESM model share the same specification. The domain differs; the structure does not.

Appendix B: Factorial-Base Conversion Reference

17 min read

This appendix provides practical conversion tables and worked examples for the factorial basis number system described throughout this book. The tables cover all integers from 0 through 120 and include the major factorial boundaries in that range. The worked examples demonstrate addition with carry, subtraction with borrow, and multiplication, each performed directly in factorial basis without converting to decimal as an intermediate step.

B.1 Notation

A factorial basis number is written as a sequence of digits in square brackets, listed from most significant to least significant: [d_k, d_{k-1}, …, d_2, d_1]. The position index runs from 1 at the rightmost digit. The digit at position i must satisfy 0 ≤ d_i ≤ i.

The scalar value of the representation is the sum of each digit multiplied by its positional weight:

n = d_k × k! + d_{k-1} × (k-1)! + … + d_2 × 2! + d_1 × 1!

The first several positional weights are:

Position Weight Maximum digit
1 1 1
2 2 2
3 6 3
4 24 4
5 120 5
6 720 6

The scope depth of a number is the index of its highest non-zero position. A number whose highest non-zero digit is at position k has scope depth k. Zero has no non-zero digits and scope depth zero (inferred state).

B.2 Decimal-to-Factorial Conversion Algorithm

To convert a positive integer n to factorial basis, apply the following steps in order. At each step, the divisor increases by one.

  1. Divide n by 2. Record the remainder as d_1. Set n to the quotient.
  2. Divide n by 3. Record the remainder as d_2. Set n to the quotient.
  3. Divide n by 4. Record the remainder as d_3. Set n to the quotient.
  4. Divide n by 5. Record the remainder as d_4. Set n to the quotient.
  5. Continue, incrementing the divisor by one at each step, until n equals zero.

The sequence of remainders, read from last to first (most significant to least significant), is the factorial basis representation.

Example: Convert 83 to factorial basis.

  • 83 ÷ 2 = 41 remainder 1. Record d_1 = 1.
  • 41 ÷ 3 = 13 remainder 2. Record d_2 = 2.
  • 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1. Record d_3 = 1.
  • 3 ÷ 5 = 0 remainder 3. Record d_4 = 3.

Result (most significant first): [3, 1, 2, 1]. Verify: 3×24 + 1×6 + 2×2 + 1×1 = 72 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 83. Correct.

B.3 Factorial-to-Decimal Conversion

Multiply each digit by its positional weight and sum. The positional weights are the factorials of the position indices.

Example: Convert [2, 3, 0, 1] to decimal.

Position 4: 2 × 24 = 48
Position 3: 3 × 6 = 18
Position 2: 0 × 2 = 0
Position 1: 1 × 1 = 1

Sum: 48 + 18 + 0 + 1 = 67.

B.4 Conversion Table: 0 through 23

Within this range, three positions suffice. The representation is [d_3, d_2, d_1].

Decimal Factorial Decimal Factorial
0 [0, 0, 0] 12 [2, 0, 0]
1 [0, 0, 1] 13 [2, 0, 1]
2 [0, 1, 0] 14 [2, 1, 0]
3 [0, 1, 1] 15 [2, 1, 1]
4 [0, 2, 0] 16 [2, 2, 0]
5 [0, 2, 1] 17 [2, 2, 1]
6 [1, 0, 0] 18 [3, 0, 0]
7 [1, 0, 1] 19 [3, 0, 1]
8 [1, 1, 0] 20 [3, 1, 0]
9 [1, 1, 1] 21 [3, 1, 1]
10 [1, 2, 0] 22 [3, 2, 0]
11 [1, 2, 1] 23 [3, 2, 1]

Structural observations: The factorial boundaries in this range are 1 = 1!, 2 = 2!, 6 = 3!, and 24 = 4! (just above the table). At each factorial boundary n!, exactly one position carries a non-zero digit and all lower positions are zero. The number 6 = [1, 0, 0] has d_3 = 1 and d_2 = d_1 = 0. The number 23 = [3, 2, 1] has every position at its maximum, confirming that 24 = 4! is the next scope boundary.
